tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Tools and Setup. This page is like packing your bag before school. It tells you what you need for Unit 1, "Computers Are Everywhere". We get our things ready first, so that later we can just play and learn with no stopping. By the end, you will have everything you need on your table. Here is what I expect from you: take your time, look at each thing on the page, and get a grown-up if you need help. There are three steps. Step 1. Read Tools and Setup. Look at the page and read the list slowly. If a word is hard, ask your grown-up to read it with you. Our main tool this unit is ScratchJr on a tablet. You will also want paper, a pencil, and some colours. A good job here means you can tell me, out loud, one thing you need for this unit. Step 2. Check each tool or setting on the list. Go one at a time, not all at once. Find the paper, the pencil and the colours, and put them on your table. Then ask your grown-up to help you open the ScratchJr app on the tablet. Tap the house, then tap the plus sign to start a new project. If ScratchJr is not there, that is okay — your grown-up can help you get it, or you can do this unit with just paper and pencil. A good job here means every thing on the list is either ready on your table, or you know a grown-up is helping you get it. Step 3. Press "My tools are ready". When your things are on the table, scroll to the bottom of the page and press the button that says "My tools are ready". Press it only after you really are ready — that button is you telling the page, "I am set!" I cannot press it for you, and I cannot tick it off. It has to be you. How will you know the page is finished? When you have read the list, checked every thing on it, and pressed "My tools are ready". Then this page is done, and we can start finding computers all around us! Great work getting set up. Come back and tell me when your tools are ready, and we will begin. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. On this page you will learn five big ideas about computers. You will find out that computers are everywhere, that they come in different sizes, what we use them for, what a program is, and how we put things into a computer. By the end, you will be able to point at a computer and say its name. You need your eyes, your ears, your voice, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Here is our plan. There are four things to do. 1. Read the five concepts, one at a time. On the page you will see five short boxes. Each box has an idea and an example. Read the first one slowly. Then press Listen and let the words be read to you. Listen all the way to the end before you move on. I expect you to do this for all five boxes, one after the other, not in a rush. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Say each example out loud, then make it your own. After you read a box, say the example out loud in a big clear voice. Then look around your room and find your own example. For example, if the box talks about a tablet, point at a real tablet or phone near you and say "this is a computer." I expect one out-loud example from you for each box. This is how the words stick in your head. 3. Press the button when you have read them all. When all five boxes are read and listened to, look at the bottom of the page. There is a button that says I studied the concepts. Press it. Only press it when you really have read every box — that button is your promise that you did the work. I expect you to be honest with yourself here, and I know you will be. 4. Do the slides under the page. Below the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same five ideas, so this is your practice. On the first slide, press Start. On each slide, use the same buttons you see there, and read or listen carefully. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next one. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you how far you have come. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to go through every slide, not skip ahead. You will know the page is finished when two things are true: you pressed I studied the concepts, and you pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and start with step 1. Read the first box, press Listen, and then come back and tell me one thing you learned. I will be right here waiting. 😊

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our Computing Words. These are the special words for Unit 1. Words like computer, laptop, tablet and keyboard. When you know these words, you can talk about computers like a real computer person. That is why we do this page. Here is what I expect from you: try every word, say it out loud, and write your own sentence. Your sentences do not have to be perfect. Trying is the important part. Get a grown-up nearby if you like. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. Do this for each word, one at a time. I expect you to look and listen, not rush. Step 2. Now say the word out loud. Say it with me, slowly. Then say the meaning in your own words. Not the same words as the page — your words. For laptop you might say, "a computer you can carry." That is a lovely answer. Step 3. Now type a sentence with the word. Then press Check sentence. A good sentence uses the word and makes sense, like "My mum has a laptop." Read what the checker says to you. If it asks you to fix something, fix it and press Check sentence again. Then do steps 1, 2 and 3 for the next word, until every word is done. Step 4. When you have done every single word, press the button that says I explored the computing words at the bottom of the page. Only press it when all the words are finished. That button tells the page you are done. Step 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same words. Press Start on the first slide. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know. Press Listen to hear the word. Say it out loud. Say the meaning your way. Type your sentence and press Check sentence. Step 7. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. Step 8. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the computing words, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now start with Step 1. Tell me which word you are on, and I will help you. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 🙂

This page is called Explore the Concept. On it you will find six little discoveries about computers. Each one shows you a picture or a model, asks you a question, and lets you type your own idea. We do this so you learn by noticing things yourself — not just by being told. By the end you will be able to name computers, say what we use them for, and point to input devices. What you need: your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. What I expect from you: look carefully first, then answer in your own words. Even a short answer is fine, as long as it is your real idea. Here are all the steps. Step 1. At the top of the page you will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. That is six discoveries. Press tab 1 first. A situation opens with a picture or a model. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Look at the picture for a moment before you do anything else. I expect you to look, not rush. Step 2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it twice. Think quietly first — what do you notice? Then type your idea in the box. Write in words, like "a tablet is a computer" or "the keyboard types letters". A full little sentence is best. Step 3. Now press Check my idea. If it says Exactly!, well done — tab 1 gets a tick. If it says Look again, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read the hint, then change your answer a little and try once more. Step 4. Now press tab 2 and do the same three things: look, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tab 3, tab 4, tab 5 and tab 6. One tab at a time, please. Do not skip ahead. Step 5. The page is finished when every one of the six tabs has a tick. Count the ticks with your finger: one, two, three, four, five, six. If one tab has no tick, go back to it and try again. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same six discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 8. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the whole page is finished when all six tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. Take your time — there's no rush.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 1. It is called "Computers Are Everywhere". This page is the Unit Overview. That means a little map of what we will learn. We do it so you know what is coming, like looking at a picture before a story. By the end of this page, you will be able to say what you will learn in this unit. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here are the 3 steps. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page about computers. If you see a small speaker picture, press Listen. Then the page reads to you. Listen all the way to the end. You can press Listen again if you want. I expect you to look at the screen and listen carefully, not rush. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, or type it to me here. It does not need to be perfect. A good answer is one or two things, like "I will learn about computers" or "I will learn about big and small computers". Your own words are best — that is how I know it is in your head. Tell me, and I will say what you did well. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have listened and told me your idea, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to the next part, where we really begin. I expect you to press it yourself. You will know this page is finished when you have listened, said your idea, and pressed Continue. Then we are ready for The Lesson! Let's start with something small. Press Listen now, and tell me when you are done. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a recipe. This page has 5 methods, one for each big idea in our unit: computers are everywhere, kinds of computers, what we use computers for, programs and apps, and input devices. We do this so you learn to work in small steps, just like a computer does. What I expect from you: press the buttons yourself, read or say every step out loud, and take your time. You need only your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step out loud. Then press the button that says "Show me the next step". A new step will appear. Say that one out loud too. Good work looks like this: you say every step, not just look at it. 2. Keep pressing "Show me the next step" again and again. Say each new step out loud as it comes. Stop when you see the words "Method complete". That means you finished that method. Well done! 3. Now do the same thing for every method on the page. There are 5. Start each new one at its first step, press "Show me the next step" until it says "Method complete". Take your time — there's no rush. When all 5 say "Method complete", the top part of the page is done. 4. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. They show the same methods, one method on each slide. On the first slide, press "Start". Then use the same buttons on the slide to move through the steps, saying each one out loud. 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. Keep going: press "Start", step through, then the arrow. 6. On the last slide, step through all of it, then press the finish button. That is the very end of the page. You will know the page is finished when all 5 methods say "Method complete" and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Go and do step 1, then tell me what your first method's first step said. I'll be right here. 😊

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's look at this page together. This page is called Code Examples. It shows you examples you can look at, one at a time. In Unit 1 our examples are about computers all around us — like a phone, a tablet, a laptop and a desktop. We are doing this so you can see the ideas, say them in your own words, and get ready to make something yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you: look carefully, say each line out loud, and tell me what you think it means. Guessing is good! Mistakes are how we learn. There are four things to do on this page. Step 1. Read each example. Look at the first example on the screen. Read it slowly, one line at a time. After each line, say out loud, "I think this means..." A good try sounds like this: "This one is flat and you touch it — I think it means a tablet." If a word is hard, ask me and I will help. Step 2. Press Copy the code. This button copies the example so you can try it yourself. If you have a tablet with ScratchJr, you can open it and try. If you do not have one, that is fine — just say the example out loud instead. Then press the button under the example to mark it done. Only press it after you have really read it. Step 3. Do the slides at the bottom. Under the examples there is a little deck of cards. Each card has one example. Press Start. Read the code on the card. Then mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next card. Keep going until the cards run out. I expect you to read every card, not skip any. Step 4. Press Go to Build It. Only press this when you have read every single example. This button takes you to the next part, where you get to make something yourself. You will know the page is finished when every example has been marked done, all the slides have been read, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Now let's start Step 1. Look at the first example on your screen and tell me what you see. What do you notice? 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of our big ideas. Looking at them helps the ideas stick in your head. You need your eyes, your finger or mouse, and your talking voice. Let's start! 1. Look at the first model: Computers are everywhere. Look at it slowly. If it moves, drag it with your finger or mouse to turn it around. Press any buttons on it to see it change. I expect you to look at every side, not just one. 2. Now say out loud what you see. Point at the picture and say, "That is a computer." Good thinking! I expect one sentence out loud, even a short one. 3. Go to the second model: Different kinds of computers. Drag it to turn it. Try to spot the desktop, the laptop, the tablet and the smartphone. I expect you to name at least two of them out loud. 4. Go to the third model: What do we use computers for. Turn it and press its buttons. Think about fun, making things, talking, and finding out things. I expect you to say one thing YOU like to do on a computer. 5. Go to the fourth model: Programs and apps. Turn it and look at the little app pictures. Remember, an app is a program. I expect you to say what one app does, like "this one draws."

6. Go to the fifth model: Input devices. Turn it and find the mouse, the keyboard, the microphone and the camera. I expect you to name one and say its job, like "the keyboard types letters."

7. Under each model there is a caption. That is the writing that tells you about the picture. Look at the caption for every one of the five models. 8. Press Listen under each caption. Listen carefully all the way to the end. If you want to hear it again, press Listen again. Take your time — there's no rush. 9. When you have looked at all five models and listened to all five captions, press I explored the models at the bottom of the page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models. That button is yours to press — I cannot press it for you. Then come back and tell me which model was your favourite. Great work today! 🌟

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with the answer already shown, step by step. We use them so you can try first, then check. By the end you will be able to say what a computer is, name the four kinds of computers, and say what apps and input devices do. You only need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you: try first, then look. Say your answer out loud before you press anything. That is what good learners do! There are 4 things to do on this page. 1. Read the first worked example. There are 6 of them, one under the other. Read the question at the top of the box. Do not press anything yet. Say your answer out loud, in a full sentence, like this: "A phone is a computer." Even a small try counts. 2. Now press Show worked solution on that box. The full answer appears. Read it slowly and compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same idea? If yes, brilliant! If not, say the right answer out loud once, so your mouth remembers it. 3. Do the same for all 6 boxes, one at a time. Try, then press Show worked solution, then compare. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It shows how many you have opened. Keep going until every one is open — no skipping, please! 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on each slide, just like before: read, say your answer, then show the solution. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? The counter at the top will show all 6 opened, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your work saved — I cannot press it for you. Ready? Start with worked example one, and tell me your answer to "A phone is a computer. True or False?" 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. Here is what this page is. It has 6 little questions about our unit, "Computers Are Everywhere". You will answer each one yourself. We do this so the words stick in your head — computer, desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, program (app), input device, keyboard. By the end, you will be able to point at a thing and say if it is a computer, and say what it does. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. What I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then answer. Try before you ask for help. It is fine to get one wrong — mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. 1. Read question one. Read it twice, slowly. Say the question out loud if that helps. Think about the answer in your head, or draw it on your paper. Only after you have thought, move to the next step. I expect real thinking first, not a fast guess. 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Type just the answer word, like tablet or keyboard. Check your spelling before you press. I expect one clear answer, not lots of words. 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. Try again after each hint before you take another one. I expect you to try once between hints — that is how your brain grows. 4. If the hints are not enough, press Show next step. It shows you one line of the working, like a helping hand. Read it, then finish the answer yourself. I expect the last bit to come from you. 5. Do the same thing for question two, then three, four, five and six. One question at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Keep going on a question until it is right, then move on. 6. When all 6 questions are right, the top part of the page is done. Well done! Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. 7. On the first slide, press Start. Then answer that slide's question the same way: type in the box and press Check my answer. Use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need them. 8. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many are left. 9. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the whole page is finished when all 6 questions show as right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and read question one. When you have your answer, come back and tell me what you chose, and I will check it with you. 🙂

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Build It. Build It is where you stop just reading and start doing. There are 8 little activities. You will find computers, match them to their names, and learn about apps and input devices. By the end, you will be able to point at a computer and say its name, and say what a mouse, a keyboard, a microphone and a camera do. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your good looking eyes. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself first, write something in every box even if it is short, and be brave. Mistakes are how we learn. Now, the steps. There are 4. Step 1. Look at the first activity on the page. Read it, and press Listen to hear it read to you. Listen right to the end. Then go and get the things it names, like your paper and pencil. Do this for every activity, one at a time. Doing it well means you never start until you know what the activity is asking. Step 2. Do the activity, then write your answer in the box. If it says circle the computers, circle them on your paper. If it says match, draw your lines. Then in the box write what you chose, like "tablet, laptop, smartphone". Or write what you noticed, like "I found 4 computers in my house". I expect a few words in every box, in your own words. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3. When you have finished one activity, press Mark complete under it. Only press it after you really did the work. Then go to the next activity and do Step 1 and Step 2 again. When all 8 say complete, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. I expect all 8 to be marked, not just some. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons you already know: Listen, then write in the box, then Mark complete. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity has Mark complete pressed, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom, and again on the last slide. Ready? Start with activity one, press Listen, and tell me when you have done it. I am right here.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Welcome to Debug It! This is my favourite part. 😊

A bug is a small mistake. Debugging means finding the mistake and fixing it. On this page you will see little cards. Each card has an idea about computers with a mistake hiding in it. Your job is to be a detective and spot it. Mistakes are how we learn — every programmer's code fails the first time! You need your eyes, your thinking, and your voice. Here is the whole page, step by step. 1. Read the first card slowly. It shows a small program or idea with a bug in it. Read it twice. Then ask yourself: does this sound right? Try to find the bug all by yourself first, before you press anything. I expect you to have a guess in your head, even if you are not sure. A guess is good thinking. 2. Now press Show the bug. This shows you where the bug is and what it should be. Look at it and compare it with your guess. Then say out loud why the wrong one was wrong. For example: "That is wrong because a phone is a computer too." I expect a short "because" sentence from you — that is the part that makes your brain remember it. 3. When you have said why, press the button on the card to mark that bug done. Then move to the next card and do the same thing: read, guess, press Show the bug, say why, mark it done. Take your time — there is no rush. Do every card on the page. 4. Now look under the cards. There is a slide deck there, with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. Read the slide and hunt for the bug, just like before. 5. On each slide, press Show the bug when you have your guess. Say why the wrong idea was wrong, in your own words. Then mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going until the slides run out. 6. When every card and every slide is finished, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. That button is yours to press, not mine — it saves the record of your good work. You will know the page is finished when all the cards say done, the slides have run out, and you have pressed I practised debugging. Ready? Go and read the first card, then come back and tell me what bug you think you found. 🔍

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are going to play the games on this page. This is our fun way to practise Unit 1, Computers Are Everywhere. Each game asks you little questions about computers, apps and input devices. By the end, you will know the words really well, and you will feel proud. Here is what I expect from you: read each question slowly, think first, then choose. Take your time — there's no rush. If you get one wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. There are three steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Pick a game and press Start game. Then answer each round. Read the question, look at every choice, and pick the one you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right. I expect you to think before you tap — not tap fast. If you are not sure, say the words out loud in your head, like "a tablet is flat and I touch it with my finger."

Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again to earn more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. So keep playing that same game until its stars are full. I expect you to try again with a smile, even if the first try was tricky. Each time you play, you will get faster and surer. Step 3: Do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, then Play again until that game has all its stars. Then move to the next game. I expect you to finish one game fully before you start a new one — that way your brain really remembers. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything special at the end. Now go on — press Start game on the first game. Tell me when you finish it, and tell me one question you got right! 🌟

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Quick Reference. Quick Reference is like a little helper page. It holds the big words and big ideas from Unit 1, all in one place. We read it so the words stay in your head. You need your eyes, your voice, and your finger to press the buttons. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say the words out loud, and try to say each idea in your own words. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page from the top. Read one line, then stop and think about it. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen. Then say the word out loud after the voice. Do that for every word: computer, desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, program (app), input device, keyboard. I expect you to read every line, not skip any. Step 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a moment, or look away from the page. Say the facts out loud in YOUR words, like you are telling a friend. For example: "A computer is a clever machine that helps us." Then say: what a desktop is, what a laptop is, what a tablet is, what a smartphone is, what an app is, and one input device. If a word is hard, peek at the page again — that is allowed! I expect your own words, not the page's exact words. That shows me you really understand. Step 3. Press Reference reviewed. Go to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says Reference reviewed. Only press it after you have read everything and said the facts out loud. That button tells the page you are done — I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when you have read every line, said the facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Start with Step 1 now, and tell me when you have read it. I am right here. 😊

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Let's do our Computing Fluency page together. 😊

This page is a little speed game. You get 6 quick questions about computers. They are all about things we already learned: what a computer is, the four kinds of computers, apps, and input devices. We do this so the words pop into your head fast, without hard thinking. You need your eyes, your fingers for typing, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here is what I expect from you: try your best on every question, answer in a few words, and do not worry about being slow. Take your time — there's no rush. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see a timer. It counts while you play. That is just for fun, not to scare you. It is fine if it counts a long time. 2. Read question one. Some questions give you two choices, like "a tablet" or "a banana". Pick the one that is a computer. Type your answer in the box. 3. Press Check & continue. This tells the page you are done with that question. Then the next question comes. 4. Do the same for all 6 questions: read, type, press Check & continue. One question at a time. If a word is tricky, think about our unit words: computer, desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, app, keyboard. 5. If you get stuck, come back and tell me. I will give you a small hint. I will not tell you the answer, because you can get this yourself! 6. When all 6 are done, the page shows how you did. You need most of them right to finish the page. 7. If you got fewer than that, do not feel sad. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Run the sprint again and try the questions once more. The second try is usually much easier. 8. You will know the page is finished when a sprint has enough right answers. The page will show you that you passed. Then you are done! Ready? Go and read question one, then tell me what you chose. Here comes question one.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Let's do this page together. 🙂

This page is called Solve Real Problems. It gives you little stories from real life — at home, at school, at the market. In each one, you use what you know about computers to work out the answer. We do this so your computer words become useful, not just words on a page. You need your eyes, your thinking, and your fingers to type. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then answer in your own words. Guessing fast is not the game. Trying is the game. Step 1. There are 4 problems on this page. Read the first one all the way to the end. Then say out loud what it is asking you. Is it asking "which one is a computer?" or "true or false?" or "what can we do on a computer?" Good work here means you know the question before you answer it. Step 2. Now work it out in your head. Think about our unit words: computer, desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, app, input device. Then type your answer in the box. Try to type a full little sentence, like "A tablet is a computer." Then press Check answer. If your brain feels stuck, press Hint first — the hint is a helper, not cheating. Step 3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little tick! Then go to the next problem and do the same thing: read, think, type, press Check answer. Keep going until all 4 problems say you are right. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, using the same buttons. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — like footprints. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 4 problems show a right answer, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it for you — you press the buttons yourself, because it is your work. Ready? Tell me what problem 1 is asking you, and we'll start there. 🌟

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Stay Safe Online. This page has three safety rules. They help keep you happy and safe when you use a computer, a tablet or a phone. By the end, you will know all three rules and be able to say them in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are three things to do. Here they are. 1. Read every rule slowly. Look at the first rule on your screen. If you see a little speaker, press Listen and let it read the rule to you. Then read the next rule, and the next. There are three rules: check before you trust, tell someone if something worries you, and respect other people's work. Do it well by going slowly — one rule at a time, no rushing. I expect you to read or listen to all three, not just the first one. 2. Say each rule in your own words, then give an example from your life. Say it out loud, like this: "If something online makes me sad, I tell my mum." Then think of a real time for you — maybe a video you did not like, or a picture you drew that is yours. Do it well by using easy words that a friend would understand. I expect one short sentence for each rule, and one example for each. Take your time — there's no rush. 3. Press I know these rules at the bottom. Only press it after you have read all three rules and said them in your own words. That button tells the page you are ready. I expect you to be honest — if one rule still feels fuzzy, read it again first, then press it. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these rules and the page moves you on. Ready to start? Read rule one now, and tell me what it says in your own words. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Explain Your Thinking" page. Here is what this page is. There are four questions. Each one asks you to tell me WHY you think your answer is right. That is called explaining your thinking. We do this because a good computer learner can say the reason, not just the answer. By the end, you will be able to say your idea in your own words, using our unit words like computer, laptop, tablet, app and input device. What you need: your eyes for reading, your voice to say your idea out loud first, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. What I expect from you: you try first, you use at least one key idea word, and you write in a full sentence. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first prompt at the top of the page. Read it slowly. Under the prompt you will see the key ideas — those are the special words I want you to use. Say the prompt out loud, then say your answer out loud before you write anything. I expect you to know what the question is really asking. Step 2. Now click in the writing box and type your explanation. Say three things: what you know, the rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example: "I know a phone is a computer. The rule is a computer is a clever machine that helps us. So a phone is a computer because it helps us call and play." Then press Check your reasoning. If it asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check your reasoning again. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Do not copy it. Just look and ask yourself: did I use the key idea words too? If you missed one, go back and add it to your own writing. That is smart learning, not cheating. Step 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for prompt two, then prompt three, then prompt four. Same buttons every time: write, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. Every explanation must use the key ideas. That is when this part is done. Step 5. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: write your explanation, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Step 7. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done! How will you know the page is finished? Every one of the four explanations uses the key ideas and has been checked, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it for you — you press the buttons, because the work is yours. 🌟

Ready? Read prompt one and tell me your idea out loud first. Then come back and tell me what you wrote.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is your Unit Challenge. The Unit Challenge is a little quiz about everything in Unit 1: computers are everywhere, the four kinds of computer, what we use computers for, programs and apps, and input devices. We do it to show what your brain has learned. By the end, you will know which parts you are strong at. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. This one is graded, so I will help you think — but I really can't give quiz answers. I promise you can get this! Here is what to do, step by step. 1. Look at the first question on the screen. Read it twice before you answer. Reading twice helps you see what the question is really asking. I expect you to read the whole question, not just the first few words. 2. Now look at the answer choices. Say each one quietly to yourself. Think: does this match what we learned in the lesson? A phone is a computer. A desktop is big. A laptop folds up. A tablet is flat. A smartphone is tiny. An app is another word for a program. Input devices put things in. 3. Tap the answer you think is best, then press Next question. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect one careful choice, not a fast guess. If two answers look the same, look for the one word that is different. 4. Keep going the same way for all 12 questions. Read, think, choose, press Next question. If one feels hard, that is okay — pick the answer that feels closest and keep going. Mistakes are how we learn. 5. At the end you will see your score. You pass with more than half of the questions right. I expect you to look at your score and tell me how it felt. 6. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing! It just means your brain gets one more practice. Come and tell me which questions were tricky, and we will go over that idea together before you try again. 7. When your score is good, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Ready? Go and read question one, then come back and tell me how it went. 🌟

project.label: Unit Project
project.text:
Hello! Today we make your Unit Project. It is called My Computer Scrapbook. You will make a little book of computers. You need paper, a pencil and some colours. A grown-up can help you cut or find pictures. We do this so you can point at each computer and say its name all by yourself. That is the big goal! Here are your steps. 1. First, read the Unit Project box on your screen. It tells you what to make. Under it there is a list of things a good project has. Read the list slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know one thing you must show in your scrapbook before you start. 2. Now make your scrapbook. Take four pieces of paper, or fold one big paper into four boxes. Box one is a desktop. It is big and stays on a desk. Draw it or stick in a picture. Then tick the first thing on the list. 3. Box two is a laptop. It folds up like a book and you can carry it. Draw it or find a picture. I expect a screen and a keyboard part in your drawing. 4. Box three is a tablet. It is flat and you touch it with your finger. Box four is a smartphone. It is small and fits in a pocket. Make the smartphone smaller than the tablet, so we can see the difference. 5. Now point at each box and say its name out loud: desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone. Say them to your grown-up. I expect all four names, said by you. 6. Next, do your Computer Hunt. Walk around your home and look for computers. A TV box, a phone, a watch, a car — all can be computers! Draw a circle on your paper for each one you find. Then draw a star on the one that is easiest to carry. 7. Last, draw your favourite app and say its job. Maybe a drawing app, or a game app. Remember, an app is a program, and a program tells the computer what to do. Say out loud: "My app is for..." and finish the sentence. 8. Now tick every thing on the list on your screen. Check each one is really done. Then press My project is finished. You will know the page is done when every item on the list is ticked and you have pressed My project is finished. 🌟

Ready? Start with step 1 and tell me when you have read the list.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our starting page. This page is called the Unit Overview. It tells you what our new unit, "Be an Animator", is all about. We do this first so you know where we are going, like looking at a map before a trip. By the end of this page, you will be able to say what you are going to learn. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Let's start with something small. There are 3 steps. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page and read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and the words will be read to you. You can press Listen more than once — that is fine. I expect you to look for two things: the new word algorithm, which means steps for a job in the right order, and the word code, which means the blocks that tell a computer what to do. If a word is tricky, you can ask your grown-up or ask me. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, or type it to me here. Do not copy the page word for word — use your own words, like you are telling a friend. A good answer is one or two sentences, like "I will learn about steps, and I will make a character move." I expect you to try even if it is not perfect. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Only press Continue after you have read the page and said your sentence. That button takes us to the next part, where the real teaching starts. I expect you to be ready, sitting comfy, with your tablet or paper near you. You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, said your own sentence, and pressed Continue and the next page opens. Now go and do Step 1. When you have read it, come back and tell me one thing you saw. Take your time — there's no rush.

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Tools and Setup. It tells you what you need for Unit 2, Be an Animator. In this unit you will make a character move, hop and talk. To do that, we need our tools ready first. A tool is a thing you use to do a job. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, check each thing with your grown-up, and only press the button at the end when everything is really ready. There are three steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Read the Tools and Setup page. Look at the page on your screen and read it from top to bottom. It will tell you about ScratchJr, which is an app on a tablet, and about Scratch, which you open in a web browser at scratch dot mit dot edu. It also says to have paper and a pencil for planning. If a word is hard, ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know, after reading, what things you need. Step 2. Check each tool, one at a time. Now go down the list and check each one. Can you find ScratchJr on the tablet? Tap it and see if it opens. Do you see the little house and the plus sign? Then check Scratch on a computer, and check you have paper and a pencil next to you. Ask your grown-up to help with anything you cannot open. I expect every item on the list to be checked, not just looked at. Step 3. Press "My tools are ready". When every tool is open or ready, scroll to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says My tools are ready. Only press it when it is true — a good computer person checks first, then clicks! You will know the page is finished when you have pressed My tools are ready and the page moves you on. That means your tools are set and you can start being an animator. Are you ready to begin Step 1? Tell me when you have read the page. 😊

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Computing Words page. This page has our seven special words for Unit 2: algorithm, step, order, code, program, block and run. We learn them because these are the words animators and coders use every day. When you know them, you can talk about your ScratchJr character like a real programmer. What I expect from you: try every word, say it out loud with a big voice, and write your own sentence for each one. Your sentence can be short and simple. Mistakes are fine — mistakes are how we learn. You need your voice, your eyes and your typing finger. A grown-up can sit near you to help. Here are all the steps. Step 1: Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Press Listen. This plays the word out loud. Listen carefully, then say the word with the sound, slowly. I expect you to copy the sound as best you can. Step 3: Now say the meaning in your OWN words, out loud. For example, for algorithm you might say, "It means steps for a job, in the right order." Your words do not have to match the page. Your own words show me you really understand. Step 4: Type a sentence with the word in it. Keep it short and about your day. Something like, "I run my program." Then press Check sentence. I expect one sentence with the word spelled right. Step 5: Read what the checker says to you. If it says well done, smile — you got it! If it asks you to try again, change one small thing and press Check sentence again. That is not failing, that is fixing. Step 6: Do steps 1 to 5 again for every word on the page. There are seven words. Go one word at a time, never two at once. If a word feels hard, tell me and I will help you make a sentence for it. Step 7: When every word has a green tick, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the computing words. This tells the page you have finished the word list. Step 8: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 9: On each slide, use the same buttons as before: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning your own way, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. Same job, new slide. Step 10: Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many slides are left. Step 11: Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is done? You will have pressed I explored the computing words, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide, with all the dots behind you. Ready? Start with word one, and tell me when you have pressed Listen. I am right here.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is The Lesson page for Unit 2, Be an Animator. On this page you meet five small ideas. They teach you what an algorithm is (steps for a job, in the right order), and how we turn steps into code so a character can move. By the end, you will be able to say what an algorithm is and name some ScratchJr blocks. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Let's start! Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see the first concept box. Read it slowly, word by word. If reading is tricky, press the Listen button and it will read to you. Listen right to the end, even if you think you know it. I expect you to read or listen to the whole box, not just the first line. Step 2. Every concept has an example. Say the example out loud in your own voice. For the first one, stand up and do the hand-washing steps in the air: turn on the tap, get the soap, scrub scrub scrub, rinse, dry. Saying it and doing it helps your brain keep it. I expect to hear your voice, not just quiet reading. Step 3. Now make it yours. Try the same idea with your own things. Say the steps for brushing your teeth, or for putting on your shoes. Use the words first, then, next, last. I expect three steps at least, in a sensible order. Step 4. Press the arrow or scroll down to the next concept box. Do the same three things again: read it, press Listen, say the example out loud. Do this for all five concept boxes, one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5. As you read, watch for our special words: algorithm, step, order, code, program, block, run. When you meet one, say the word out loud and say what it means in your own words. I expect you to try, even if it comes out a bit wobbly. Wobbly is fine! Step 6. When you have read every one of the five concepts, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after all five — that button is your promise to me that you really read them. Step 7. Under the page there is a deck of slides. They show the same five ideas, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Then read that slide and press the same buttons on it, just like you did above. Step 8. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Do one slide at a time, and do not rush past any. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. Well done — that is the last thing to press! You will know the page is finished when two things are true: the button I studied the concepts has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1, then come back and tell me one thing you learned from the first concept. I will be right here waiting. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello, animator! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here is what it is. There are 6 little discoveries. Each one shows you a situation and a picture. You think, then you type your own idea. It is like being a detective for steps and order. Why we do it. This unit is all about algorithms — steps for a job, in the right order. When you work the idea out yourself, it sticks in your head much better than if I just tell you. What I expect from you. Look carefully. Think before you type. Write your own words, even if they are short. Trying is the important part, and mistakes are how we learn. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. Here are all the steps. There are four. 1. Find the numbered tabs at the top. Press tab 1 first. Read the little situation and look at the picture or model. Take your time — there is no rush. I expect you to look at the picture and say out loud what you can see before you type anything. 2. Now read the discovery question under it. Think of your answer in your head first. Then type your idea in the box and press Check my idea. A good answer uses words from our unit, like step, order, algorithm or block. If it says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint, read it, change one thing, and try again. When it says Exactly!, that tab gets a tick — well done! 3. Now do the same for the other tabs: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. One at a time, in order — just like an algorithm! Press the tab, read, think, type, press Check my idea. I expect all six tabs to have a tick when you are done. Come and tell me if one tab keeps saying Look again, and I will give you a small hint. 4. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. They show the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? Every one of the 6 tabs has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is the whole page done! Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you can see. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello, animator! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our picture museum. This page has 5 visual models. A visual model is a picture that shows an idea. Some of them move! We look at them so the big ideas of this unit stick in your head — steps, order, code, and making a character move. You need your eyes, your finger to drag and tap, and your voice to say what you see. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: look slowly, press the buttons, and say out loud what you notice. Not fast clicking. Slow looking! Step 1. Find the first model, "Everyday steps (what is an algorithm?)". Look at it carefully. If it moves, put your finger on it and drag to turn it around. Press any buttons on it to change it. Then tell me one thing you see. A good answer is like: "I see steps in a row."

Step 2. Under that model there is a caption — that is the little bit of writing. Read it, then press Listen to hear it out loud. Listen all the way to the end. Then say the caption back in your own words. I expect you to use the word algorithm, which means steps for a job in the right order. Step 3. Go to model 2, "Follow the steps, in order". Drag it to turn it and press its buttons. Watch what happens when the order changes. I expect you to notice this: if the steps get mixed up, we get a muddle. Tell me one silly order you can think of, like socks on top of shoes! Step 4. Read the caption under model 2 and press Listen. Then answer me in your head: does the order matter, yes or no? Say your answer out loud in a full sentence. Step 5. Go to model 3, "Code and programs". Look at it, drag it, press its buttons. This one is about code — the blocks that tell a computer what to do. I expect you to spot that a computer only does what the blocks say. It cannot guess! Step 6. Read the caption under model 3 and press Listen. Then tell yourself what a program is. A program is code that does a job. Say it once, slowly. Step 7. Go to model 4, "Be an animator! Make it move in ScratchJr". Drag it to turn it and press its buttons to make it change. Look for the colours: yellow starts, blue moves, red stops. I expect you to point at the yellow start block with your finger. Step 8. Read the caption under model 4 and press Listen. Then say the order out loud: Start, Move, Hop, End. That is our little program! Step 9. Go to model 5, "Make it talk, and tap to start". Drag it and press its buttons. This one has the purple Say block, which makes a speech bubble. I expect you to remember: purple talks, and Start on Tap means the program runs when you tap the character. Step 10. Read the caption under model 5 and press Listen. Now check yourself: did you look at all 5 models? Did you press Listen under every caption? If you missed one, go back — that is good work, not a mistake. Step 11. When you have really looked at all 5, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Press it only after you have done all of them, because that button tells the page you finished. You will know the page is done when you have turned all 5 models, heard all 5 captions, and the I explored the models button has been pressed by you. Ready? Start with Step 1, then come back and tell me one thing you see. Take your time — there's no rush.

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Code Examples. Code is the blocks that tell a computer what to do. On this page we read blocks that already work. We read them like a little story, from top to bottom. By the end you will know what each block does, and you will be ready to build your own. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help. Ready? Here are your steps. Step 1: Read each code example, line by line. Look at the first example on the page. Start at the top line and point at it with your finger. Say out loud what you think that line does. Then move down to the next line and do the same. For example, the yellow "Start on Green Flag" line means the program begins. The blue "Move Right" line means the character walks across. The red "End" line means stop. I expect you to say something out loud for every line, even if you are not sure. Guessing is good thinking! Step 2: Press Copy the code, then mark it done. Under the example there is a button that says Copy the code. Press it. If you have ScratchJr on a tablet, put those same blocks in a row, like a jigsaw, and tap the green flag to run it. Blocks must touch! If you cannot try it today, that is fine. When you have read the example, press the button under it to mark it done. I expect you to only press done after you have read every line, not before. Step 3: Do the slides at the bottom of the page. Scroll down. There is a deck of slides, with one code example on each slide. Press Start. Read that code the same way, line by line, out loud. Then mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going until there are no more slides. I expect you to say the colour of each block too: yellow starts, blue moves, purple talks, red stops. Step 4: Press Go to Build It. When you have read every example and every slide, press the button that says Go to Build It. That is where you become the animator and make your own character move. I expect you to press this last, after all the reading, so your brain is ready. You will know the page is finished when every example has been marked done, all the slides are read, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Now start with Step 1. Read the first example out loud, then tell me what you think the blue line does. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello, my animator! Today we are on the "Learn the Method" page. A method is a way to do a job step by step. This page shows you 5 methods from our unit. You will read each step, one at a time, and say it out loud. This helps the steps stick in your head, just like an algorithm — steps for a job, in the right order. What I expect from you: a calm voice saying each step out loud, one step at a time, and no skipping. Take your time. There is no rush. Here are your steps. Step 1: Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step. Say it out loud in your own words. If a word is tricky, ask your grown-up or ask me. Step 2: Now press the button that says "Show me the next step". A new step will pop up. Read that one out loud too. Good work means you say every step, not just look at it. Step 3: Keep pressing "Show me the next step" until the page says "Method complete". That means you have reached the end of that method. Well done — that is one finished! Step 4: Now do the same thing for the next method. Read step one, press "Show me the next step", say each step out loud, and stop when it says "Method complete". Do this for all 5 methods. Step 5: Under the page there is a deck of slides. The same methods are there, one method on each slide. On the first slide, press "Start". Step 6: On each slide, use the same buttons as before. Press "Show me the next step" and say each step out loud until that slide is done. Step 7: To move to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. Keep going, slide by slide. Step 8: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How you know the page is finished: all 5 methods say "Method complete", and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with the first method and tell me when you get to "Method complete". I am right here! 🌟

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello, animator! Today we are on the Guided Practice page. This page has 6 small questions about our unit, Be an Animator. They are about algorithms (steps for a job, in the right order), code, and the ScratchJr blocks. We practise so the words stick in your head and your fingers know what to press. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a pencil and paper if you like. I expect you to try each one yourself first, even if you are not sure. Mistakes are how we learn. Here is the whole plan, step by step. Step 1. Look at the first question on the page. Read it slowly. Read it twice. If it helps, say it out loud. Then work out your answer on paper or in your head. I expect you to think for a moment before you type anything — no fast guessing. Step 2. Type your answer in the box. Use the words from our unit, like algorithm, order, code, block, or the block name like Move Right. Then press Check my answer. I expect a real try in the box, even a short one. Step 3. If you feel stuck, do not worry. Press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint helps a bit more. Try again after each hint before you press it again. That is good, brave thinking. Step 4. If you are still stuck after the hints, press Show next step. It shows you one line of the working. Read that line, then finish the rest yourself. I expect you to still type your own answer — the last bit must come from you. Step 5. Now do the same for every question: read, think, type, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need them. Keep going until each of the 6 questions is right. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is your practice round — you already know these answers, so it should feel easier this time. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. I expect you to answer from your own memory first now. Step 8. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished, and only you can press it — I cannot press it for you. How will you know the page is finished? All 6 questions are marked right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Ready? Go and read question one, then tell me what you typed. 🙂

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Quick Reference. It is like a little poster with all the important words and facts from Unit 2, Be an Animator, in one place. We read it so the words stay in your head: algorithm, step, order, code, program, block, run. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here are the three things to do. 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page slowly, from the top to the bottom. Read one word, then read what it means, then stop and think for a moment. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. I expect you to go slowly, not fast. Reading it twice is even better. 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a second and say them out loud, like you are teaching a friend. Try these: "An algorithm is steps for a job, in the right order." "Code is the blocks that tell a computer what to do." "A program is code that does a job." I expect your own words, not perfect words. If you get stuck, peek at the page, then say it again without looking. Saying it out loud is what makes it stick! 3. Press Reference reviewed. When you have read the page and said the facts out loud, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says Reference reviewed. Only press it after you have really read it — that button is your promise that you did the work. I cannot press it for you. It saves your work, so it must come from you. You will know the page is finished when you have read every word, said the key facts in your own words, and the Reference reviewed button has been pressed. Now go and start step 1. When you finish reading, come back and tell me one word you remember, and I will listen. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with all the thinking shown. It is like watching me do a puzzle, then doing one yourself. We do this so you learn how a good answer looks. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit near you and help you read. Here is what I expect from you: try each question in your head FIRST, before you peek. Guessing and trying is not cheating — it is learning. Mistakes are how we learn. There are four things to do on this page. Here they are, one at a time. Step 1: Look at the first worked example. There are 6 of them. Read the question out loud, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Now think for a moment and say your own answer out loud, like "the order does matter" or "the blue arrow makes it move". A good try is any answer you say before you look. I expect one guess from you for every question, even if you are not sure. Step 2: Now press the button that says Show worked solution. Read the answer slowly, line by line, and compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? If yes, smile — you got it! If not, that is fine. Just say the right answer out loud once, in your own words, so it sticks in your head. Step 3: Do the same for every one of the 6 examples: think first, then press Show worked solution. At the top of the page there is a counter — a little number that tells you how many you have opened. Watch it grow: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. I expect you to open all six, not just the easy ones. The page is finished when the counter shows all of them open. Step 4: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on each slide: think of your answer first, then press the button to show the solution. Try to say your answer before you press — that is the important part. Step 5: To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. That takes you to the next slide. Under the slide there are little dots — they show you where you are in the deck. When you reach the very last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to go through every slide, slowly, not rushing. How you will know the page is done: the counter at the top shows all 6 worked examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are all done! Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have done Step 1, and tell me what you guessed. I will be right here. 🙂

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Build It. Build It is the doing part of our unit. You made your brain ready with the words algorithm, step and order. Now your hands get busy! You will put steps in order, match blocks, and make a character really move. By the end you will be an animator — someone who makes pictures move. Get these ready: a pencil, some paper or your printed activity page, colours, and a tablet with ScratchJr if you have one. A grown-up can sit near you to help. Here is what I expect from you: try first, then write. Even a short answer is good. Neat is nice, but trying is what counts most. There are 8 build-it activities on this page. Here is your whole plan. 1. Read the first activity and press Listen. Listen tells you the words out loud, so you hear them as well as see them. Each activity says what to use and what to do. Get those things before you start. I expect you to read it once, listen once, then say to yourself, "I know what to do."

2. Do the activity with your hands, not just your eyes. For "Put the Steps in Order", write 1, 2 and 3 next to the hand-washing steps. Think: what must happen FIRST? I expect three numbers, and no box left empty. 3. Write your answer, or what you noticed, in the box under the activity. Your notice can be short, like "soap comes before drying". I expect one line at least. Nobody writes it for you — the words come from you. 4. Press Mark complete under that activity. This tells the page, "I did this one." I expect you to press it only after you really finished it, not before. 5. Now do the next activities the same way: Listen, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. In "Follow the Path" trace the bird's path with your finger, then your pencil, and say each move out loud: right, right, hop. In "Match the Block" draw lines: yellow starts, blue arrow moves right, blue hop jumps up, red stops. Take your time — there's no rush. 6. Keep going through all 8. "Put the Code in Order" and "Put the Blocks in Order" want numbers in the boxes — remember, the start block always comes first and the red stop block comes last. "Make it Move in ScratchJr" and "Build it in ScratchJr" want the real tablet: press the plus for a new project, add a character, join the blocks in a row with no gaps, then tap the green flag to run it. "Draw Your Character Moving" wants your drawing with arrows to show it moving. I expect every one to have its box filled and Mark complete pressed. 7. When all 8 have Mark complete, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Only press it when every single one is marked. That button saves your good work. 8. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same activities, one on each slide, big and clear. Press Start on the first slide. Do that activity, use the same buttons as before, then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 9. Keep pressing the arrow until the last slide. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity shows Mark complete and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom, and again on the last slide. Ready? Start with activity one: read it, press Listen, and tell me when you have your pencil in your hand. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I'm your teacher today. This page is our Games page. Games are how we practise the big ideas from Unit 2: algorithm, step, order, code and program. Each game asks you short questions. When you play, the words stick in your brain. What I expect from you is simple: read each question, think for a moment, then choose. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are the three things to do, in order. 1. Pick a game and press Start game. Look at the game cards on the page and choose one you like. Press Start game on that card. Now a round appears. Read the question. Read all the choices before you tap one. Then tap the answer you think is right. You earn a star for every round you get right. If you get one wrong, that's fine — mistakes are how we learn. Just read the little explanation and try to remember it. I expect you to think before you tap, not tap fast. 2. Press Play again to earn more stars. When the game ends, press Play again. You will see the questions once more. This time you know more, so you should get more right. Keep pressing Play again until that game has all its stars. When a game has all its stars, it is mastered — that means you really know it. I expect you to stay with one game until its stars are full, then move on. 3. Master every game. Go back to the game list and pick the next game. Do the same thing: press Start game, answer the rounds, then press Play again until all the stars are full. Do this for every game on the page. Some games ask about the same words in a new way — that is on purpose, so your brain gets strong. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything else. Full stars on every game means you are done. Now go ahead: choose your first game and press Start game. Tell me which game you picked, and how the first round went. 🌟

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello, my clever animator! Today we are bug hunters. 🐛

A bug is a small mistake in a program. Every programmer gets bugs — even grown-up ones! On this page you will look at little programs, find the mistake, and learn how to fix it. This makes you good at checking your own work in ScratchJr. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Here is the whole page, step by step. 1. Look at the first card. Each card shows a small program with one bug hiding in it. Read it slowly, from the top line to the bottom line, like you are the computer. Ask yourself: is the order silly? Is a block missing? Are the blocks touching? I expect you to make a guess out loud before you press anything — a guess is not cheating, it is thinking! 2. Now press Show the bug. It will tell you where the bug is and what it should be. Then say why it was wrong, in your own words, like "the End block came first, so nothing moved." After you have said it, press the button to mark that bug done. I expect a real sentence from you, not just a nod. 3. Do the same for every card on the page. Read, guess, press Show the bug, say why, mark it done. Take your time — there's no rush. If a card feels hard, tell me and I will give you a small hint. 4. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. This is a little deck with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. 5. On each slide, hunt for the bug first, all by yourself. Then press Show the bug to check. Say why it was wrong, mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next slide. I expect you to guess before you peek — that is how your brain grows. 6. Keep going until you have seen every slide. Then press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. You will know the page is finished when every card and every slide is marked done and the I practised debugging button has been pressed. Ready? Start with card one. Read it to me, and tell me what you think the bug is!

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Let's get ready for our Computing Fluency sprint. 🌟

This page is a quick game. You answer six short questions about our unit, "Be an Animator". They are all about things you already know: what an algorithm is, why order matters, and what code and blocks do. We do this so the words come to you fast, like knowing your own name. You need your eyes, your reading voice, and your fingers for typing. What I expect from you: try your best, answer in a few words, and don't worry about being perfect. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just for fun — take your time, there's no rush. Speed comes later, when the words feel easy. 2. Read question one out loud, softly. Reading it out loud helps your brain hear it. Look at the question again — what is it really asking? 3. Type your answer in the box. A short answer is fine, like "a set of steps" or "yes". I expect you to write words, not just guess a letter. 4. Press Check & continue. This tells the page you are done with that question and shows you the next one. 5. If your answer was not right, that is okay. Read the little help message, say the right answer once out loud, and keep going. That is how it sticks. 6. Do the same for all six questions: read, type, press Check & continue. One question at a time, first to last — just like the steps in an algorithm! 7. At the end you will see your score. You need most of them right to pass the sprint. 8. If you got fewer right, press Run the sprint again. This is not a bad thing! Doing it a second time makes you faster and stronger. 9. You will know the page is finished when a sprint has enough right answers. The page will show you it is done. A little tip before you start: think about washing your hands. Soap first, then rinse, then dry. Those steps in the right order have a special name — and that name will help you with question one. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me how it goes. I'm right here. 😊

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. Here is what it is. There are 4 little problems from real life. Each one asks you to use what we learned in Be an Animator. That means steps, order, code and blocks. Why do we do it? Because knowing a word is good, but using it is even better. By the end you will be able to put steps in the right order and pick the right block, all by yourself. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a pencil and paper if you like to plan. What I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then type. Do not guess quickly. If you get stuck, that is fine — press Hint, and try again. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps.
