Step 1. Read the first problem carefully. Read it twice — once fast, once slow. Then ask yourself: what is this problem really asking me? Some ask you to put steps in order, like washing hands. Some ask you to choose the right block, like the yellow start block. Tell yourself the job out loud in your own words. That is how I know you have understood it. Step 2. Now work it out, then type your working and your answer in the box. Working means showing your thinking, not just the answer. For example you can write, first this, then this, then this. Then press Check answer. If you feel stuck, press Hint first and read it, then try again. I would rather you try and be wrong than not try at all. Step 3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little smile! Then move on to the next problem and do the same thing: read it twice, think, type your working, press Check answer. Keep going until all 4 problems say right. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. The same problems are there, one problem on each slide. On the very first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons you already know on each slide: read, think, type, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Step 5. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. More dots to go means more slides to do. Step 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. Well done, animator! How will you know the page is finished? All 4 problems show that your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the page is complete. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me what the first problem is asking you to do. Take your time — there's no rush.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Stay Safe Online page. This page is about staying safe and kind when you use a tablet or computer. We do it because computers are fun, but we need safe rules too, just like we have safe rules for crossing the road. By the end, you will know the rules and be able to say them in your own words. You need your eyes, your ears, and your talking voice. There are three steps. Here we go! Step 1: Read every rule slowly. On the page you will see the safety rules. Read one rule, then stop and think for a moment. If you see a speaker picture, press Listen and hear the rule read out loud. Listen right to the end. I expect you to go slowly and not skip any rule. Ask your grown-up to help you read any tricky word. Step 2: Say each rule in your own words. Do not just copy the words on the screen. Say it like you would say it to a friend. For example, one rule says: if something online worries you, stop and tell a grown-up you trust. In your own words that might be, "If something scares me, I go and tell Mum." Then give an example from your own life. A good answer has two parts: what the rule means, and one real example from your day. Step 3: Give an example for the other rule too. The other rule is about respecting other people's work. Pictures, songs and stories belong to the person who made them. Your work belongs to you, so put your name on it. Say that rule your own way, then tell me one example, like, "I will not say my friend's drawing is mine."

Step 4: Press the button. When you have read every rule and said them all in your own words, press I know these rules at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have really read them all. That button is how the page saves your work, so I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these rules and you can say both rules without looking. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read the first rule. 🙂

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's do this page together. This page is called Explain Your Thinking. On it, you tell me what you know in your own words. That is how we make an idea stick. You will need your voice, your fingers to type, and a grown-up nearby to help with spelling if you like. Take your time — there's no rush. What I expect from you: a short answer, but a thinking one. Use the unit words — algorithm, step, order, code, program — and say WHY. Even one good sentence is enough for Grade 1. Step 1. Look at the first prompt at the top of the page. Read it out loud, slowly. Under the prompt there are key ideas — little words like "step" or "order". Read those too. I expect you to spot which key words you must use in your answer. Do not type yet — just read and think. Step 2. Now click inside the answer box and type your explanation. Try to say three things: what you know, which rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example: "It is the blue arrow block. That block means move. So it makes the character go across." Then press Check your reasoning. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check your reasoning again. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare. Read it and ask yourself: did I use the same key words? You do not need the same words as the model — but your answer should have the key ideas in it. If yours is missing one, go back and add it. Step 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for prompt two, prompt three and prompt four. There are 4 prompts in all. Each time: read the prompt, read the key ideas, type your answer, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. Go one prompt at a time. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 5. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is your practice round — say the answer again, in your own words, a little better this time. Step 6. On each slide use the same buttons: type your answer, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — count them to see how many are left. Step 7. On the last slide, do the same thing, then press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I cannot press it for you — the record of your work comes from you. How you will know the page is finished: all 4 explanations are written and checked, every one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read me the first prompt, and tell me what you already know about it.

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Unit Project. This is the big finish of Unit 2, "Be an Animator". You will make your own character move, hop and talk. We do this to show that you can turn steps into code. An algorithm is steps for a job in the right order. Code is the blocks that tell a computer what to do. You will need a tablet with ScratchJr, and a pencil and paper for planning. A grown-up can sit with you. What I expect from you: try each step yourself first, join your blocks with no gaps, and tap the green flag to test. Tell me when a step is done, and I will check it with you. Here are the steps. Step 1. Read the Unit Project on the page. Read the box that says what you will make. Then read the list of things a good project has. That list is your checklist. Read it slowly with your grown-up, and point at each line with your finger. I expect you to be able to tell me one thing from the list in your own words. Step 2. Plan your steps on paper. Write or draw your algorithm first, before you touch the tablet. Think: start, move, hop, stop. Say each step out loud. I expect four little steps in the right order. Step 3. Open ScratchJr and start a new project. Tap the house, then tap the plus. Then tap the plus at the top left to add a character. Pick any animal or person you like! I expect one character on your screen. Step 4. Build your first blocks. Find the yellow Start on Green Flag block. Drag it into the row at the bottom. Then add the blue Move Right block. Push them together like a jigsaw, with no gap. I expect two blocks touching. Step 5. Add the hop and the end. Add the blue Hop block after Move Right. Then add the red End block last. Now tap the green flag to run it. I expect your character to move across and then hop. Step 6. Fix it if it looks wrong. Nothing moved? Check your blocks are touching. Hopped first? Check the order. Every programmer's code fails the first time, so this is normal. I expect you to change one thing, then run it again. Step 7. Add a friend character. Tap the plus at the top left again and pick a second character. This friend will talk to us. I expect two characters on your screen. Step 8. Make your friend talk on a tap. Give the friend the yellow Start on Tap block. Then the purple Say block, and type Hello. Then a blue Move block, then the red End block. Tap your friend to run it. I expect a speech bubble and then movement. Step 9. Tick your checklist. Go back to the list on the page. Look at each line and check your project really does it. Tick each one as you check it. I expect you to test, not guess. Step 10. Press My project is finished. Only press it when every item on the list is ticked. That button tells the page you are done. I expect your project to be running before you press it. You will know the page is finished when every item on your list has a tick and you have pressed My project is finished. Start with Step 1, and tell me when it is done. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello, animator! This page is your Unit Challenge. It is 12 questions about everything we learned in "Be an Animator" — algorithms, steps, order, code, programs and blocks. We do it to see what your brain has kept. It is not scary. I will not tell you any answers, because this one is yours to show off. All you need is your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you: read every question all the way to the end, think for a moment, then choose the answer you believe. No rushing. Guessing fast is not the game — thinking is the game. Step 1. Look at the first question on the screen. Read it twice. Read the question again, and ask yourself: what is it really asking? Some questions ask "what does this word mean?" Some ask "what should you do when this happens?" Knowing which kind it is helps a lot. Step 2. Now look at all the answer choices before you pick. Do not tap the first one that looks nice. Read them all, then choose the one that matches the question best. Tap your answer, then press Next question. Step 3. Keep going the same way for all 12 questions. Read, think, choose, press Next question. Take your time — there's no rush. If a word feels tricky, remember our unit words: algorithm means steps for a job in the right order, code means the blocks that tell a computer what to do, and a program is code that does a job. Step 4. If one question feels too hard, do your best thinking and pick the answer that feels closest. Then move on. A hard question is not a mistake — it is just a hard question. Step 5. At the end you will see your score. You pass with more than half right. Look at it kindly. Every question you got right is something you really learned. Step 6. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is good news, not bad news! Going round a second time is how the ideas get stuck in your head. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 7. When your score is high enough, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue after a passing score. Then come back and tell me your score — I would love to hear about it, and we can look at any question that felt wobbly. Ready? Read question one, and off you go. Good luck, animator! 🎬

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Welcome to Unit 3: Be a Data Detective. Here is what this unit is about. Data is a big word that means information. Data can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds. A detective looks for clues. A data detective looks for data! By the end of this unit you will sort things into groups, count them, and colour a block graph. Today we are only on the Unit Overview page. That page is like a map. It shows you where we are going. What I expect from you today: eyes on the words, ears open, and your own voice at the end. You will need a comfy seat and your grown-up nearby if you want help reading. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the page and read what this unit is about and what you will be able to do. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen. Then the words are read out loud to you. Do it well by listening all the way to the end, not stopping halfway. If a word feels hard, press Listen again. I expect you to hear or read the whole overview once. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the words on the screen. Just say it out loud, like telling a friend. A good answer sounds like this: "I think I will learn about data and how to sort things into groups." One or two sentences is plenty. I expect you to use at least one new word, like data or sort. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. That button takes you to the next part, where the real teaching begins. Only press it after you have done Step 1 and Step 2. I expect you to press it yourself, so the page knows you are ready. How will you know this page is finished? When you have listened or read the overview, said in your own words what you will learn, and pressed Continue. Then The Lesson opens, and that means you are done here. Great work today! Come back any time you want to practise. 🌟

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello, data detective! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. It teaches you five big ideas about data. Data just means information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds. By the end you will be able to say what data is, sort things into groups, count each group, and put things in order. You need a pencil, some paper, and a few small things from home, like blocks, spoons or crayons. Let's begin! 1. Start at the top of the page. There are five concept cards. Read the first one slowly. Then press Listen, and let it read the card to you while you follow along. Do this for every card, one at a time. I expect you to go slowly and not skip any card. Five cards, five Listen presses. 2. On each card there is an example. Say that example out loud, in your own voice. Then try it for real with your own things. For the sorting card, tip out your blocks and make a group where every one is the same colour. For the counting card, touch each block and count: one, two, three. I expect to hear you talking and see you touching real things — that is how it sticks in your brain. 3. When you have read and tried all five cards, scroll down to the bottom. Press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really have read every card. That press tells the page you finished this part. Well done — that is the reading part done! 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. They show the same five ideas, one idea on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Look at the slide and say the idea back in your own words, like you are teaching a friend. Use the same buttons on each slide. 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. More dots filled means you are getting closer to the end. Take your time; there is no rush. 6. Keep going until you reach the last slide. On that last slide, press the finish button. That means you have been all the way through the deck. Brilliant work! You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then come back and tell me one thing you learned. I would love to hear it! 🌟

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello, detective! I am your teacher today. This page is called Tools and Setup. It tells you what things you need before we start Unit 3, Be a Data Detective. We do this first so nothing stops us later. A detective needs their kit ready! In this unit you will sort things into groups, count them, and colour a block graph. Most of it is done with your hands and eyes — not on a screen. What I expect from you: read slowly, get your things, and only press the button when everything is really there. It is fine to ask your grown-up to help. Here are our three steps. Step 1: Read the Tools and Setup page. Look at the list on your screen from top to bottom. Read it with your grown-up if the words are tricky. For this unit the list is small: paper (or the printed activity page), a pencil, and some colours like crayons or pencil crayons. I expect you to be able to tell me one thing from the list in your own words. Step 2: Check each tool, one at a time. Do not just look — go and fetch each thing and put it on your table. Touch each one and say "got it". Check your pencil is not broken and your colours still work. If something is missing, ask your grown-up for it or find something like it. I expect all your things sitting in front of you before you move on. Step 3: Press "My tools are ready". This button is at the bottom of the page. Only press it when every thing on the list is really on your table. Pressing it tells the page you are set up and ready to learn. That press must come from you — I cannot do it for you. How you will know the page is finished: after you press "My tools are ready", the page will show you it is done and let you go on to the next part of the unit. Now tell me one thing: what have you put on your table so far? 😊

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello, my Data Detective! Today we learn our six special computing words. They are: data, computing device, sort, group, count, order. These words help you talk about your work like a real detective. You need your voice, your ears, and your fingers for typing. Here is our whole plan, step by step. 1. Look at the first word card on the page. Read the word. Then read the little line that tells you what it means. Take your time — there is no rush. 2. Press Listen. This says the word out loud for you. Listen carefully. I expect you to hear it once, then press Listen again if you want. 3. Now say the word out loud yourself. Say it with me, slowly. Big voice! Saying it helps your mouth remember it. 4. Now say the meaning in your OWN words. Do not copy the page. For example, for data you might say, "Data is information, like numbers and pictures." That is what I expect: your own simple words. 5. Now type a sentence with the word in the box. Your sentence should show you know the word. A good one is like this: "I count the mangoes in the bowl." A weak one is "Data is data." Make it about your real life — your toys, your food, your family. 6. Press Check sentence. Then read what the checker says to you. If it says well done, smile! If it asks you to try again, change one small thing and press Check sentence again. Mistakes are how we learn. 7. Do steps 1 to 6 again for every word: data, computing device, sort, group, count, order. One word at a time. Do not rush — six words is a lot of good work. 8. When every word is done, press I explored the computing words at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have really done them all. 9. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of our words. Press Start on the first slide. 10. On each slide, do the same things: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning your own way, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. 11. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 12. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the computing words, and the last slide's finish button too. Then you have all six detective words in your pocket! Ready for word one? Tell me what you think data means, and let's start. 🕵️

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello, my Data Detective! Today we are on the Explore the Concept page. This page has 6 little discoveries about data. Data means information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds. You will look, think, and type your own idea. By the end, you will be able to sort things into groups, count them, and read a block graph. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up nearby to help you type. Here is what I expect from you: try your own idea first, even if it feels wobbly. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs — little buttons with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1. A discovery opens. Read the little story and look at the picture. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to LOOK carefully before you type anything. 2. Now read the discovery question. Think for a moment. Then type your idea in the box. Use your own words — even a few words is fine. Then press Check my idea. I expect a real try from you, not an empty box. 3. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint. Read the hint slowly, then change your answer a little and press Check my idea again. When it says Exactly!, the tab gets a tick. Well done — that tick is yours. 4. Now press tab 2 and do the same three things: look, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tab 3, tab 4, tab 5 and tab 6. One tab at a time, please. Six tabs, six ticks. 5. When every tab has a tick, look under the page. There is a deck of slides — the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — like a path. 7. Keep going, slide by slide, until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. I am right here with you. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello, data detective! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures of our big ideas. Some of them move! Looking at a picture helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what data, sort, count and order mean. You need your eyes, your finger to tap, and your voice to say the words out loud. That is all. Let's look at that together. There are 5 models, then the captions, then one button at the end. Here are all the steps. Step 1: Find the first model. It is called "Data is all around us". Tap it. If it moves, drag it slowly with your finger to turn it around. Press any buttons on it and watch what changes. I expect you to say out loud one thing that is data — like the number of mangoes in your bowl. Step 2: Go to model 2, "Sorting into groups". Drag it and press its buttons. Watch how the things go into groups. Remember: sort means to put things into groups that are the same in some way. I expect you to point at one group and say how they are the same — "these are all red". Step 3: Go to model 3, "Count each group and make a block graph". Turn it and press its buttons. Look at the rows of blocks. One block means one thing. I expect you to point to the longest row and say, "this group has the most". Step 4: Go to model 4, "Putting things in order". Drag it to turn it. Order means putting things in a line — small to big, or 1, 2, 3. I expect you to point at the smallest one first, then the biggest one last. Step 5: Go to model 5, "Be a data detective!". Turn it and press its buttons. This one shows all the detective steps: ask, collect, count, colour the graph, read the answer. I expect you to say the first thing a data detective does — ask a question! Step 6: Now the captions. A caption is the little bit of writing under each picture. Go back to model 1 and read the caption. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Say it along quietly with the voice. Step 7: Do the same for models 2, 3, 4 and 5. Read each caption, press Listen, and say it with the voice. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 8: When you have looked at all 5 models and heard all 5 captions, scroll to the bottom. Press the button that says I explored the models. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models and the page shows it is done. That button is yours to press — I cannot press it for you! Start with Step 1 now, and tell me when you have looked at the first model. 🕵️

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello, my Data Detective! Today we are on the Learn the Method page. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. On this page there are 5 methods from our unit — like sorting into groups, counting, making a block graph, and putting things in order. We do this so your brain learns the order of the steps, just like a real detective follows clues. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Ready? Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first method box on the page. Read the first step out loud. If a word is tricky, ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to say each step out loud before you press — saying it helps you remember it. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Say every new step out loud, slowly. Do not rush and do not skip. Keep going until the page says Method complete. That is how you know that method is finished. 3. Now do the very same thing for the next method. Read the first step, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and keep going until it says Method complete. I expect you to finish all 5 methods this way, one at a time, from the top of the page to the bottom. 4. When all 5 say Method complete, scroll down. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide shows one method again. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on that slide to move through the steps, saying each one out loud. 5. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Keep going slide by slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when every method says Method complete, and the last slide has had its finish button pressed. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you press your first Show me the next step, and tell me what the step said. I will check it with you. 🕵️

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello, my Data Detective! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with all the thinking shown, like watching me solve it on the board. We do this so you learn HOW to think, not just the answer. You need your eyes, your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. Here is our plan — six examples, then the slides at the bottom. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Now think for a moment: what would YOUR answer be? Say it out loud or write it down. I expect you to try first, even if you are not sure. Trying first is what makes the next part work. 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read it slowly, line by line. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? Did I miss a bit? If it is different, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. I expect you to notice ONE thing the solution shows that you did not think of. 3. Do the same for all six worked examples: read, think, then press Show worked solution. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It tells you how many you have opened. The page is finished when all six are open, so keep going until the counter says six. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one slide each. On the first slide, press Start. This is a second go at the same ideas, and second goes make our brains strong. 5. On each slide, do exactly what you did before: read the question, think of your answer, then press the button to show the solution. Take your time — there is no rush. 6. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all six opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready to start with worked example one? Tell me what you think the answer is, and I will help you check it. 😊

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello, data detective! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our reading page. 📖

Here is what this page is. It shows little examples from our unit about data. Data is a fancy word for information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds. In Grade 1 we do not type real computer code yet, so our examples are short and easy, like counting fruit or sorting things into groups. We read each one and say what it means. Why we do it: reading examples helps the idea stick, so later you can do it on your own. By the end, you will be able to say what data is and how we sort and count it. What you need: your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. A pencil and paper are nice too. What I expect from you: read slowly, say each line out loud, and tell me in your own words what it means. Guessing is allowed. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 things to do on this page. Here they are. Step 1. Read each example line by line. Point with your finger at one line at a time. After each line, say out loud, "This line means..." and finish the sentence. Do it well by going slowly, one line, then the next. I expect you to say something for every line, even a small guess. Step 2. Press the button that says Copy the code. This copies the example so you can try it yourself if you have paper or a device. Try it if you can — write it or say it again. Then press the button under that example to mark it done. I expect you to press it only after you have read the whole example. Step 3. Scroll down to the slides at the bottom. Press Start. You will see one example on each slide. Read the words on the slide, say what they mean, then mark it done. Press the arrow to go to the next slide. Do this for every slide. I expect you to keep going until there are no more arrows left. Step 4. When you have read every example, press Go to Build It. That button takes you to the next part, where you get to do the work yourself. Press it only when everything above is marked done. How you will know the page is finished: every example has been marked done, all the slides are finished, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me what your first example says. Take your time — there's no rush. 🌟

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello, my Data Detective! Today we are doing Guided Practice. Guided Practice means you try questions and I help you. There are 6 questions about data — counting groups, reading a block graph, and putting things in order. We do this so the words data, sort, count and order stick in your brain. Get a pencil, some paper, and your thinking cap. Here is your guide. 1. Read the first question carefully. Read it twice — slowly. Then work it out on paper or in your head. If it says count, touch each picture as you count: one, two, three. If it says which has the most, look for the longest row, not the top row. I expect you to think first, before you type. 2. Now type your answer in the box and press Check my answer. Type just what the question asks — a number like 4, or a word like mango. If the page says it is right, give yourself a little cheer! 3. If you feel stuck, do not worry. Press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint tells you a bit more. Try again after each hint before you press for another one. Mistakes are how we learn. 4. If the hints are still tricky, press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working — one small piece, not the whole answer. Read it, then finish the rest yourself. I expect you to try again after every hint or step. 5. Do this for every question — question 1, then 2, then 3, all the way to 6. Keep going on a question until it is right. Take your time — there's no rush. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Say your answer out loud too — that helps you remember it. 8. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 questions are right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me question 1 when you have read it, and we will look at that together. 🕵️

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello, data detective! Today we are on the Quick Reference page. This page is like a little card that holds all the big ideas of Unit 3 in one place. We read it so the words stay in your head: data, computing device, sort, group, count, order. By the end, you will be able to say what data is, all by yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. There are three steps. Here they are. Step 1: Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page from the top to the bottom. Read it slowly, one line at a time. Where you see a speaker button, press Listen and listen to the words. Say each key word out loud after you hear it. I expect you to go slowly and not rush — take your time, there's no rush. Step 2: Say the key facts in your own words. Now cover the page with your hand, or look away. Say out loud: what is data? What is a computing device? What does sort mean? A good answer sounds like your own talking, not the exact words on the page. For example: "Data is information. It can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds." I expect at least three key words said in your own way. If one is stuck, peek at the page, then try again. Step 3: Press Reference reviewed. This button is at the bottom of the page. Press it only after you have read the page and said the facts out loud. That press tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when you have listened, said the facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me when you have read it, and I will listen to your own words. 😊

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Hello, my Data Detective! Today we are on the Build It page. Here you do real detective work with data. Data just means information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds. You will sort things into groups, count them, colour a block graph, and put things in order. Get a pencil, some colours and a sheet of paper. Ready? Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first activity box. There are 8 activities on this page. Each one tells you what to use and what to do. Read it, then press Listen so you can hear it too. Now go and get the things it names — maybe your pencil, your colours, or some toys to sort. I expect you to have everything in front of you before you start. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Now do the activity. Really do it — with your hands, not just in your head. Sort the things into groups, or count them, or colour one block for each thing. Then write your answer in the box, or write what you noticed. A good answer says how many, or which group has the most. Even one word or one number is fine. 3. When that activity is done, press Mark complete under it. Then move to the next activity box and do the same thing: read, press Listen, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. I expect you to do all 8 that way, one at a time, not rushing ahead. When every one is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same build-it activities, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Do that activity just like before, and use the same buttons on the slide. 5. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. One dot lights up for the slide you are on. Do every slide, one by one. 6. On the last slide, press Finish activities. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the page is finished when all 8 activities show Mark complete, you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom, and you have pressed Finish activities on the last slide too. Start with step 1 now, and tell me when your first activity is done. I will check it with you. 😊

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text: Hello, data detective! Today I am your teacher for the Debug It page. A bug is a small mistake. On this page you will find mistakes about data, sorting, counting and order. Fixing a mistake is called debugging. We do this because finding your own mistakes makes your thinking strong. Mistakes are how we learn. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first card at the top of the page. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Each card shows a little bit of work with one bug hiding in it. I expect you to try first, all by yourself, before you press anything. Say out loud: "I think the mistake is..." Even a guess is good thinking. 2. Now press Show the bug. This tells you where the mistake is and what it should be. Look at it and compare it with your guess. Then say why it was wrong, in your own words, like "Data is not only numbers — pictures are data too." Then press the button to mark that bug done. I expect one sentence from you for each bug, said out loud. 3. Do the same for every card on the page. Go one card at a time: read, guess, press Show the bug, say why, mark it done. Take your time — there's no rush. Remember our unit words: sort means making groups, and order means putting things in a line, small to big. 4. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. This is a deck of cards with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. 5. On each slide, find the bug first with your own eyes. Then press Show the bug to check. Say why it was a mistake, then mark it done. I expect you to guess before you peek — that is the detective part! 6. Press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going: find, Show the bug, say why, mark done, arrow. Do this until there are no slides left. 7. When every card and every slide is done, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. I cannot press it for you — you press it, because it is your work. You will know the page is finished when all the cards are marked done, all the slides are finished, and you have pressed I practised debugging. Ready? Go and look at the first card, then tell me what you think the bug is. 🕵️

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello, data detective! Today we do a quick sprint called Computing Fluency. It is six short questions about the things you already learned in this unit — data, sorting, counting and order. We do it fast because these ideas should feel easy now, like knowing your own name. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper nearby. Ready? Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just to show you how quick you are. Do not worry about it. Take your time — there's no rush. Being right matters more than being fast. 2. Read question one. Say it out loud to yourself, slowly. Most questions are about the fruit block graph — mango, banana and apple. Some ask you to count. Some ask which row is longest or shortest. I expect you to look at the picture first, before you answer. 3. Type your answer in the box. Write just what the question asks. If it asks "how many", write a number, like 5. If it asks "which fruit", write the fruit name, like apple. 4. Press Check & continue. This shows if you were right and moves you to the next question. Press it once, then wait a moment. 5. Do the same for all six questions: read, look, type, press Check & continue. When a question asks you to put things in order, remember: order means a line, smallest first, like 1, 2, 3. 6. If a question feels tricky, remember our two words. Sort means making groups. Order means making a line. That little rhyme helps a lot. 7. At the end you will see how many you got right. You need most of them right to finish the page. Getting some wrong is fine — mistakes are how we learn. 8. If you got too few right, press Run the sprint again. Then try once more. This time go a bit slower and point at each block as you count it. 9. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. The page will tell you. Then you have done it! Now start with question one, and tell me how it goes. I am right here with you. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello, data detective! Today we are on the Solve Real Problems page. This is where you use what you know about data in real life — at home, at school, at the market and in our community. There are 4 problems. You will sort things into groups, count how many, and put numbers in order. Get a pencil and a piece of paper, and let's begin. What I expect from you: try each one by yourself first, say your thinking out loud, and write your answer in a full sentence like "There were 4 mangoes." Guessing fast is not the goal. Thinking is the goal! 1. Read the first problem slowly. Look at the little words that tell you what to do — sort, count, or order. If it says "circle the fruit", you are sorting into a group. If it says "how many", you are counting. If it says "smallest first", you are putting things in order. Point at each word with your finger as you read. I expect you to tell yourself what the question is really asking before you answer. 2. Now work it out on your paper. For counting, touch each thing one time as you say the number, so you do not count one twice. For sorting, ask "how are these the same?" For ordering, find the smallest first, then the next. Then type your working and your answer in the box and press Check answer. If your brain feels stuck, press Hint — that is a smart thing to do, not a silly thing. 3. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little clap! Then go to the next problem and do the same three things: read, work it out, press Check answer. If it says not quite, do not worry — mistakes are how we learn. Look again, fix one small thing, and press Check answer once more. 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same problems, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the problem the same way, using the same buttons. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — count them to see how many are left. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 4 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you can tell me one thing you counted or sorted today. I will be right here if you get stuck — just tell me which problem, and we will look at it together. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello, my clever Data Detective! Today we are on the Games page. These games are little quizzes about our unit words: data, sort, group, count and order. We play them so those words stick in your head like glue. All you need is your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here are your steps. Step 1: Look at the games on the screen. Pick one you like and press Start game. A question will come up with some answers under it. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then tap the answer you think is right. Do this for every round. Each round you get right gives you a star. I expect you to think before you tap — no fast guessing. If you are not sure, ask yourself: does this sentence match what our unit said? Remember, sort means groups, and order means a line. Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again. You will see the questions again, and you can win more stars. A game is mastered when all its stars are filled in. I expect you to keep going even if you got one wrong the first time. Mistakes are how we learn. Try to remember the right answer and use it next time. Step 3: Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again until that game has all its stars. Then move to the next game. I expect you to finish one game before starting another — that helps your brain hold the words. How you will know you are done: when every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not have to press anything special at the end. Off you go — press Start game on your first game. When you finish a round, come back and tell me how it went! ⭐

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello, my Data Detective! Today we are on the Stay Safe Online page. This page has three safety rules for using the internet. We do this because a good detective is a safe detective. By the end, you will know what to do if something online worries you. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what we will do. Three steps. Step 1: Read every rule slowly. Look at the first rule on the page. If you see a little speaker button, press Listen and hear the words. Read along with your finger. Then do the same for the next rule, and the next. Do not rush. I expect you to look at all three rules, not just one. The rules are about checking if something is true, telling a grown-up when something worries you, and being kind about other people's work. Step 2: Say each rule in your own words. This is the important part! Look at one rule. Then say it out loud like you are telling a friend. For example, if the rule says "tell someone if something worries you", you might say: "If I see something scary on the tablet, I stop and I tell my mum." Then give an example from your own life for each rule. I expect a full sentence out loud for every rule — not just a nod. Say it to your grown-up, or say it to me here. Step 3: Press the button. When you have read all the rules and said them in your own words, look at the bottom of the page. Press I know these rules. Only press it when you really have read them all — that button is your promise. How will you know the page is finished? When you have pressed Listen on every rule, said all three rules in your own words, and pressed I know these rules at the bottom. Then this page is done. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read the first rule. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello, data detective! Today we do the "Explain Your Thinking" page. On this page you tell me, in your own words, what you know about data, sorting, counting and putting things in order. We do it because saying an idea out loud makes it stick in your brain. You need your voice, and maybe a grown-up to help you type. There are 4 things to do, and I will take you through them one at a time. Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Under the prompt there are little words called key ideas, like data, sort or group. Those words are your helpers — your answer should use them. I expect you to point at each key idea and say it out loud before you write. Step 2. Now click in the answer box and write your explanation. Say three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example: "Data is information. The rule is that data can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds. So a photo of a goat is data." Then press Check your reasoning. If it says to add more, add one more sentence and press it again. I expect a try from you first — even one sentence is a great start. Step 3. Press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Do not copy it — just look and ask yourself, "Did I use the key ideas too?" If you missed one, add it to your box. Then do the same for prompt two, prompt three and prompt four. Four prompts, one at a time, no rush. Step 4. Now scroll under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: write your answer, press Check your reasoning, then Show model explanation. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all four explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Remember to press the buttons yourself — that is how the page saves your good work. Ready? Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me the first prompt, and we will do it together.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello, data detective! Today we do the Unit Challenge. It is 12 little questions about everything you learned in this unit: data, computing devices, sorting, counting and order. We do it to see what your brain has kept safe. You need your eyes, your reading voice, and a calm, slow mind. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what I expect from you: read every question twice, choose the answer YOU think is right, and try all 12 on your own. This one is your quiz, so I will cheer for you, but I cannot give you answers. That is the rule, and I know you can do it. 1. Look at the first question on your screen. Read it slowly, all the way to the end. Then read it one more time. Reading twice helps your brain hear it properly. 2. Now read every choice before you pick. Sometimes the second or third one is the best. Point at each one with your finger as you read it. 3. Think about the key word in the question. Is it asking about data (that means information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds)? Or about a computing device (a machine that works with data, like a phone or a watch)? The key word tells you where to look in your head. 4. If the question says sort or group, remember: sort means making groups where things are the same in some way. If it says order, remember: order means a line, small to big, or 1, 2, 3. Sort equals groups. Order equals a line. 5. Choose your answer by clicking it. Then press Next question. Do this for every question, one at a time, until you have done all 12. 6. If one question feels hard, take a breath and pick the answer that sounds most like what we learned. Guessing your best is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. 7. At the end you will see your score. You pass with more than half right. Look at it and tell me the number — I would love to hear it! 8. If your score is not high enough, do not feel sad. Press Try again and go through the questions once more. Second tries make us stronger. If you want, come back and ask me to explain any idea a different way first. 9. When your score is good, press Continue. That is the last button on this page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue and the page moves on. Then you have earned your Data Detective badge! 🕵️ Go and start question one now, and come back and tell me how it went.

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing your Unit Project. It is called My Data Detective Project. Here is what it is. You will ask people one question, write down their answers, count them, and colour a little graph. Then you will look at your graph and find the answer. That is what a real data detective does! Why we do it: it puts everything from this unit together — data, sort, count, and order. What you need: a pencil, some colours, a sheet of paper, and a few people to ask (family or friends). What I expect from you: ask each person only once, make one mark for every answer, colour one block for each person with no gaps, and then tell me the favourite fruit. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Read the Unit Project on your screen. It tells you what you will make and shows a list of things a good project has. Read the list slowly with your grown-up. That list is your checklist — it tells you exactly what "finished" looks like. I expect you to know your question before you start: which fruit do people like best — mango, banana or apple? Step 2: Now make your project, and tick each thing on the list as you do it. Do it in this order. First, ask each person: "Mango, banana or apple?" Second, make one mark on your paper for each answer. Third, count each group, touching each mark as you count. Fourth, colour one block for each person, starting at the bottom, with no gaps. Fifth, look at the longest row — that is your class favourite! Tick each item on the list only after you really did it. Step 3: When every single item on the list is ticked, press "My project is finished". Do not press it early. Press it only when your graph is coloured and you can point to the favourite fruit. That press is what saves your work on the page. You will know the page is finished when all the items on the list are ticked and you have pressed "My project is finished". Ready? Tell me your question and who you will ask, and we will start Step 1 together. 🕵️

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's start Unit 4. It is called "Be a Designer". This page is the Unit Overview. That means it tells you what the unit is about before we begin. It is like looking at a picture of a cake before you bake it. Doing this helps your brain get ready. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 things to do on this page. Here they all are. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen and read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let it read to you. Listen all the way to the end. I expect you to hear or read two big words: algorithm, which means steps in the right order, and outcome, which means what happens. Try to spot them! Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the screen. Just talk, like you are telling a friend. You could say something like, "I think I will learn to make a character move." A good answer has one idea and your own words. I expect one or two sentences, said out loud or typed to me. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have read the page and said your idea, find the button that says Continue and press it. That takes you to the next part, where we really start learning. I expect you to press it only after Step 1 and Step 2 are done. You will know this page is finished when you have listened, said your own idea, and pressed Continue. Then the new page will open. That is how you know it worked! Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read it. 🙂

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello, my Program Designer! Today we get our tools ready. This page is called Tools and Setup. It tells you what you need for Unit 4, "Be a Designer". In this unit you will join coloured blocks to make a character move. Blocks are picture instructions. So first we make sure your tablet or computer is ready. What I expect from you: look at each thing, try it once, and ask your grown-up if you need help. There are 3 steps. Step 1: Read the Tools and Setup page. Read it slowly from the top. Your grown-up can read it with you. It tells you two tools. One is ScratchJr, an app for a tablet. The other is Scratch, a website. I expect you to point at each tool name and say it out loud. Step 2: Check each tool, one at a time. For ScratchJr: open the app on a tablet. Tap the house. Tap the plus sign to start a new project. Can you see the coloured blocks at the bottom? Good, that one is ready. If the app is not there, ask your grown-up to get it. It is free and made for children your age. Step 3: Check the other tool, Scratch. Ask your grown-up to open scratch.mit.edu on a computer or tablet. Click Create. Can you see blocks on the left side? Then it is ready too. You do not need to make anything yet. Just checking is enough. Only your grown-up should type the website. Step 4: Get your paper things ready. You will also need paper, a pencil and some colours. Put them next to you. We use them to plan our steps before we build. Good designers plan first! Step 5: Press the button. When your tools are all set up, press My tools are ready at the bottom of the page. Press it yourself, because that is how your work gets saved. I cannot press it for you. How you know the page is finished: you have looked at both tools, you have your pencil and paper, and you have pressed My tools are ready. Now tell me how you got on. Which tool did you find first? 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called The Lesson, in Unit 4: Be a Designer. Here is what it is. The page has 5 short ideas about coding. They teach you one big thing: when we change the steps, we change what happens. By the end you will know what an algorithm is, and how a blue block, an orange block and a yellow block change what a character does. Here is what I expect from you. Read slowly. Say things out loud. Try each example with your fingers, your toys, or your feet. It is fine to go slowly. Take your time — there's no rush. Now here are all the steps. There are 4. Step 1. Read the first concept, then press Listen. The Listen button reads it to you. Read with your eyes while you listen with your ears. Do this for every concept, one at a time, from the first to the fifth. I expect you to stop after each one and think: what is this idea about? If a word feels hard, say it again with the Listen button. Step 2. Say the example out loud, then try it yourself. For example, if it says "move right 3", say "hop, hop, hop" and hop 3 times, or hop your finger along 3 stones. Then change the number and try again with 5. I expect you to use your own things — buttons, blocks, toy cars, or your own feet. That is how the idea sticks. Step 3. When you have read all 5 concepts, press the button that says I studied the concepts at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you really did read them all. I expect you to be able to tell me one thing you learned before you press it. Step 4. Go to the slides under the page. There is a small deck of slides with the same 5 ideas, one idea on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Use the same buttons on each slide. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going until the last slide, and there press the finish button. How you will know the page is finished: you have pressed Listen on all 5 concepts, you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. All the dots will be behind you. Ready? Start with Step 1 now, and tell me when the first concept is done. 🙂

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello, designer! Today we learn the special words for Unit 4, Be a Designer. These are the words we use when we make a program. When you know them, you can talk about your code like a real programmer. You will need your voice, your eyes, and your fingers for typing. Let's start with something small. 1. Look at the first word card on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to hear it once, then say it back quietly to yourself. Do this for one word at a time — do not rush ahead. 2. Now say the word out loud in a big, clear voice. Then say the meaning in your OWN words, not the page's words. For example, for the word step you might say, "a step is one thing I do." Then type a sentence with the word in the box and press Check sentence. A good sentence uses the word properly and tells me something real, like "My algorithm has three steps." Read what the checker says to you, and if it asks you to try again, change your sentence and press Check sentence one more time. Do steps 1 and 2 for every word on the page — there are ten words, like algorithm, step, outcome, change, speed, program, block, run, predict and ScratchJr. 3. When you have listened to every word and typed a sentence for every word, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the computing words. Only press it when you really have done them all. That button tells the page you finished this part. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons as before: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning your own way, and type your sentence, then press Check sentence. 5. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which word you are on and how many are left. Take your time; there is no rush. 6. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the deck. You will know the whole page is finished when two things are true: you have pressed I explored the computing words, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with word number one and press Listen. Tell me when you have done it, and tell me your sentence — I will check it with you. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello, my Designer! Today we explore together. This page is called Explore the Concept. It has 6 little discoveries. Each one shows you a picture and asks you one question. You think, you type your idea, and the page tells you if you got it. We are doing this so you learn the big idea of Unit 4: when we change the steps, we change what happens. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your fingers for typing. A grown-up can sit near you to help with typing. Here is what I expect from you: try your own idea FIRST, before any hint. Even a small guess is good. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1. A discovery opens up. Read the little story and look at the picture or model. Take your time — there's no rush. Good looking means you can tell me out loud what you see. Step 2. Now read the discovery question under the picture. Think first. Count with your finger if it is about frogs and steps. Then type your idea in the box. Write a few words, not just one letter. Then press Check my idea. Step 3. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint. Read the hint slowly. Then change your idea a little bit and press Check my idea again. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a tick. That tick means: done and correct! Step 4. Press tab 2 and do the same three things: look, think, type, press Check my idea. This one is about fast and slow. Remember my teacher tip: fast means quick, it does not mean far. Step 5. Press tab 3. This one is about how far a frog goes. Look at the two numbers of steps. The bigger number goes further. Type your idea and press Check my idea. Step 6. Press tab 4. This one is about ScratchJr blocks and their colours. Yellow, blue, orange, red — each colour does a different job. Match them, type your idea, and press Check my idea. Step 7. Press tab 5. This one asks you to predict. Predict means guess before you run it. Read the blocks like a story, from the first block to the last. Type your guess and press Check my idea. Step 8. Press tab 6. This one is the ScratchJr try-it. If you have a tablet, open ScratchJr and make a character move. Then type what happened and press Check my idea. If you have no tablet, type what you think WOULD happen. Step 9. Check all six tabs. Every tab should have a tick. If one has no tick, press it and finish that question. That is how you know the top part of the page is done. Step 10. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides. They show the same six discoveries, one on each slide. This is your practice round, to make the learning stick. Step 11. On the first slide, press Start. Read it, think, type your idea, and press Check my idea, just like before. Use Hint if you need one. Step 12. Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Do every slide the same way. Step 13. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How you will know the page is finished: all six tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the whole Explore the Concept page is complete. Ready? Press tab 1 now, and tell me what you see. I am right here. 🐸

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello, my Program Designer! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of the big ideas in Unit 4. Some of them move, so you can drag them and press their buttons. We do this so you can SEE what a step, a speed and a block really do — seeing helps your brain remember. By the end you will be able to say each idea in your own words. All you need is your eyes, your finger, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are 7 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Find the first model, "Steps in order (what is an algorithm?)". Look at it slowly. If it moves, drag it with your finger to turn it, and press its buttons. Then read the caption under it and press Listen. I expect you to point at the steps and count them out loud, 1, 2, 3 — in order. Step 2: Go to the second model, "Change the steps, change what happens". Drag it and press its buttons. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say what changed when you pressed a button — did it go faster, further, or a different way? Step 3: Go to the third model, "Turning steps into blocks (meet ScratchJr)". Drag it to turn it and press its buttons. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to name the colours you see: yellow starts, blue moves, orange is speed, red stops. Step 4: Go to the fourth model, "Change a block, change the outcome; and guess first". Before you press anything, guess out loud what will happen. Then press the buttons and see. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect a guess FIRST, then a check. That is what predict means. Step 5: Go to the fifth model, "Be a Program Designer (the Boat project)". Drag it and press its buttons. Read the caption and press Listen. I expect you to say what your boat does, like "my boat sails slowly to the right". Step 6: Now check yourself. Did you look at all five models? Did you press Listen under every caption? If you missed one, go back and do it now. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 7: When all five are done, press the button at the bottom that says "I explored the models". That button is how your work is saved, so only you can press it. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed "I explored the models" at the bottom. Then come and tell me which model was your favourite, and why. 🙂

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello, designer! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Code Examples. Code examples are little programs written down as a list of blocks. We read them like a story, from the top line to the bottom line. We are doing this so you can look at blocks and know what will happen before you even run them. That is called predict. You need your eyes, your finger to point with, and your voice to say each line out loud. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here are the steps. There are four. Step 1: Read each code example. Put your finger on the first line and say what it does out loud. Remember the colours: yellow means start, orange sets the speed, blue moves the character, red means end. So "Move Right (11) (blue)" means the character moves right eleven steps. I expect you to say something for every single line, not just look at it. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Press Copy the code. That copies the blocks so you can build them in ScratchJr on a tablet if you have one. Try making the same program and tap the green flag to run it. Then press the button under the example to mark it done. I expect you to only press it after you have read all the lines. Step 3: Go down to the slides at the bottom of the page. Press Start. One example shows on each slide. Read that code the same way, out loud, then mark it done, then press the arrow to go to the next one. I expect you to read every slide, not skip ahead. Step 4: When you have read every example, press Go to Build It. You will know the page is finished when every example is marked done and you have pressed Go to Build It. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read the first example.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello, my little Program Designer! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with all the thinking already shown. It is like watching me do one, then doing one yourself. We do this so you learn how to think about steps, speed and blocks. Then the quiz will feel easy! You need your eyes, your finger for counting, and maybe a pencil and paper. Ready? Here are your steps. Step 1: Look at the first worked example. Read the question slowly. If you cannot read a word, ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know what the question is asking before you do anything else. Step 2: Try it yourself first, in your head or on paper. Say your answer out loud, like "I think the 8-step frog goes further." Even a guess is good. Trying first is the part that makes your brain grow. Step 3: Now press Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line with your finger. Ask yourself: is my answer the same? I expect you to compare, not just peek. Step 4: If your answer was the same, say "Yes! I got it." If it was different, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Look for the one small bit that was different, and say it out loud. Step 5: Do the same for worked example 2, then 3, then 4, then 5, then 6. Every time: read, try it yourself, then press Show worked solution and compare. Six examples, one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 6: Look at the counter at the top of the page. It counts how many examples you have opened. When it shows all six are open, the top part of the page is done. If a number is missing, go back and find the example you did not open. Step 7: Now scroll down to the slides under the page. There is a little deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8: On each slide, do the same thing as before: read the question, say your answer, then press the show button to see the working. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Step 9: Look at the little dots under the slide. They show where you are in the deck. Keep pressing the arrow on the right until you reach the last slide. Step 10: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? Two things: the counter at the top shows all six examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Off you go with Step 1. Tell me when you have read the first question, and tell me your own answer before you open the solution. 🌟

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello, designer! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to do a job, step by step. On this page there are 5 methods. They show you how to work with steps in order, how changing a step changes what happens, how to turn steps into blocks in ScratchJr, and how to guess first before you run. By the end, you will know how to read a method one step at a time — just like a computer does. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Let's begin! 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step out loud. Then press "Show me the next step" to see the next one. Do it slowly. I expect you to say the step out loud, not just look at it — hearing it helps it stick in your head. 2. Keep pressing "Show me the next step" again and again. Say each new step out loud as it appears. Keep going until the page says "Method complete". That means you have reached the end of that method. I expect you to press it every time and not skip ahead. Take your time — there's no rush. 3. Now do the same for every method. There are 5 of them. For each one: read step one out loud, press "Show me the next step", keep going until it says "Method complete". When all 5 say "Method complete", the top part of the page is done. I expect all five, not just your favourite one! 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods on it. On the first slide, press "Start". Then use the same buttons on the slide to move through the steps, saying them out loud. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — they help you see how many slides are left. Keep going slide by slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 5 methods say "Method complete", and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. When you are done, come back and tell me one thing you learned. I would love to hear it! Off you go — start with method one. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello, my designer! Today we are on the Guided Practice page. This page has 6 little questions about our Unit 4 words: algorithm, step, speed and blocks. We do it so you can practise what you learned — thinking about steps in order, and how changing a step changes what happens. By the end, you will be able to answer all 6 on your own. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: try first, then check. Guessing without thinking is not our way. Reading the question twice is our way. Step 1. Read the first question slowly. Say it out loud if that helps. Work the answer out in your head, or draw it on paper. If it is about frogs and steps, use your finger and count the hops. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Type your answer in the box. Use short, simple words, like "a set of steps" or "the fast hare". Then press Check my answer. I expect you to type your OWN idea first, before any hint. Step 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint helps a little more. Press it one at a time and think in between. Do not press all three at once. Step 4. If you are still stuck after the hints, press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working — just one small piece, not the whole answer. Read it, then try typing your answer again yourself. Step 5. If your answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, look at what it is really asking, then type a new answer and press Check my answer again. Step 6. Do this same thing for all 6 questions, one after the other, until every question is right. That is when the top part of the page is finished. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. I expect you to try the answer yourself first, every time. Step 9. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done, designer! You will know the page is finished when all 6 questions are marked right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me what question 1 says, and let's start together.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Quick Reference. It is like a little pocket of our best words and facts from Unit 4, all on one page. We read it to help the words stick in our head, so we remember them next time. You need your eyes, your reading voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here are the three steps. Step 1: Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page slowly, from the top to the bottom. You will see our unit words like algorithm, step, outcome, speed and predict. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Do it well by reading one line, stopping, and thinking "do I know this?" I expect you to read every line, not just look at the pictures. Step 2: Say the key facts in your own words. Now cover the page with your hand, or look away. Say out loud what an algorithm is. Say what happens when we change a step. You do not need the same words as the page — your own words are best. A good answer sounds like: "An algorithm is steps in order," and "If I change a step, what happens changes." I expect you to say at least two facts out loud, in a full sentence. Step 3: Press Reference reviewed. Go to the bottom of the page. When you have really read it and said your facts, press the button that says Reference reviewed. Only press it after Step 1 and Step 2, because that button tells the page you did the work. I expect you to be honest — pressing it means "I read it and I can say it."

You will know the page is finished when you have read every line, said two facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Ready? Start Step 1 now, and tell me when you have read it. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Build It. Build It means you do things, not just read. There are 8 little activities. In them you will hop a frog, spot fast and slow, and make a boat sail in ScratchJr. We do this because a designer learns by trying: when we change the steps, we change what happens. Get these ready: a pencil, some paper, and a tablet with ScratchJr for the last few. A grown-up can sit with you. What I expect from you: try each one yourself first, count carefully with your finger, and write what you noticed in your own words. Even one short sentence is great. Step 1. Look at the first activity on the page. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen all the way to the end. Then go and get the things it names, like your pencil and paper.
