Do this for each new activity as you reach it. Step 2. Now do the activity. Take your time, there is no rush. Then write your answer in the box. A good answer says what you did or what you saw, like "The frog landed on stone 4." If it is a ScratchJr one, write what happened when you tapped the green flag. Step 3. When that one is done, press Mark complete under that activity. Then start the next one the same way: Listen, do it, write, Mark complete. Keep going until all 8 have been marked. When every one is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do that activity and use the same buttons on the slide. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 5. Keep going slide by slide until the dots show you are at the last one. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when all 8 activities show as marked complete, you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom, and you have pressed Finish activities on the last slide too. Ready? Start with number one and press Listen. When you have done it, tell me what you wrote, and I will check it with you. 🐸

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text: Hello, my Program Designer! Today we are doing "Debug It". A bug is a little mistake in a program. Debug means to find the mistake and fix it. We do this because every programmer's code fails the first time — even mine! Finding bugs makes you a strong coder. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is our whole plan. There are 4 parts. 1. Look at the first card. Each card shows a tiny program with one bug hiding in it. Read it slowly, from the top block to the bottom block, like a story. Point with your finger at each block and say out loud what it does. Then ask yourself: "Does this do the right job?" I expect you to make a guess before you press anything — even a wrong guess is good thinking. 2. Now press Show the bug. It will show you where the bug is and what it should be. Read it, then say out loud WHY it was wrong. Use your own words, like "the yellow start block was not first" or "the blocks had a gap". Then press the button to mark that bug done. I expect one sentence from you for every card — saying why matters more than being right. 3. Next, scroll down to the slides at the bottom of the page. There is one bug on each slide. Press Start. Find the bug yourself first, then press Show the bug, then mark it done, then press the arrow to go to the next slide. Do this for every slide, one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. 4. When all the cards and all the slides are done, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. That button is yours to press, not mine — it saves your good work. Here are three bugs to watch for, because they hide a lot: the yellow start block must be first, blocks must click together with no gap, and fast means quick — it does not mean far. You will know the page is finished when every card is marked done, every slide is marked done, and you have pressed I practised debugging. Ready? Start with card one. Tell me what you think the bug is, and I will help you check.

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Computing Fluency. Fluency means knowing something so well that it comes quickly. On this page you will answer six quick questions about our unit, Be a Designer. It is like a little running race for your brain. You need your eyes, your fingers for typing, and your best quick thinking. A grown-up can sit beside you if you like. Here is what will happen, step by step. 1. Get ready first. Sit comfortably and look at the top of the page. There is a timer there, counting your time. Do not worry about the timer. Quick is nice, but right is better. 2. Warm up your brain. Say these three things out loud with me: an algorithm is steps in the right order; fast means quick, not far; a bigger number of steps goes further. These ideas will help you in nearly every question. 3. Read question one carefully. Read it twice, slowly. Then type your answer in the box. I expect a short, clear answer in your own words, not a guess you did not think about. 4. Press Check & continue. This tells the page you are done with that question and takes you to the next one. Press it only once, after you have typed your answer. 5. Do questions two, three and four the same way. Read, think, type, then press Check & continue. Some questions are about which one is faster, and which one goes further. Remember, those are two different things! Fast is about speed. Far is about the number of steps. 6. Do questions five and six the same way too. These ones may ask about the coloured blocks in ScratchJr. Picture them in your head: the yellow flag block is the GO block at the start, and the red block is the stop block at the end. 7. Look at your score at the end. You need most of the six right. If you got enough right, wonderful — you have finished! 8. If you got too few right, do not feel sad. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Run the sprint again and have another go. The second try is nearly always better, because your brain has just practised. 9. If a question feels too hard, come and tell me which one, and I will give you a small hint. I will not give you the answer, because the answer needs to come from you — I'll help you get there. 10. You will know the page is finished when a sprint has enough right and the page tells you so. Then come back and tell me your score, and we will talk about which part you were strongest at. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me when you have pressed Check & continue for the first time. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. Here is what it is. There are 4 little problems about our unit, Be a Designer. Each one asks you about steps, blocks, or speed. We do this so you can use what you know in real life, not just remember words. By the end, you will be able to look at a program and say what will happen. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your fingers for typing. Take your time. There is no rush. Here is what I expect from you. Read each problem twice. Then say your answer in a full sentence, like "The frog goes further because 8 is bigger than 2." I want your thinking, not just one word. Now, the steps. There are 4. Step 1. Read the first problem out loud, slowly. Ask yourself: what is this really asking me? Is it about the order of the blocks? Is it about speed? Is it about how far something goes? Point at the words with your finger as you read. When you know what it is asking, you are ready. Step 2. Work out your answer in your head or on paper first. Then type it in the box and press Check answer. Write your thinking too, not only the answer. If you feel stuck, press Hint and read it, then try again by yourself. I would love to see a sentence like "First the yellow block, because that one says GO."

Step 3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little cheer! Then go to the next problem and do Step 1 and Step 2 again. Do all 4 problems this way, one at a time. Remember our big rule: fast means quick, far means a long way. They are not the same. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it with the same buttons, Check answer and Hint. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 4 problems will say your answer is right, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your work saved, so please do press it — I cannot press it for you. Off you go with Step 1. Tell me what the first problem is asking, and we will check it together.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is our Games page for Unit 4, "Be a Designer". Games are how we practise. Each game asks you little questions about steps, blocks, speed and order. When you play, the words stick in your head. By the end you will know your Unit 4 words really well. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a comfy seat. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the games on the page. Pick one you like. Press Start game. A question will come up with some answers to choose from. Read it slowly, then pick the one you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right. I expect you to think first, not tap fast. If you are not sure, there is a clue to help you. 2. When the game ends, press Play again. You can play the same game more times. Each time you can earn more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep trying if you missed one. Mistakes are how we learn. Say the answer out loud to yourself before you tap it. 3. Now do this for every game on the page. Press Start game, play, then Play again until that game has all its stars. Then move to the next game. I expect you to finish one game before you start another. Take your time — there is no rush. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. The page finishes by itself when they are all mastered. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, then tell me how it went. 🌟

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello, my Grade 1 friend! Today we are learning our online safety rules. Being safe online is just as important as looking both ways before you cross the road. By the end of this page, you will know two big rules and be able to say them in your own words. You only need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Let's begin! 1. Read every rule slowly. Look at the first rule on the page. Read it word by word, out loud if you can. Where you see a little speaker, press Listen and hear the rule read to you. Then read the second rule the same way, and press Listen there too. I expect you to read both rules all the way to the end, not just look at them. Slow is good here — there is no rush. 2. Say each rule in your own words. Now cover the words with your hand and tell yourself the rule, but in YOUR way of talking. For rule one, you might say: "If something online makes me feel funny or scared, I stop and tell a grown-up I trust." For rule two, you might say: "Pictures and songs belong to the person who made them, so I ask and I say thank you." I expect a full sentence for each rule, not just one word. 3. Give an example from your own life. Next to each rule, think of a real thing that happened to you or could happen to you. For rule one, maybe: "If a video pops up that scares me, I close it and call Mum." For rule two, maybe: "My friend drew a cat, so I put her name on it, not mine." I expect one small, real example for each rule. Say it out loud — that helps it stick in your head. 4. Press I know these rules. When you have read both rules, said them your own way, and given your examples, look at the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I know these rules. Only press it after you have really done all the steps, because that button is your promise that you know them. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these rules and the page says it is done. Then come and tell me one rule you remember — I would love to hear it! Great work today, my careful little learner. 🌟

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today you are a Program Designer. That is a person who makes a program and then changes it to see what happens. In this Unit Project you will make a Boat sail across the sea in ScratchJr. Then you will change one block and watch the Boat do something new. We do this because it shows the big idea of our unit: when we change the steps, we change what happens. You will need a tablet with ScratchJr, and maybe a grown-up nearby to help you tap. Here are all the steps for this page. 1. First, read the Unit Project box on your screen. It tells you what to make and shows a list of things a good project has. That list is your tick list. Read each line slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know one thing before you start: my Boat must sail when I tap the green flag. 2. Open ScratchJr and tap the plus sign to start a new project. Pick a sea background, so your Boat has water to sail on. Then tap the plus at the top to add your Boat. A duck or a fish is fine too! 3. Drag your Boat to the LEFT side of the screen. This is important. If the Boat starts in the middle, it has nowhere to sail to. 4. Now join your blocks in a row, like a jigsaw. Start on Green Flag (yellow), then Set Speed slow (orange), then Move Right (blue), then End (red). Push them together with no gaps. If there is a gap, only the first block will run. 5. Tap the green flag to run it. Your Boat should sail slowly to the right. Well done — that is your first tick: my Boat sails across the sea when I tap the green flag. 6. Now change ONE block. Tap the orange Set Speed block and change slow to fast. But first, guess: will the Boat stop in the same place, or a new place? Say your guess out loud before you tap. Guessing first is a real tick on your list too. 7. Tap the green flag again. Watch carefully. The Boat is quicker, but it stops in the SAME place. Fast means quick. It does not mean far. That is two more ticks: I made my Boat go fast, and I made a guess before I ran it. 8. Now change the blue arrow block to Move Left instead of Move Right. Run it again. Your Boat sails the other way! That is your next tick: I changed the arrow and my Boat went the other way. 9. Go back to the tick list on your page and tick each thing you have done, one by one. Only tick it if you really did it. I expect you to check your Boat against every line. 10. When every single item on the list is ticked, press the button that says My project is finished. You will know the page is done when all the ticks are filled in and you have pressed My project is finished. Then you can say it proudly: I am a Program Designer! Ready to start? Tell me when your Boat is on the sea. 🚤

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello, designer! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just pick an answer. You say WHY. You use your own words to tell me how you worked it out. We do this because a real designer can explain their steps. When you can say why, the idea sticks in your head. You need your eyes, your thinking, and the box on the page to type in. A grown-up can help you type if you like. There are four steps. Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Under it you will see key ideas — small words like algorithm, step, outcome, change or speed. Those words are your helpers. I expect you to read the prompt out loud if you can, and say which key word you will use. Step 2. Now type your answer in the box. Write what you know, then the rule you used, then why your answer makes sense. For example: "I know the boat moves. The rule is fast changes the speed. So it goes quicker." Then press Check your reasoning. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check your reasoning again. I expect a full sentence, not one word. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This shows you a good answer. Compare it with yours. Did you use the key words too? It is fine if your words are different. I expect you to spot one thing the model answer says that you could add next time. Then do Step 1 and Step 2 again for prompt two, prompt three and prompt four. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has the same prompts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same things: read, type, press Check your reasoning, then Show model explanation. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when every explanation you wrote uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Go and read prompt one, then tell me which key word you will use. I am right here.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for the Unit Challenge. The Unit Challenge is the last part of Unit 4, "Be a Designer". It is a set of 12 questions about the things you learned: steps in order, changing steps, and blocks in ScratchJr. We do it so you can show what you know, and so we can see which bits you are strong at. You need only your eyes, your thinking, and a calm brain. A grown-up can sit with you and read the questions out loud if that helps. Here is what I expect from you: read every question twice before you choose, pick your own answer, and take your time. I will not tell you any answers — but I promise you can get this. Step 1. Read question one slowly. Look at the answer choices, one at a time. Say quietly to yourself, "does this one match?" When you are sure, tap the answer you think is right, then press Next question. I expect one careful choice, not a fast guess. Step 2. Keep going the same way for all 12 questions. Some questions ask what a word means. Think of our unit words: algorithm means steps in the right order, step means one thing you do, outcome means what happens, speed means how fast, block means one picture instruction, run means to make it go, predict means to guess first. Press Next question after each one. Step 3. Some questions ask about a mix-up, like "fast means far". Remember our floor game: fast means quick, and far means a long way. They are two different things. Think about which answer explains that clearly, then press Next question. Step 4. Some questions are about order. Remember: the yellow Green Flag block always goes first, and the red Stop block always goes last. Blocks must click together with no gap. Use that to help you choose, then press Next question. Step 5. If a question feels hard, read it again and look at the first few words of each choice. Choose the one that best matches what our unit taught. Do not leave a question empty — a thoughtful choice is always better than none. Then press Next question. Step 6. After the last question, your score will show. You pass with more than half right. Look at your score and feel proud of the questions you got right. Step 7. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing at all. Mistakes are how we learn. Read even more slowly the second time. Step 8. When your score is good, press Continue. That is the page finished! You will know you are done when you have pressed Continue and the page moves you on. Take your time — there's no rush. Come back and tell me how it went, and I will help you with any bit that felt tricky. 🌟

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 5. It is called "We Can Network". This page is the Unit Overview. That means it is a little peek at what we will learn. We will learn about a network — that is two or more computers or devices joined together, so they can talk and share. By the end of this page, you will know what is coming next. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 steps. Here they are. 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on your screen. If you see a little speaker button, press Listen. Then the words are read to you. Read along and listen at the same time. Listen for two special words: network and internet. I expect you to listen right to the end, without rushing. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, to me or to your grown-up. You do not need big words. A short answer like "I will learn how computers join together and talk" is perfect. I expect one or two sentences, in YOUR words, not copied from the screen. If you get stuck, start with "I think I will learn about..." and finish it. 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. This is the button at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have listened and said your sentence. I expect you to be ready to learn, with a pencil and paper near you, because soon we will draw a little network! You will know this page is finished when you have listened to the overview, said your own sentence out loud, and pressed Continue and the next page opens. Ready? Do step 1 now, and tell me when you have listened. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson page in Unit 5, "We Can Network". On this page you will learn five little ideas about networks. A network is two or more computers or devices joined together. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, name devices that can join, and tell me what the internet is. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, listen carefully, and say things out loud. Talking out loud helps the words stick. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see five concept cards. Read the first one slowly, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Read along with the voice. I expect you to read all five, one at a time, not in a rush. Step 2. Each card has an example. Say that example out loud in your own voice. Then try it your way. For example, point to two things at home, like a phone and a tablet, and say "these two are joined, so they make a network." I expect one out-loud sentence from you for each card. Step 3. When you have read all five cards, and said all five examples, press the button at the bottom that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after you have really read them all. That button tells the page you did the work. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has the same idea, one idea on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Listen and read that slide. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Use the same buttons on every slide, and on the last slide press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when two things are true: the I studied the concepts button has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me one thing you learned from the first card. Take your time — there's no rush.

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher. This page is called Tools & Setup. It is like packing your bag before a trip. It tells you what things you need for Unit 5, We Can Network. We do this first so that later, when we build networks, nothing stops us. You need your eyes to read, and a grown-up nearby if you want help. Here is what I expect from you today: read carefully, find your things one by one, and only say you are ready when you really are ready. That is what a good learner does. Ready? Here are the three steps. Step 1. Read the Tools and Setup page. Look at the words and pictures on the screen. Read them slowly, from the top to the bottom. If a word is hard, point at it and ask your grown-up to read it with you. For Unit 5 you will mostly need simple things: paper, a pencil, and some colours. You may also want playdough for our fun project later. I expect you to read every line, not just look at the pictures. Step 2. Check each tool or setting on the list. Go one thing at a time. Say the thing out loud, then go and find it. Like this: "Pencil... yes, I have it." Then: "Paper... yes." Then: "Colours... yes." If something is missing, tell your grown-up now, before we start the lessons. I expect you to touch or see each thing, not just guess. Step 3. Press "My tools are ready" at the bottom. When you have all your things next to you, scroll down to the bottom of the page. Find the button that says My tools are ready. Press it once. Only press it when it is true! That button is your promise that you are set up and ready to learn. You will know the page is finished when you have read it, found your things, and pressed My tools are ready. Then Unit 5 can begin. Off you go — find your pencil first. Tell me when you have it. 😊

words.label: Computing Words
words.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Computing Words page. On this page we meet the six special words of Unit 5: network, connect, communicate, device, share and internet. We learn them because these are the words we use to talk about computers joined together. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, your eyes, and your typing finger. Let's start! Step 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word and read what it means. Then press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Listen carefully — I want you to hear how the word sounds from beginning to end. Step 2. Now say the word out loud yourself. Say it slowly, then say it again a bit faster. It is fine to say it two or three times. A good try is when your mouth says it the same way the Listen button did. Step 3. Say the meaning in your own words. Do not copy the page — use your words. For example, for the word device you might say, "a machine like a tablet or a phone." I expect a short, simple meaning, said out loud. Step 4. Now type a sentence with the word in it, then press Check sentence. Make your sentence about your real life, like your home, your school or your family. A good sentence has the word in it and makes sense, like "My tablet is a device."

Step 5. Read what the checker says about your sentence. If it says well done, smile — you did it! If it asks you to change something, fix that one small thing and press Check sentence again. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 6. Now do steps 1 to 5 again for every word on the page: network, connect, communicate, device, share and internet. Do one word at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 7. When you have done every single word, press the button that says I explored the computing words at the bottom of the page. Only press it after all six words are done, because that button tells the page you finished your work. Step 8. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 9. On each slide, do the same things as before: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning, type your sentence and press Check sentence. Same job, new place — this is your practice. Step 10. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 11. Keep going, one slide at a time, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all six words have a checked sentence, you have pressed I explored the computing words, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with word one and tell me when you have pressed Listen. I am right here with you.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. On this page you will find out about networks. A network is two or more computers or devices joined together so they can talk and share. You will do six little discoveries. By the end you will be able to say what a network is, name devices that can join one, and say what the internet is. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your fingers for typing. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what I expect from you: try your own idea first, in your own words, even if it is short. A good answer uses our words like network, device, connect, share or internet. Guessing is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Look at the numbered tabs. Press tab number 1. Read the little story and look at the picture or model. Tell yourself out loud what you can see. Step 2. Now read the discovery question under it. Stop and think for a moment. Ask yourself: what do I already know about this? Step 3. Type your idea in the box. Write a short sentence, not just one word. For example, start with "A network is..." Then press Check my idea. Step 4. If it says Look again, that is okay. Press Hint, read it slowly, then change one part of your sentence and press Check my idea again. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a tick. Well done! Step 5. Now press tab number 2 and do the same three things: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going through tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6 the same way. Do one tab at a time. Step 6. When every tab has a tick, the top part of the page is finished. Look how far you have come! Step 7. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. They have the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, do just what you did before: read, think, type your idea, press Check my idea, and use Hint if you need it. Step 9. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going, one slide at a time. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when every tab has a tick and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab number 1 now, and tell me what you see. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Visual Models. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of the big ideas in Unit 5. Looking at a picture helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, and name devices that can join one. All you need are your eyes, your finger to drag and press, and your voice to say what you see. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here are your steps. Do one, then the next. 1. Look at the first model, "What is a network?". Touch it and drag it slowly to turn it around. Press its buttons to make it change. I want you to see the line that joins two devices — that line is the join. Then say out loud: "A network is two or more devices joined together."

2. Now the second model, "Which things can join a network?". Drag it and press its buttons again. Look for the devices: a laptop, a tablet, a phone, a smartwatch and a printer. Then point to one and name it. I expect you to name at least two devices you can see. 3. Next is the third model, "What a network lets us do". Turn it and press its buttons. Watch a message or a photo travel along the line. Then tell me one thing a network lets us do — send a message, share a photo, or share one printer. 4. Now the fourth model, "The internet, the biggest network of all". Drag it around slowly, because this one is big! Look at how many devices are joined, all over the world. Then say one thing we can do on the internet: chat with friends, share pictures, or play games. 5. Last is the fifth model, "Make a network". Turn it and press its buttons. This one shows a little network you could build yourself with playdough. I expect you to count the devices in it and say how many there are. 6. Under each model there is a caption — a short bit of writing that tells you what the picture shows. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listening and reading together helps the words stay in your memory. 7. Do step 6 for all five models, one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Good looking is slow looking, not fast clicking. 8. When you have looked at all five models and heard all five captions, press the button at the bottom that says "I explored the models". You will know the page is finished when you have pressed "I explored the models" and it shows as done. That button is yours to press — it saves your work, not mine. Ready? Start with step 1, then tell me what you see. 😊

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Code Examples. On this page you look at little examples one at a time. In our unit "We Can Network", the examples show how devices join together to make a network. A network means two or more computers or devices joined together. By the end you will be able to look at an example and say what it shows in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is what I expect from you: look carefully, say each part out loud, and press the buttons yourself. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Read each code example, line by line. Look at the first example on the page. Read it slowly, one line at a time, with your finger under each line. After each line, say out loud what you think it does. A good answer sounds like this: "This line joins the tablet to the phone." If you are not sure, say what you SEE first, like "I see a tablet and a line." That is a great start. Step 2. Press Copy the code, then try it yourself. Under the example there is a button that says Copy the code. Press it once. Now you can try it yourself if you have a screen to try it on. If you cannot try it on a screen, that is fine — draw it instead. Draw two devices on paper and join them with a line. Then press the button under the example to mark it done. I expect you to press it only after you have really read the example. Step 3. Do the slides at the bottom of the page. Scroll down. Under the examples there is a deck of slides, with one example on each slide. Press Start. Read the code on the slide slowly, the same way you did before. When you understand it, mark it done. Then press the arrow to go to the next one. Keep going until you have seen every slide. I expect you to say one sentence out loud for each slide, like "These two devices are joined, so they can share."

Step 4. Press Go to Build It. When you have read every example and every slide, press Go to Build It. This takes you to the making part, where you build your own network. Only press it when you have finished the reading — that is how good learners work. How you will know the page is finished: every example has been marked done, every slide has been marked done, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Now start with Step 1. Read the first example, and tell me what you think the first line does. I'm right here with you.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's learn the method together. This page is called "Learn the Method." A method is a way to do something, step by step — like the steps for washing your hands. Here you will see 5 methods about networks. A network is two or more devices joined together. By the end, you will be able to say the steps out loud all by yourself. You need your voice, and a grown-up close by if you want help reading. Here is what I expect from you: press one button at a time, say each step out loud, and take your time. There is no rush. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then say it out loud in your own words. When you are ready, press the button that says "Show me the next step." I expect you to say the step out loud before you press — that is how it sticks in your head. 2. Keep pressing "Show me the next step" again and again. Each press gives you one new step. Say every step out loud as it appears. Keep going until the page says "Method complete." That means you finished that one method. Well done! 3. Now do the very same thing for every method on the page. There are 5 in all. For each one: read the first step, say it out loud, press "Show me the next step," and keep pressing until you see "Method complete." I expect all 5 methods to say "Method complete" when you are done. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide holds one method again. Press "Start" on the first slide. Then use the same buttons on the slide, just like before, until that slide is done. To move on, press the arrow on the right side. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — count them if you like! Keep going slide by slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 5 methods say "Method complete," and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when your first method says "Method complete."

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page in Unit 5, We Can Network. Worked examples are questions with the answer already shown, step by step. We use them so you can try first, then check. By the end you will be able to say what a network is, name devices that can join one, and say what the internet is. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here are the steps. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question slowly, all by yourself. Say your answer out loud, or write it on your paper, before you look at any solution. I expect a guess from you every time — even a wobbly guess is good thinking. 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line and compare it with your own answer. Ask yourself: is my answer the same, nearly the same, or different? If it is different, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. 3. Do the same for all 6 worked examples. Read, think, answer, then press Show worked solution and compare. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It tells you how many you have opened. Keep going until every one is open. 4. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 5. On each slide, do the same thing as before: read the question, say your own answer first, then use the same buttons on the slide to see the solution. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 6 worked examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now start with step 1. Read worked example 1 and tell me your answer. Take your time — there's no rush.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today we are on the Quick Reference page. This page is like a little memory card for Unit 5, We Can Network. It puts all our big words and big ideas in one place. We do this so the words stay in your head, not just on the screen. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Here are our three steps. Step 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page from the top to the bottom, slowly. You will see our six words: network, connect, communicate, device, share, internet. Next to each word is what it means. Where you see a little speaker, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. I expect you to read every word once, and to press Listen at least one time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now cover the page with your hand, or look away. Say out loud: what a network is, and what the internet is. A good answer sounds like this: "A network is two or more devices joined together." And: "The internet is the biggest network in the world." I expect your own words, not the exact words on the page. Then name one device that can join a network, and one thing that cannot. You can say it to me, or to your grown-up. Step 3. Press Reference reviewed. This button is at the bottom of the page. Press it only after you have read the words and said the facts out loud. That press tells the page you are done. I cannot press it for you — the record of your work comes from you. You will know the page is finished when you have read all six words, said the facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read the page.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in Unit 5, We Can Network. This page gives you 5 small questions about networks. We do it so the big words stick in your head: network, connect, device, share, internet. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is and what we can do on the internet. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a pencil and paper if you like. Here is what I expect from you. Try each question yourself first. Answer in your own words — you do not need long sentences. If you get stuck, that is fine; use the hints, not a guess-and-rush. 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Think about it in your head, or say it out loud to your grown-up. You can write your idea on paper first. I expect you to think before you type — even ten seconds of thinking helps a lot. 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Keep it short and clear, like "two or more devices joined together". If you are stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints, so press it again if you need more. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try the hint first, before the next step. 3. Do this for every question, one at a time, until each one is right. If an answer is not right, do not worry — mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint, change your answer, and press Check my answer again. When all 5 questions are right, that part of the page is done. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, with Check my answer, Give me a hint and Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 5 questions are marked right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now, off you go — start with question one, and tell me what you typed. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Build It page. Build It means we make and do things about networks. A network is two or more computers or devices joined together. On this page you will circle, match, colour, draw, and even make devices from playdough. By the end you will be able to say what a network is, name devices that can join one, and say one thing we can do on the internet. You will need a pencil, some paper, colours, and playdough if you have it. A grown-up can sit with you. There are 8 activities on this page, plus the same 8 again on the slides at the bottom. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first activity box. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen carefully, then go and get the things it names, like paper and a pencil. I expect you to have your things ready before you start. Step 2. Do the activity with your hands. Circle the things that CAN join a network, and cross the things that cannot. A good answer circles the tablet, the phone, the printer and the laptop, and crosses the bicycle, the ball and the chair. Step 3. Now write in the box. Write your answer, or one thing you noticed. Even a few words is lovely, like "a bicycle cannot join". I expect one true sentence in your own words. Step 4. Press Mark complete under that activity. Only press it when you really did the activity and wrote in the box. That button tells the page you are done with that one. Step 5. Do the same three things for every activity: read and press Listen, do it, write in the box, then press Mark complete. Take your time. There is no rush. Step 6. Here is what each activity asks, so you know what a good job looks like. Match the Device: draw a line from each device to what it does. What Can a Network Do: colour send a message, share a photo, share a printer, and leave the silly one. On the Internet: circle chat with friends, share pictures, play games. Send a Photo: write 1, 2, 3 to put Maya's steps in the right order. Step 7. Draw a Little Network: draw two devices and join them with a line. Make your network: use playdough to make two or more devices, then join them with playdough strings. Tell your partner: point at your network, name each device, say they are joined so they can share, and say one thing you can do on the internet. I expect you to use our words: network, connect, device, share, internet. Step 8. When all 8 activities have Mark complete pressed, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Do not press it early. Press it only when every single one is marked. Step 9. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same build-it activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 10. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, do the activity, write in the box, then Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 11. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity shows Mark complete, and you have pressed Finish activities on the page and on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me when your things are ready. 😊

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Debug It. To debug means to find a mistake and fix it. On this page you will see cards. Each card has a little mix-up about networks — something that is not quite true. Your job is to spot it, like a detective with a magnifying glass. We do this because finding mistakes helps the right idea stick in your head. By the end, you will know what a network really is, and you will be able to fix wrong ideas all by yourself. What you need: your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a grown-up nearby. A pencil and paper are nice too, but not needed. What I expect from you: read each card slowly, guess the bug BEFORE you press anything, and say the fix out loud in your own words. Guessing wrong is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first card. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Ask yourself: is this true about networks? Remember, a network is two or more computers or devices joined together. If the card says something like "a network is just one computer", that is your bug. Try to find it yourself first, before you press any button. 2. Now press Show the bug. The card will show you where the mistake was and what it should say. Look at it and compare it with your guess. Then say out loud WHY it was wrong, like this: "It is wrong because one computer alone is not a network. You need two or more, joined together." Saying the why is the most important part. 3. When you have said the why, press the button to mark that bug done. That tells the page you finished this card. Then move to the next card and do the same three things again: find the bug, press Show the bug, say why. Do this for every card on the page. Take your time — there's no rush. 4. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom of the page. This is a little deck of cards, with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. It works just like the cards above, so you already know how! 5. On each slide, read the bug and think first. What is the mix-up? Then press Show the bug to check. Say the fix in your own words, then mark it done. After that, press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going, one slide at a time, until you have seen them all. 6. When every card and every slide is done, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. Do not press it early — press it only when you have really done them all. How will you know the page is finished? Every card will be marked done, every slide will have been shown, and the I practised debugging button will be pressed. That is the whole page complete! I am here beside you. If a card puzzles you, tell me which one, and I will give you a small hint — not the answer, because you can get this yourself. Ready? Start with card one. 🕵️

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is our Games page for Unit 5, "We Can Network". Games are how we practise. Each little game asks you questions about networks — joining devices, sharing, and the internet. Playing them helps the words stick in your head. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you: read each question slowly, think first, then choose. Guessing fast is not our way. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1: Look at the games on the page. Pick one and press Start game. Now questions come, one at a time. Read the question. Read every choice. Then tap the one you think is right. Every time you get a round right, you earn a star. If you are not sure, think back to our big rule: a network is two or more devices joined together. I expect you to try every round, even the tricky ones. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you more stars. Playing again is good — the same idea comes back, and your brain gets faster at it. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. Keep pressing Play again on that game until its stars are full. I expect you to stay with one game until it shines with all its stars. Step 3: Now do the same with every other game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again, fill up the stars. One game at a time, please — finish one before you start the next. I expect you to master them all, not just your favourite one. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not press anything special — the stars tell the story. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, then come and tell me how it went. 🌟

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for the Computing Fluency page. This page is a quick sprint. You will answer 5 short questions about networks, as fast as you can. We do it so the big words from Unit 5 — network, device, connect, share, internet — come to your mind quickly, without stopping to think hard. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, and what we can do on it, straight away. You need your eyes, your typing finger, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. What I expect from you: try every question by yourself, type a short answer in your own words, and do not worry about being perfect. Speed is nice, but a real try is better. Step 1. Warm up your brain first. Say these three things out loud to yourself: a network is two or more computers or devices joined together; a device is a machine like a tablet, a phone or a printer; the internet is the biggest network in the whole world. This little warm-up makes the sprint much easier. I expect you to say all three out loud before you start. Step 2. Start the sprint. Look at the top of the page — your time will show there and start counting. Read question one carefully, then type your answer in the box. A good answer is short, like one word or one small sentence. Then press Check & continue. Step 3. Keep going, one question at a time. After each answer you press Check & continue to move on. Do not stop to worry if one feels tricky — write your best guess and keep moving. I expect you to answer all 5, not to skip any. Step 4. Think about the words as you go. Some questions ask you to finish a sentence, like "the internet is the biggest ______". Some ask true or false, like "a bicycle can join a network". Remember: only things made to connect can join, so a ball, a chair or a bicycle cannot. I expect you to use the unit words in your answers. Step 5. Look at your score at the end. You need most of them right to pass the sprint. If you got enough right — brilliant work! If you got fewer, that is completely fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 6. Try again if you need to. Press Run the sprint again. You will get the questions once more, and this time you will already know the tricky ones. I expect you to try again cheerfully, not sadly. How you will know the page is finished: when one sprint has enough right answers, the page counts as done. That is your finish line. Ready to begin? Tell me when you have said your three warm-up sentences out loud, and I will cheer you into question one.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Stay Safe Online" page. This page has four safety rules. They help you stay happy and safe when you use a tablet, a phone or the internet. Remember, the internet is the biggest network in the world — lots of people are on it, so we need good rules. By the end, you will be able to say each rule in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. 1. Read every rule slowly. Look at the first rule on your screen. If you see a little speaker, press Listen and hear the words read out loud. Then read the rule again with your eyes. Do this for all four rules, one at a time — no rushing. I expect you to finish one rule before you start the next one. 2. Say each rule in your own words, and give an example from your own life. Say it out loud, even if you are alone. For example, for the rule about private information you might say, "I keep my name and where I live secret," and your example could be, "I would not type my house address into a game." A good answer has two parts — the rule in your words, and one example from your day. I expect you to do this for all four rules. 3. Press I know these rules at the bottom. Only press it after you have read all four rules and said them in your own words. That button tells the page you are done, so it must be you who presses it. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Listen on every rule, said all four rules in your own words with an example, and pressed I know these rules. One last thing from your teacher: if anything online ever worries you, tell a grown-up you trust straight away. Please tell your parent or teacher — this is exactly what grown-ups are for. Now go and start step 1. Tell me when you have read the first rule, and I will check it with you.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. On this page you use what you learned about networks in real life. There are 4 little problems about devices, sharing, and the internet. Doing them helps the words stick in your head: network, connect, device, share, internet. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your fingers for typing. A grown-up can sit with you to help with the typing. Here is what I expect from you. Read slowly. Think first. Then type your own answer in a full sentence, like "A bicycle cannot join a network." Your own words are always best. Step 1. Look at the first problem on the page. Read it two times, slowly. Ask yourself: what is this question really asking me? Is it asking about a device, or about the internet, or about sharing? I expect you to know what the question wants before you type anything. Step 2. Now think of your answer in your head. Say it out loud to yourself first. If the question says true or false, choose one and think why. Good thinking sounds like this: "False, because a bicycle is not a device."

Step 3. Type your answer in the box. Write your thinking too, not just one word. Then press Check answer. I expect a full sentence, with a capital letter at the start if you can. Step 4. If you feel stuck, do not worry. Press Hint. The hint gives you a little help, not the answer. Read the hint, then try again yourself. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 5. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done! Now go to the next problem and do the same thing: read twice, think, type, press Check answer. Keep going until all 4 problems say you are right. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is your practice round, so you can show me you really know it. Step 7. On each slide, do the same as before: read, think, type, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many are left. Step 8. On the last slide, do the problem, then press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when all 4 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read problem one now, and tell me what you think it is asking you. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just pick an answer. You tell me HOW you know. That is what real computer thinkers do. It helps the idea stick in your head. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. What I expect from you: use our unit words in your answers — network, connect, communicate, device, share, internet. Say what you know, then say why. Even one or two sentences is great. Step 1: Read the prompt. There are 4 prompts on this page. Read the first one slowly. Under it you will see some key ideas, like network or device. Those little words are your helpers. I expect you to read the prompt twice before you write. Reading twice helps you see what it is really asking. Step 2: Write in the box, then press Check your reasoning. Click inside the answer box and type your thinking. A good answer has three little parts: what you know, the rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example, for a bicycle you might write: "A bicycle cannot join a network. A network needs devices that connect. A bicycle is not a device, so it cannot connect." Then press Check your reasoning. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check your reasoning again. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3: Press Show model explanation and compare. This opens a good example answer. Read it and look for the key ideas. Ask yourself: did I use those words too? If you missed one, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. You can go back, add that word, and check again. Do Steps 1, 2 and 3 for all 4 prompts. Step 4: Do the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same prompts. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons as before: write your answer, press Check your reasoning, and press Show model explanation. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? When all 4 explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! One last thing from me: I expect you to try writing before you peek at the model answer. Your own words matter most. Ready? Read prompt one, and tell me what you think it is asking. 😊

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing our Unit 5 Project: We Can Network. Here is what it is. You will make your very own network out of playdough. A network is two or more devices joined together. You will make devices, join them, and then talk about them. We do this because making something with your hands helps the idea stick in your head. What I expect from you: try your best, use your own words, and tell me when each step is done. You will need playdough, paper, and a pencil. A grown-up can sit with you. Step 1. Read the Unit Project box on your screen. It tells you what you will make. Under it is a list of things a good project has. Read the list slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know two things after reading: what you are making, and how many devices you need. You need two or more. Step 2. Now make your project. Roll playdough into devices. Maybe a tablet, a phone, and a printer. Make them flat and neat so we can tell them apart. I expect at least two devices. Step 3. Join your devices with thin playdough strings. Every device must touch a string. That string is the connection. Now you have a network! Step 4. Draw your playdough network on paper. Draw each device, then draw the lines that join them. Neat lines, please. Step 5. Point at each device and say its name out loud. "This is my tablet. This is my phone." I expect you to name every one. Step 6. Tell your grown-up or partner one thing you can do on the internet. Chat with a friend, share a picture, or play a game. Say it in a full sentence. Step 7. Look at the tick list on the page. Tick each thing you have done. If one is not ticked, go back and finish it first. Step 8. When every box is ticked, press My project is finished. You will know the page is done when all the boxes have ticks and you have pressed My project is finished. Then come back and tell me what you made — I would love to hear it!

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is our Unit Challenge. It is like a friendly game to show what you know about networks. You do not need paper — just your eyes, your thinking, and one finger to press the buttons. Take your time. There is no rush. Here is what we will do, step by step. Step 1. There are 12 questions. Read the question slowly. Then read every answer choice before you pick one. Think back to our unit words: network means two or more devices joined together, connect means to join, share means to let others use the same thing, and internet means the biggest network in the whole world. Pick the answer you think is right by pressing it. I expect you to try every question yourself — even the tricky ones. I will not tell you answers, but I can give you a hint if you ask. Step 2. After you pick your answer, press Next question. Then do the same thing again: read, think, choose, press Next question. Keep going until all 12 are done. If one question feels hard, take a breath and read it one more time. Reading the question twice really helps. Step 3. At the end you will see your score. You pass when more than half are right. I expect you to look at your score and tell me how you did. If your score is not high enough, that is okay — mistakes are how we learn. Press Try again and have another go. You can ask me to explain any idea before you try again. Step 4. When your score is good enough, press Continue. That finishes the page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen a passing score, and pressed Continue. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me when you are done or if you get stuck. 🙂

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. Our unit is called Be a Problem Solver. By the end of it, you will put steps in the right order, find a wrong step, and fix a mistake in a program. A mistake in a program has a special name: a bug. Finding it and fixing it is called debugging. You do not need anything for this page — just your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Let's go! 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page and read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen. Then the page will read it to you while you follow along. I expect you to listen to the whole thing, not rush. Try to catch two words: algorithm, which means a list of steps in the right order, and bug, which means a mistake in a program. A grown-up can read with you if you like. 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the words on the page — use your own. You can say it out loud, or say it to me here in the chat. A good answer is one or two little sentences, like "I will learn to put steps in order" or "I will learn to fix a mistake." I expect you to try, even if it is not perfect. There is no wrong answer here, because it is your own thinking. 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have read the page and said your idea, find the button that says Continue and press it. That takes you to the next part, where we start learning properly. Only press it when you are ready — take your time. You will know this page is finished when three things are true: you have read or listened to the whole overview, you have said in your own words what you will learn, and you have pressed Continue. That is it! Now let's start with step 1. Read the Unit Overview and press Listen if you see the speaker. Tell me when you are done. 😊

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Tools and Setup. It is the page where we get ready before we learn. In this unit, Be a Problem Solver, we will put steps in the right order and fix mistakes called bugs. To do that, we need our tools ready first — just like we get the flour ready before we make anjero. There are three small jobs. I will give you all three now, and you do them one at a time. 1. Read the Tools and Setup page. Look at the screen and read the list from the top to the bottom. It tells you what you need for this unit. You can read it out loud, and your grown-up can read it with you. I expect you to look at every line, not just the first one. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Check each tool on the list, one by one. For this unit you need a tablet with the ScratchJr app, some paper, a pencil, and colours if you have them. Point to each thing and say "yes, I have it." ScratchJr is the free app where we join picture blocks to make a character move. If ScratchJr is not on the tablet yet, ask your grown-up to help you get it — this is a grown-up job, not yours. 3. Open ScratchJr once, just to look. Tap the ScratchJr app, then tap the house, then tap the plus to start a new project. You do not have to build anything today. I just want you to see the coloured blocks and the green flag at the top. Then you can close it again. 4. Put your paper and pencil next to you. We will draw and write little steps in this unit, like 1, 2, 3. Having them ready means you will not have to stop later. I expect your table to be tidy and ready, like a good problem solver's table. 5. Press the button that says My tools are ready. It is at the bottom of the page. Only press it when you really have everything — the tablet with ScratchJr, your paper and your pencil. Pressing it tells the page you are ready to start. You will know the page is finished when you have checked every tool and pressed My tools are ready at the bottom. Then this page is done and we can begin the fun part! Now start with step 1 and tell me when you have read the page. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. On this page you learn how to be a problem solver. That means putting steps in the right order, finding a wrong step, and fixing a mistake in a program. A mistake in a program is called a bug. Fixing it is called debugging. What I expect from you: read slowly, say things out loud, and try each example yourself. It is fine to go slowly. Get a pencil and paper ready. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. There are 5 short concepts. Each one is a small idea with an example. Read the first one slowly, out loud if you can. Then press Listen so you can hear it read to you. Listening and reading together helps the words stick. 2. Now say the example out loud. For the anjero one, say: "First mix, then pour, then cook." Then try it with your own things. Use your own steps, like getting ready for school: wake up, eat breakfast, walk to school. I expect you to say three steps in the right order, in your own words. 3. Do the same for all 5 concepts, one at a time. Read, press Listen, say the example, then try your own. Do not rush. When you have read every single one, go to the bottom and press I studied the concepts. Only press it after you have truly read all five. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. The same 5 concepts are there, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 5. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read it, press Listen, and say the example out loud. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 6. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, then tell me when you have read the first concept. Take your time — there's no rush. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Explore the Concept page. This page is about being a problem solver. You will look at 6 little discoveries. Some are about putting steps in the right order, like making anjero. Some are about finding a wrong step. Some are about bugs in ScratchJr. A bug is a mistake in a program, and finding it is called debugging. What I expect from you: look carefully, think a little, then type your own idea in your own words. Short is fine. Guessing wrong is fine too — mistakes are how we learn. You just need the page and your thinking brain. Maybe a grown-up nearby to help you type. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab number 1. A discovery will open. Read the little story and look at the picture or model. Take your time — there is no rush. I expect you to look at the picture before you answer. 2. Now read the discovery question under the picture. Stop and think first. What do you notice? Then type your idea in the box. One short sentence is enough, like "Mix it first." Then press Check my idea. 3. If the page says Look again, that is okay. Press Hint. Read the hint, think again, and type a new idea. Try once more. When the page says Exactly!, that tab gets a little tick. Well done — that means you got it! 4. Now press tab number 2 and do the same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tab 3, tab 4, tab 5 and tab 6. One tab at a time, please. I expect every tab to have a tick when you finish. 5. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides. They show the same discoveries, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read, think, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are. 7. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you will know the page is finished: all 6 tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. When you are ready, press tab number 1 and tell me what you see. I am right here with you!

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Computing Words page. These are the special words of Unit 6, "Be a Problem Solver". Words like step, order, algorithm, error, bug and debug. We learn them so we can talk about our mistakes and fix them like real problem solvers. By the end, you will know each word and be able to use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, your eyes, and your fingers to type. There are four things to do. Here they are, one at a time. Step 1. Look at the first word card. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to listen at least once, and then whisper the word back to yourself. Do this for every word on the page. Step 2. Now say the word out loud in a big clear voice. Then say what it means in YOUR own words — not the same words as the page. For example, for bug you might say, "a bug is a mistake inside a program." Then type a sentence using the word, and press Check sentence. Read what the checker tells you. A good sentence shows what the word means, like "I fixed the bug in my blocks." If the checker says try again, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Do this word by word, all the way down the page. Step 3. When you have done every word — listened, said it, and checked a sentence — press the button at the bottom that says I explored the computing words. Only press it after every word is done, because that button tells the page you finished this part. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on each slide: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? Easy! Every word has a sentence you checked, the I explored the computing words button has been pressed, and the last slide's finish button has been pressed too. Take your time — there's no rush. Start with word number one, and tell me when you have pressed Listen. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello, my problem solver! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of the big ideas in this unit. Looking at a picture helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what an algorithm is, what a bug is, and how we fix one. All you need is your eyes, your finger, and your voice. Let's look at them together. There are 5 models. Here are your steps. Step 1: Find the first model. It is called "Steps in the right order". Touch it with your finger and drag it to turn it around. Look at the steps for making anjero. I want you to say out loud: first mix, then pour, then cook. Good thinking! Step 2: Under that model, read the little caption. Then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listen right to the end. I expect you to hear one new word: algorithm. It means a list of steps in the right order. Step 3: Now go to model 2, "Find the wrong step". Drag it to turn it. Press any buttons you see to change it. Look hard for the step that goes the wrong way. Then press Listen for its caption. I expect you to point at the wrong step with your finger and say "that one is wrong". Step 4: Go to model 3, "Meet ScratchJr: make a character walk". Turn it with your finger. Look at the yellow block at the top and the blue arrow blocks under it. Press Listen. I expect you to say what the yellow green flag block does. It starts the program. Step 5: Go to model 4, "Bugs: find and fix the mistake in a program". Drag it and press its buttons to see it change. Press Listen. I expect you to remember two words: bug means a mistake in a program, and debug means find it and fix it. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 6: Go to model 5, "Be a problem solver: the Mini-Project". This is Leo walking to the park. Turn it and follow his path with your finger. Press Listen. I expect you to say which way Leo goes first: right, or up? Step 7: Take one more slow look. Make sure you looked at all 5 models and pressed Listen on all 5 captions. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 8: Now press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. That saves your work. You will know the page is finished when all 5 models have been turned, all 5 captions have been heard, and you have pressed I explored the models. When you are done, come and tell me one thing you saw. I would love to hear it!

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello, my problem solver! Today we learn methods. A method is a way to do a job step by step. We are doing this so you can plan your steps like a real programmer, and so mistakes stop being scary. You need your eyes, your voice, and a comfy seat. Here is our plan. 1. Look at the top of the page. There are 5 methods. Start with the first one. Read its very first step out loud, slowly. I expect to hear your voice saying it — reading out loud helps the step stick in your brain. 2. Now press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will pop up. Read that one out loud too. Take your time — there's no rush. 3. Keep pressing Show me the next step, again and again. Say every step out loud as it appears. Stop pressing when the page says Method complete. That means you finished method one. Well done! 4. Now do the same thing for method two, then three, then four, then five. Same buttons, same job: read out loud, press Show me the next step, keep going until it says Method complete. I expect you to finish all 5, not just one. 5. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one method on it, just like above. On the first slide, press Start. 6. On each slide, press the same buttons to see the steps, and say them out loud. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right side. That takes you to the next slide. 7. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show where you are. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when every method says Method complete and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with method one, and tell me when it says Method complete. I will be right here. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello, problem solver! Today we work on the Worked Examples page together. A worked example is a question with the answer already shown, step by step. We look at them to learn how a good answer is built. By the end, you will know how to put steps in order, spot a wrong step, and say what a bug is. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a pencil and paper. Here are your steps. Step 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question by yourself, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Say the answer out loud, or write it on your paper first. I expect you to TRY first, even if you are not sure. Trying first is what makes your brain grow. Step 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read the answer slowly, line by line. Compare it with what you said or wrote. Ask yourself: is my answer the same? If it is different, that is fine — find the one line where yours and theirs go apart. That is the bit you just learned. Step 3. Do the same for all six worked examples. Read, try, then press Show worked solution. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It tells you how many you have opened. Keep going until every single one is open.
