I expect you to open all six, not just the easy ones. Step 4. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. They show the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on each slide: try the question first, then show the solution. Step 5. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Take your time. There is no rush. Step 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that closes the deck. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all six examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me when you have tried the first question. I am right here. 😊

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello! Today we are on the Code Examples page. Code examples are little bits of a program for you to look at. In this unit our code is made of picture blocks, like the yellow start block and the blue arrow blocks in ScratchJr. We read them so we can see what each block tells the character to do. By the end, you will be able to look at blocks and say what will happen when you tap the green flag. You need your eyes, your finger to point, and your talking voice. A grown-up can sit with you and listen. There are 4 things to do. Here they all are. 1. Read each code example. Put your finger on the very first line at the top. Say out loud what you think that line does, like "this one starts the program" or "this one moves him 3 steps right." Then move your finger down to the next line and do the same. I expect you to say something for every line, even if you are not sure. Guessing out loud is good thinking, not a mistake. 2. Press Copy the code. This copies the code so you can try it yourself. If you have a tablet with ScratchJr, build the same blocks and tap the green flag to watch it run. If you do not have a tablet, that is fine — just read it again with your finger. When you have finished with that example, press the button under it to mark it done. I expect you to press it only after you have really read the whole thing. 3. Do the slides at the bottom of the page. Scroll down until you see the slide deck. Press Start. One code example will show on each slide. Read it line by line like before, say what it does, then mark it done. Then press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going until there are no more slides. Take your time — there is no rush. 4. Press Go to Build It. Do this only when you have read every single example and marked them all done. That button takes you to the next part, where you get to build something yourself. You will know the page is finished when every example has its done button pressed, the slides have no more arrows to press, and you have pressed Go to Build It. One little question before you start: what does the yellow start block do?

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello, my Problem Solver! Today we are on the Guided Practice page. This page gives you five little questions about steps, order and bugs. We do it so your brain gets strong at putting steps in the right order and finding mistakes. By the end, you will be able to spot a wrong step all by yourself. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a pencil and paper if you like. A grown-up can sit near you and read with you. Here is what to do, step by step. 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then work it out on paper or in your head. Think: what comes first, next and last? I expect you to think before you type. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Type your answer in the box. Use your own words. Then press Check my answer. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint tells you a little bit more. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try first, then use a hint — hints are for helpers, not for skipping. 3. Keep going until every question is right. If an answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint, change one small thing, and press Check my answer again. I expect you to try again with a smile. When all five questions are right, this part is done. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Answer the question in the box and press Check my answer, just like before. The same hint buttons are there if you need them. 5. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Do every slide the same way: read, think, type, check. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. I expect you to press it yourself, because it saves your good work. You will know the page is finished when all five questions are marked right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me what you think the answer is. I am right here with you. 😊

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello, my problem solver! Today we are on the Quick Reference page. This page is like a little memory card. It holds the most important words and facts from Unit 6 in one place. We read it so the words stay in your head: step, order, algorithm, error, bug, debug. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. There are three things to do. Here they are, all together. 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page and read it slowly, one line at a time. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen and let the words be read to you. Listen once, then say the word out loud yourself. Do not rush. I expect you to read every box, even the short ones, and to point with your finger as you read. 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a moment and try to remember. Say out loud: "A step is one thing I do." "Order is what comes first, next and last." "An algorithm is a list of steps in the right order." "A bug is a mistake in a program." "Debug means find the mistake and fix it." I expect you to use your own words, not perfect words. If you forget one, look back at the page, then say it again without looking. You can also tell me here and I will listen. 3. Press Reference reviewed. When you have read everything and said the facts out loud, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says Reference reviewed. Only press it after you have really read the page. That button is how the page remembers your good work, so I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when you have read every box, said the key facts out loud in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed at the bottom. Now start with step 1. Read the page slowly and press Listen where you see a speaker. Tell me when you are done, and I will check what you remember. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Build It page. On this page you do 8 little activities. In them you put steps in the right order, you find a wrong step, and you make a character walk in ScratchJr. We do this because a job only works when the steps come in the right order. You cannot cook the anjero before you mix it! By the end, you will be a problem solver: you will find a mistake and fix it. You will need a pencil, some paper, and a tablet with ScratchJr for the last ones. A grown-up can sit with you. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first activity box on the page. Read it, then press Listen so you can hear it too. Listen right to the end. Then go and get the things it names, like your pencil and paper. I expect you to have your things ready before you start. Step 2. Now do that activity. Take your time — there's no rush. Say the steps out loud with your finger, first, then next, then last. Then write your answer in the box under the activity. Even a short answer is good, like "Mix is 1" or "the step should say up". I expect your own thinking, not a guess. Step 3. When you have written in the box, press Mark complete under that activity. That tells the page you have finished it. Only press it after you really did the activity — that is what a good learner does. Step 4. Now do the same thing for every one of the 8 activities, one at a time. Read, press Listen, get your things, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. Never skip the writing box. If something feels hard, stop and ask me — I will give you a small hint, not the answer. Step 5. Some activities need ScratchJr on the tablet. Open ScratchJr, tap the plus to start a new project, pick a background, tap the blue plus to add a character, then join the blue arrow blocks under the yellow green-flag block. Tap the green flag to run it. If nothing moves, that is a bug — just a mistake we can fix. Every programmer's code fails the first time. Step 6. When all 8 boxes say complete, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Check first that no activity is left without its tick. Step 7. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the slide the same way as before, using the same buttons. Step 8. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going, one slide at a time, until the dots run out. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity says complete, and you have pressed Finish activities on the page and on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have pressed Listen on the first activity. 🙂

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello, my problem solver! Today we are on the Debug It page. A bug is a mistake in a program. Finding the bug and fixing it is called debugging. By the end you will be able to look at a little program, spot the wrong step, and say what it should be instead. You just need your eyes, your finger to point, and a happy "I can try" heart. Remember: everyone makes bugs, even grown-ups who build games. Here is the whole page, step by step. Step 1. Look at the first card. Each card shows a small program with one bug in it. Read it slowly, from the top block to the bottom block, like a computer would. Ask yourself: what should happen? Then ask: does every step match that? I expect you to try to find the bug yourself first, before any button. Point at the step you think is wrong and say out loud, "This one is wrong."

Step 2. Now press Show the bug. It will show you where the bug is and what it should be. Check it against your guess. Then say why that step was wrong, in your own words, like "It says down, but the star must go up." Saying why is the important part, so please do not skip it. I expect a full little sentence, not just "wrong."

Step 3. When you have said why, press the button to mark that bug done. Then move to the next card and do the same three things again: find it yourself, press Show the bug, say why. Take your time with every card. There is no rush at all. Step 4. Scroll down to the slides at the bottom of the page. This is a deck of slides, and each slide has one bug. Press Start to begin. Step 5. On the slide, find the bug first with your own eyes. Then press Show the bug. Then mark it done. Then press the arrow to go to the next slide. Do that same little pattern on every slide: look, Show the bug, done, arrow. Step 6. When all the cards and all the slides are finished, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. You will know the page is finished when every card is marked done, every slide is marked done, and you have pressed I practised debugging. Two teacher tips. Usually only one step is wrong, so look for one small thing, not lots. And watch the directions carefully — up is not the same as down, and left is not the same as right. Off you go with card one. Tell me which step you think is the bug, and I will be right here. 🙂

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's do the Computing Fluency page together. 🙂

What this is: it is a quick sprint of 5 short questions about our unit, Be a Problem Solver. It is like a running race for your brain. We do it so the words step, order, algorithm and bug come to you fast, without thinking hard. What I expect from you: try your best, answer quickly, and stay happy even if one is wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Get ready: sit up, have your pencil near, and look at the timer at the top. It counts your time. Do not worry about the clock — quick is nice, but right is better. Step 1. Press the button to start the sprint, then read question one. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check and continue. I expect one short answer, not a long story. Tip: think about the two start blocks in ScratchJr — one waits for a tap, one waits for the green flag. Step 2. Read question two and answer it the same way, then press Check and continue. This one asks the special word for a mistake in a program. It is a tiny word with three letters, and a real moth once caused it! Say the word in your head first, then type it. Step 3. Question three asks you to put steps in order: mix, pour, cook. Type the order you think is right, then press Check and continue. I expect you to picture making anjero in your kitchen. Ask yourself: can I cook it before I mix it? Your finger can help you count 1, 2, 3. Step 4. Question four is about the Moon. The Moon should go up, but one step says down. Type what the step should say, then press Check and continue. Point your arm up in the air first — that helps you feel the right direction. I expect an answer that names the direction and the number of steps. Step 5. The last question is a Move step. Read it slowly, type your answer, then press Check and continue. Read the question twice before you answer. When you finish, the page will show how you did. Step 6. Now look at your score. You need most of them right. If you got fewer, that is fine — press Run the sprint again and try once more. Each time you go, you will get faster and surer. That is exactly what practice is for. How you know the page is finished: when one sprint has enough right answers, the page marks itself done. You must press the buttons yourself — I cannot press them for you. When you are ready, press start and tell me how question one goes. Take your time — there's no rush.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Games page for Unit 6, Be a Problem Solver. These little games ask you questions about our unit words: step, order, algorithm, error, bug and debug. We play them so those words stick in your head, like a song you remember. By the end, you will be quick at saying what a bug is and why order matters. All you need is your finger to tap, and your thinking brain. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read each question slowly, think before you tap, and stay happy if you get one wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. That is exactly what a problem solver does. 1. Look at the list of games and pick one. Press Start game. A question comes up with a few answers. Read the question twice, then tap the answer you think is right. You earn a star for every round you get right. I expect you to try each round on your own first, and if you are not sure, use the clue on the screen. 2. When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you more rounds and more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep pressing Play again on that same game until its stars are full. If you get one wrong, read the little explanation, then try that game again. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Pick the next game, press Start game, answer the rounds, and press Play again until all its stars are full. Do this until every game is mastered. I expect you to finish one game before starting a new one, so you do not get muddled. You will know the page is finished when every game shows all its stars. Then the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything else. Ready? Pick your first game and press Start game. Tell me which one you picked! ⭐

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today we are learning how to stay safe online. This page has three safety rules. Rules keep you safe, just like looking both ways before you cross the road. By the end, you will know what to do if something online feels wrong. You only need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say each rule out loud in your own words, and think of one example from your own life. There are three steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Read every rule slowly. Look at the first rule on your screen. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and hear the words too. Then move to the next rule, and the next. There are three rules: check before you trust, tell someone if something worries you, and respect other people's work. Do it well by reading each one twice — once with your eyes, once with your ears. Step 2. Say each rule in your own words, and give an example from your life. Do not read the words on the screen. Say it your way, out loud. For example, for the first rule you might say, "Not everything on the internet is true, so I ask my mum." For the second, you might say, "If a game makes me feel scared, I tell my teacher." For the third, you might say, "If I use someone's picture, I say who drew it." I expect one sentence for each rule, plus one small example. You can tell your grown-up your examples too — they will love hearing them. Step 3. Press the button. When you have read all three rules and said them your own way, press I know these rules at the bottom of the page. Press it only when you really have read them all — that button is your promise that you know them. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I know these rules and the page shows it is done. Then you can tell me one thing you will do to stay safe online. 🙂

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello, problem solver! Today we work on the page called Solve Real Problems. On this page you get four little problems from real life. You will use what you know about steps, order, and bugs to solve them. This helps you think like a computer person: slow, careful, one step at a time. You need your eyes for reading, your brain for thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here is what I expect from you today. I want you to read each problem twice. I want you to think first, then type. And I want you to keep smiling if you get one wrong, because mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Look at the first problem on the page. Read it slowly. Ask yourself: what is it asking me to do? Some problems ask which block starts the program. Some ask what a mistake in a program is called. Some ask about moving up or down. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Now work it out in your head, or say it out loud. Then type your answer in the box. Try to write a small full sentence, not just one word. For example, do not just type a letter — type words like "The step should say..." Then press Check answer. Step 3. If you are stuck, press Hint. The hint gives you a little push, not the answer. Read the hint, then try again in the box. It is fine to try two or three times. Every programmer's code fails the first time. Step 4. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little cheer! Then move down to the next problem and do the same thing: read, think, type, press Check answer. Do this for all four problems. Step 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer that slide the same way you did above: read it, think, type, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Step 6. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. More dots filled in means you are getting closer to the end. Step 7. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last slide. Answer it, then press the finish button on that last slide. That tells the page you have finished the whole deck. How will you know the page is finished? All four problems will show that your answers are right, and the slide deck will be at the last slide with the finish button pressed. Then you are done! Ready? Start with problem one, and tell me when you have read it. I am right here with you. 😊

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Unit Project: Be a Problem Solver. You will help Leo walk to the park. First you plan the steps, then you build it in ScratchJr, then you find and fix a bug. You need a tablet with ScratchJr, plus paper and a pencil. What I expect from you is this: try, check, and keep smiling when something goes wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are the three things on this page. 1. Read the Unit Project. On the page you will see what you will make, and a list of things a good project has. Read the list slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. The list says: I planned Leo's steps, I built Leo in ScratchJr, I tapped the green flag to check, I found and fixed the bug, and I added one thing to make it better. I expect you to know what each one means before you start. If one sounds hard, tell me and we will look at it together. 2. Make your project step by step, and tick each thing on the list as you do it. Plan first: look at the little map, put your finger on Leo, and move it to the park. Write your steps on paper, like "move 3 steps right, move 2 steps up." That list of steps is your algorithm. Then open ScratchJr, tap the big plus for a new project, tap the picture button for a background, and tap the blue plus to add Leo. Drag the yellow Start on Green Flag block, then join your blue arrow blocks. Tap the green flag and watch. If Leo goes the wrong way or does not move, that is a bug — find the one wrong block, change it, and run it again. Change one thing at a time. Then add one nice extra, like a new background or one more move. Tick each thing on the list only when you really did it. I expect honest ticks, not fast ticks. 3. Press "My project is finished" when every item on the list is ticked. Look at your list one more time first. Ask yourself: did Leo really reach the park? Did I fix my bug? When all the boxes are ticked, press the button "My project is finished". That button is how the page saves your work, so it must be you who presses it. You will know the page is done when every item on the list has a tick and you have pressed "My project is finished". Now let's start with something small. Tell me: which way does Leo go first on your map — right, left, up or down?

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is our Unit Challenge. The Unit Challenge is a little quiz about everything in Unit 6, Be a Problem Solver. We do it to see what your brain has kept: steps, order, algorithms, errors, bugs and debugging. By the end, you will know which parts you are strong at. You need only your eyes, your thinking, and a calm, slow finger for tapping. This one is graded, so I will help you think — but I will not give you answers. Here is the whole page, step by step. Step 1: Read question one slowly. Read it twice. Ask yourself, "What is this question really asking?" Look for a key word you know, like step, order, bug or green flag. I expect you to think first, then choose. No fast guessing. Step 2: Tap the answer you think is right. Then press Next question. Do this for every question, one at a time. There are 12 questions in all. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3: If a question feels hard, remember our unit. Steps must be in order, because you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it. A mistake is an error. A mistake in a program is a bug. Finding it and fixing it is debugging. I expect you to try every question, even the tricky ones. Step 4: Keep going until you have answered all 12. Then the page shows your score. You pass with more than half right. I expect you to look at your score with a happy face, whatever it says. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 5: If your score is not high enough, press Try again. Go through the questions once more, slowly. Think about the ones that felt hard last time. Trying again is exactly what a problem solver does. Step 6: When your score is good enough, press Continue. That takes you onward. You will know the page is finished when you have seen your score, it is more than half right, and you have pressed Continue. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me how you get on. I am right here. 🙂

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. 📝

On this page you say WHY, not just what. You will use our unit words: step, order, algorithm, error and bug. Doing this helps the words stick in your head, so you can teach them to someone else. You need your reading eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. Here is our whole plan, step by step. 1. Read the first prompt out loud. There are 4 prompts on this page. Under each one you will see some key ideas — little words like step, order or bug. Read the prompt twice, then read the key ideas. I expect you to point at the key ideas and say them out loud before you write. Those words are your helpers. 2. Now write your explanation in the box. Say three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example, if the prompt is about putting steps in order, you might write what comes first, then say the rule (steps must go in the right order), then say why (you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it). Then press Check your reasoning. If the page says it wants more, do not worry — that is normal. Add one more sentence using a key idea and press Check your reasoning again. 3. Next, press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare. Read it and ask yourself: did I use the key ideas too? You do not have to copy it word for word. Your own words are best. If you missed a key word, go back to your box, add it, and check again. Do this for all 4 prompts, one at a time. Take your time — there is no rush. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one per slide. On the first slide, press Start. Use the same buttons on each slide: write in the box, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 4 explanations use the key ideas, and the last slide's finish button has been pressed. That is your work saved. 🌟

Ready? Read prompt one, then tell me what you think the answer is. I am right here with you.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher. Let's look at that together. This page is the Unit Overview. It is like peeking at a map before a trip. This unit is called "Computers Control Things". It teaches you a big secret: tiny computers hide inside things like a washing machine, a microwave and even some toys. By the end, you will be able to say what a computer controls, what a robot is, and how a computer tells us things. You need your eyes, your ears, and your talking voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and listen carefully. Read it slowly, not fast. I expect you to find one thing that surprises you — maybe that a fridge has a computer inside! Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, to me or to your grown-up. Do not copy the words on the page — use your own. A good answer is one sentence, like "I will learn about computers hiding inside things." I expect one sentence from you, in your voice. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Only press it when you have read the page and said your sentence. That button takes you to the next part, where we start learning properly. I expect you to press it yourself, when you feel ready. You will know the page is finished when you have read it, said your own sentence, and pressed Continue. Then the lesson opens, and off we go! Now, step 1 — go and read it. Tell me one thing you noticed. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 7: Computers Control Things. This lesson has five little ideas, called concepts. They teach us a big secret: tiny computers hide inside things like a washing machine, and they are the boss. By the end you will know what a robot is, and what output means. You need your eyes, your listening ears, and your voice. Maybe a pencil too. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say things out loud, and think about your own home. Ready? Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first concept box on the page. Read it slowly, word by word. Then press Listen and let it read to you while you follow along. Do this for the first concept only, then think for a moment: what is this one about? I expect you to be able to tell me the idea in your own small words, like "computers hide inside things". 2. Now find the example under that concept. Say the example out loud, in a big clear voice. Then try it with your own things at home. For example, look around and say "our fridge has a computer inside, and it keeps our food cold". I expect one real thing from your own home for each concept — that is how the idea sticks. 3. Do the same for concept two, three, four and five. Read, press Listen, then say the example out loud. Take your time, there is no rush. As you go, try to remember these four words: control means to tell something what to do, robot means a machine that does a job by itself, android means a robot that looks like a person, and output means what a computer shows us. I expect you to meet all five concepts, not skip any. 4. When you have read every single concept, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really did read them all. That button tells the page you finished the reading part. 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same concepts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Read that slide carefully, just like before, and use the same buttons on the slide. I expect you to read the slide, not just click past it. 6. When you finish a slide, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are, and how many are left. Keep going, one slide at a time, using the same buttons on each one. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the slide deck. Well done! You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. When you are done, come back and tell me one thing you learned. I would love to hear it! 😊

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our getting-ready page. Here is what Tools & Setup is. It is a short list of the things you need for Unit 7, "Computers Control Things". In this unit we find computers hiding inside everyday things, we meet robots, and later we build our very own robot from boxes. We do this page first so nothing stops us in the middle of the fun. By the end you will have all your bits and pieces in one place, ready to go. What I expect from you: read slowly, get each thing before you tick it, and ask your grown-up for help if you need to. There are three steps. Step 1. Read the Tools & Setup page from the top to the bottom. Use your finger to follow the words, or ask your grown-up to read them with you. Look for the things you need — for this unit that is paper, a pencil, some colours, and for our robot later, cardboard boxes, tubes and bottle caps. A good read is a slow read, where you can tell your grown-up one thing you need. Step 2. Check each tool on the list, one at a time. Go and find it, then put it on your table in a little pile. If something is missing, tell your grown-up now, not later. You do not need a fancy thing — an old box from the kitchen is perfect. I expect you to touch and check every item, not just look at the list. Step 3. When everything is on your table, press the button that says "My tools are ready" at the bottom of the page. Press it only after you really have your things, because that button tells the page you are set to start. If you are still missing one thing, wait and press it after you find it. How will you know the page is finished? When your pile of tools is on the table and you have pressed "My tools are ready", this page is done. Then we can start hunting for the computers hiding inside things! 🙂

Tell me when Step 1 is done, and I will check in with you.

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our Computing Words for Unit 7. These are the special words about how computers control things — like computer, device, control, output, robot and android. We learn them so you can say what a hidden computer does, and talk like a real computer scientist. You will need your voice, your eyes, and your hands for typing. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first word card on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen and hear the word said out loud. I expect you to listen carefully and look at the word at the same time. 2. Now say the word out loud yourself. Say it slowly, like the Listen button did. Then say the meaning in your own words — not the same words as the page. For example, for device you might say "a machine that does a job for us". I expect a short, clear sentence from your own mouth. 3. Next, type a sentence with that word in the box, then press Check sentence. A good sentence uses the word properly and comes from your own life, like "My fridge is a device." I expect one sentence with the word spelled the same as on the card. 4. Read what the checker says back to you. If it says well done, smile and move on. If it says try again, change one small thing and press Check sentence again. I expect you to read the message, not just skip it. 5. Do steps 1 to 4 again for every word on the page. Take your time — there is no rush. I expect you to try every word, even the tricky ones like output and android. 6. When you have done every word, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the computing words. That tells the page you finished this part. I expect you to press it only after all the words are done. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you used before: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning in your own words, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. I expect a new sentence here, not the same one you typed before, if you can think of one. 9. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 10. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to finish every slide, one at a time. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the computing words, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then all your work is saved. Off you go with step 1 — tell me when you have listened to your first word, and I will help you with the meaning. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for this page. It is called Explore the Concept, and it is all about Unit 7: Computers Control Things. We are doing it because tiny computers hide inside lots of things at home, and today you will find them. By the end you will be able to say what a computer controls, what a robot is, and what output means. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your fingers for typing. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see six little numbered tabs, like six little doors. Press number 1 first. A picture or a model will open. Look at it carefully and read the little story next to it. I expect you to really look — not rush past. Ask yourself: what is this thing, and does it have a computer inside? 2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it slowly. Think first, then type your own idea in the box. Even a short answer is good, like "yes, a washing machine has a computer inside." Then press Check my idea. I expect your own words — not copied words. Your own thinking is what makes it stick. 3. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read the little clue, then change your answer a bit and press Check my idea again. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a tick. That tick means: done and correct! 4. Now do the same for tab 2, then 3, 4, 5 and 6. One tab at a time, please. Press the tab, look, read, think, type, press Check my idea. The page is finished when all six tabs have a tick. 5. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides waiting for you. They have the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need a clue. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. 7. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is you telling the page, "I did it!" I cannot press it for you — the record of your work comes from you. You will know the page is finished when every one of the six tabs has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have opened tab 1, and tell me what you see. I am right here with you. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes that show our big ideas. Our big idea this unit is control — a computer tells a machine what to do. Looking at pictures helps the idea stick in your head. You just need your eyes, your finger or mouse, and your talking voice. Here we go. 1. Find the first model, "Computers hide inside things". Look at it carefully. If it moves, put your finger on it and drag slowly to turn it around. Press any buttons on it to see what changes. I want you to spot the hidden computer inside the machine. Then say out loud: "A computer hides in here."

2. Now the second model, "Which things have a computer?". Drag it to turn it, and press its buttons. Look at the two groups: has a computer, and no computer. I expect you to point at one thing in each group and name it, like "a spoon has no computer" and "a tablet has a computer."

3. Next is the third model, "Meet the robots". Turn it with your finger and press the buttons. Look at the robot's shape. Remember, a robot is a machine that does a job by itself. Tell me one thing this robot could do. And remember the happy truth: a robot cannot feel happy or sad. 4. Now the fourth model, "Output: how computers tell us things". Output means what a computer gives back to us. Drag it and press its buttons. Find a speaker, a screen and a printer. I want you to say what each one does: speaker to hear, screen to see, printer to put it on paper. 5. Last is the fifth model, "Design and build a robot". Turn it and press its buttons. Look at the parts — the body, the arms, the head. Think about YOUR robot. What job will it do? Say your idea out loud, like "My robot waters the plants."

6. Now read the caption under each model. A caption is the little bit of writing below the picture. Press the Listen button to hear it read to you. Listen carefully, and try to say one word from it back to me. 7. When you have looked at all five models and heard all the captions, scroll to the bottom. Press the button that says "I explored the models". That button tells the page you are done — I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed "I explored the models" at the bottom. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you finish one model, and I will be right here! 😊

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Code Examples page in Unit 7, Computers Control Things. Here is what this page is. It shows you little examples of how computers control things and how they tell us things. Reading them helps you see the idea, not just hear it. By the end, you will be able to say what a computer inside a machine does, and name an output device like a speaker, a screen or a printer. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you. Look at every example slowly. Say each line out loud in your own words. Do not rush. Guessing and trying is good — mistakes are how we learn. There are four steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read each code example. Look at the first example on the page. Read it one line at a time, from the top. After each line, say out loud, "I think this line tells the computer to..." A good job sounds like this: "This line tells the machine to make a sound." You do not need to be perfect. You just need to try each line. Step 2: Press Copy the code. That button copies the example so you can use it. If you have a computer to try it on, ask your grown-up and try it. Watch what happens. Then press the button under the example to mark it done. I expect you to press Copy the code first, and only mark it done after you have really read it. Step 3: Do the slides at the bottom. Under the examples there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one example. Press Start. Read the code on the slide. Then mark it done. Then press the arrow to go to the next one. Keep going until there are no more slides. I expect you to read every slide, not skip any. Step 4: Press Go to Build It. Do this only when you have read every example and every slide. That button takes you to the next part, where you build something yourself. I expect you to be ready to say one thing you learned before you press it. How will you know the page is finished? Every example will have its done button pressed, every slide will be marked done, and then you press Go to Build It. That is it — page complete! Ready for Step 1? Tell me when you have read the first example, and tell me one line you understood. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are on Guided Practice for Unit 7, Computers Control Things. This page is where you show what you know about computers hiding inside things, robots, and output. We practise so the ideas stick in your head. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. Here are the steps. Step 1: Read the first question slowly. There are 5 questions on this page. Say the question out loud if that helps. Work it out on paper or in your head first, before you type anything. I expect you to think for a moment, not rush. Step 2: Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. Try to write a whole little sentence, like "A washing machine has a computer inside." That tells me you really understand. Step 3: If you feel stuck, do not worry. Press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. Using a hint is smart, not naughty. Step 4: If your answer is not right, read the hint and try again. Mistakes are how we learn. I expect you to try again, not to give up. Step 5: Do the same for every question, all 5 of them, until each one is right. Question, think, type, Check my answer. One at a time, no rushing. Step 6: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7: On each slide, use the same buttons: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Step 8: When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Step 9: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when all 5 questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now, off you go — read question one and tell me what you think the answer is. Take your time — there's no rush.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Quick Reference page. This page is like a little treasure box. It holds the most important words and facts from Unit 7, all in one place. We read it so the big ideas stick in your head — computers hiding inside things, robots, and output. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. There are three steps. 1. Read the Quick Reference slowly. Look at the page and read from the top. Do not rush. Where you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Say the word back after the voice. I expect you to read every part, even the parts you think you know. If a word looks tricky, stop and ask me — I am right here. 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now cover the page with your hand or look away. Say out loud: "A computer hides inside a washing machine and it controls it." Then say: "A robot is a machine that does a job by itself. It cannot feel happy or sad." Then say: "Output is what a computer shows us — a speaker to hear, a screen to see, a printer for paper." I expect your own words, not the exact same words as the page. That is how I know you really understand. You can say them to me here, and I will listen. 3. Press Reference reviewed. When you have read everything and said the facts your own way, scroll down to the bottom of the page and press the button that says Reference reviewed. Only press it when you have really done steps 1 and 2 — that button is your promise that you read it. I cannot press it for you; it must come from you. You will know the page is finished when you have read it all, said the three key facts out loud in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Let's start with step 1. Read the page slowly now, and press Listen on any speaker you see. Tell me when you are done, or tell me any word that felt tricky. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today we are on the Worked Examples page for Unit 7, Computers Control Things. A worked example is a question with the answer already shown, step by step. We use these to learn HOW to think, not just what the answer is. By the end, you will be able to say which things have a computer inside, what a robot is, and what output means. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain! Here is what I expect from you: always try the question yourself FIRST, before you look at the answer. Even a guess counts. That is how your brain grows. Step 1. Look at the first worked example on the page. Read the question slowly. If reading is tricky, ask your grown-up to read it with you. Say the question back in your own words. Step 2. Now try it yourself. Say your answer out loud, or write it on your paper. Do not peek yet! A good answer is a full sentence, like "The tablet has a computer inside."

Step 3. Now press Show worked solution. Read the answer line by line. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? It is fine if you did not — that is how we learn. Step 4. Do the same for worked examples 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. There are 6 in all. Read, try it yourself, then press Show worked solution. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 5. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It shows how many examples you have opened. Keep going until every single one is open. All 6 open means this part is done! Step 6. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. The same examples are there, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: read the question, try it yourself, then show the solution. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are. Step 8. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter shows all 6 examples opened AND you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me when you have read the first question. 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to work something out, one small step at a time. On this page there are 5 methods about computers that control things. We do this so your brain learns to go slowly and follow steps — just like a computer does. By the end, you will be able to say the steps out loud all by yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Let's go! 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step. Say it out loud in your own voice. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to read each step slowly, not rush. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Say every step out loud as it appears. Keep going until the page says Method complete. That message means you finished that one — well done! 3. Now do the same thing for every method. There are 5 in all. Read, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and stop when you see Method complete. I expect all 5 to say Method complete, not just one or two. 4. Now look under the page. There is a little deck of slides with the same methods, one method on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons to move through the steps. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the very last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 5 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have done step 1, and I will check it with you! 🌟

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Build It page. This is our hands-on part of Unit 7, "Computers Control Things". You will find the hidden computers inside everyday things, meet robots, and learn about output — what a computer shows us. Get a pencil, some paper, and colours. Your grown-up can sit beside you if you like. What I expect from you: try each activity yourself, then write or draw your answer in the box. Short answers are fine. Your own words are always best. Here are the steps. 1. There are 8 build-it activities on this page. Start with the first one. Read it, then press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen carefully. Then go and get the things it names, like paper, a pencil, or boxes. I expect you to have your things ready before you begin. 2. Now do the activity. Take your time — there's no rush. When you finish, write your answer in the box. If the activity asks you to circle or draw, do it on your paper, then write in the box what you found. For example, you might write, "A washing machine has a computer inside." A good answer says what you did and what you noticed. 3. When one activity is done, press Mark complete under it. Then move to the next one and do the same: Listen, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. Do this for all 8. When every activity is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same build-it activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: Listen, write in the box, then Mark complete. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when all 8 activities show as complete, and you have pressed Finish activities. That press is important — it saves your work, so please do it yourself. Ready? Go to activity one, press Listen, and tell me when you have your things. I'll be right here. 🌟

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Debug It. A bug is a little mistake. On this page, each card shows a small mistake about computers and robots. Your job is to be a bug detective and find it. We do this because finding mistakes helps us understand things better. Mistakes are how we learn. By the end, you will be able to spot a wrong idea and say the right one. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are four steps. Here they are. Step 1. Look at the first card. Read the little program or idea on it slowly. Ask yourself: what is wrong here? Try to find the bug all by yourself first, before you press anything. I expect you to think for a moment, not rush. You can say the bug out loud, like "that is wrong because a robot is not alive."

Step 2. Now press the button that says Show the bug. It will show you where the bug is and what it should say. Read it. Then tell me, or tell your grown-up, WHY it was wrong. Saying why is the important part! After that, press the button to mark that bug done. Do this for every card on the page, one card at a time. Step 3. Now look under the cards. There is a slide deck with one bug on each slide. Press Start. Look at the bug and think first, just like before. Then press Show the bug, say why it was wrong, and mark it done. Then press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going until you have done every slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 4. When all the cards and all the slides are finished, scroll to the bottom. Press the button that says I practised debugging. Only press it when you have really done them all — that button is your record of your good work. You will know the page is finished when every card is marked done, every slide is marked done, and you have pressed I practised debugging. Ready? Go and read the first card. When you have a guess about the bug, come back and tell me what you think it is.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Unit 7 games. These games are all about computers that hide inside things, robots, and output. Playing them helps the words stick in your head, like practising a song until you know it. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a click or a tap. Here is the whole plan. 1. Look at the games on your screen and pick one. Press Start game. Read the question slowly, all the way to the end. Then read every choice before you pick one. Tap the choice you think is right. If you get it right, you earn a star! I expect you to think first and tap second — no fast guessing. 2. Keep answering each round until the game ends. Some rounds ask "which one has a computer inside?" Some ask about robots. If you get one wrong, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Just read the little explanation, then remember it for next time. I expect you to try every round, even the tricky ones. 3. When a game ends, press Play again to have another go. Each time you play, you can earn more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. I expect you to keep playing that game until its stars are full. You will get faster and surer each time — that is your brain learning. 4. Now do the same for the next game. Press Start game, answer the rounds, then Play again until all its stars are full. Do this for every game on the page. Take your time — there is no rush. 5. Here is how you know you are done: when every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not need to press anything special at the end. Now go and press Start game on your first game. Tell me when you have played one round, and tell me what the question was. I will be right here waiting! ⭐

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Computing Fluency. Fluency means "quick and sure". You already learned about computers hiding inside things, robots, and output. Now we make those ideas fast in your head. It is like reading a word you know without stopping to sound it out. You need your eyes, your thinking, and your fingers for typing. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: answer with what YOU think first, not a guess from me. I will not give you the answers, but I will help you get there. Short answers are fine, like "yes", "no", or "speaker". Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see a timer, showing your time. Do not worry about the clock. Take your time — there's no rush. It is just there to show you how fast your thinking is getting. 2. Read question one. Read it twice, slowly. Think: is this about things with a computer inside, about robots, or about output? Knowing that helps you find the answer. 3. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check & continue. I expect a real try every time, even if you are not sure. A try teaches you more than an empty box. 4. Keep going the same way for all five questions: read, think, type, press Check & continue. There are five in the sprint. If one feels hard, say the word out loud first, then type it. 5. When the five are done, the page shows how you did. You need most of them right to finish. That means getting more right than wrong. 6. If you got fewer than that, press Run the sprint again. This is not a bad thing! Mistakes are how we learn. The second sprint is usually much easier, because your brain now knows the questions. 7. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. The page will tell you. Then you are done, and you can smile — you earned it. Now, step one: look at the top of the page and find the timer. Tell me when you can see it, and we will start question one together.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are on the Solve Real Problems page. This is where you take what you know about hidden computers, robots and output, and use it to answer real questions from home, school and out in the world. It helps the ideas stick in your head. You need your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up nearby to help with typing. Let's start with something small. Here is the whole page, in 4 parts. 1. First, read the problem. There are 4 problems on this page. Read the first one slowly, all the way to the end. Ask yourself: what is this question asking me to do? Is it asking me to pick a thing with a computer inside, or to say what a computer does, or to say if a robot is alive? I expect you to read it twice before you answer. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Next, think, then type. Work out your answer in your head first. Then click in the answer box and type it in. Try to answer in a full sentence, like "The tablet has a computer inside." Then press Check answer. If your brain feels stuck, press Hint — the hint gives you a nudge, not the answer. That is a smart thing to do, not a silly one. 3. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done — now move on to the next problem and do the same three things: read, think, type, press Check answer. Do this for all 4 problems. If one says "not quite", that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the problem again, change one word in your answer, and press Check answer again. 4. Last, the slides at the bottom. Scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check answer, press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 4 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it for you — you press the buttons, so the page remembers your good work. Ready? Read problem one and tell me what you think it is asking you to do. 🙂

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Let's do this page together. I am right here with you. This page is called Explain Your Thinking. On it, you tell me HOW you know something, not just the answer. We do this because a good computer thinker can say why. By the end, you will be able to explain your ideas using our unit words: computer, device, control, output, robot and android. You need your eyes, your thinking, and your hands for typing. Ready? Here are all the steps. Step 1. There are 4 prompts on this page. Read the first prompt slowly. Under it you will see key ideas — those are the words I want you to use. Read the prompt twice, and say it out loud if you like. I expect you to point at the key ideas and think, "how can I put these words in my answer?"

Step 2. Now click in the writing box and type your explanation. Say three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example, you might write, "I know a fridge is a device. The rule is that a computer controls a device. So the computer keeps my food cold." Then press Check your reasoning. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check your reasoning again. I expect a real try, in your own words — even one or two sentences is great. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This shows you a good answer so you can compare. Look for the key ideas in it. Ask yourself, "did I use those words too?" You do not need the same words as the model — but you do need the key ideas. Then do the same for prompts 2, 3 and 4: read, type, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same prompts. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: type your answer, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. To move on, press the arrow on the right. The little dots under the slide tell you which slide you are on. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? When all 4 prompts have your own explanation with the key ideas in it, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Nice and clear! Now go and read prompt 1. Tell me what it asks, and we will think about it together. Take your time — there's no rush.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Stay Safe Online page. This page has three safety rules. They help you stay happy and safe when you use a computer or tablet. By the end, you will be able to say each rule in your own words. You need your eyes for reading, your voice for talking, and your ears for listening. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Read the rules slowly. Look at the top of the page. Read the first rule all the way to the end. If you see a little speaker button, press Listen and hear it read to you. Then do the same for the next rule, and the next. I expect you to read all three rules, not just the first one. Go slowly — take your time, there's no rush. Step 2: Say each rule in your own words. Now cover the words with your hand. Say rule one out loud in YOUR words, like you are telling a friend. Then add one example from your own life. For example, for "tell someone if something worries you", you might say: "If a game shows me something scary, I will tell my mum." I expect a short sentence in your own words, plus one real example — for all three rules. You can say them to your grown-up. Step 3: Press the button at the bottom. When you have read all three rules and said them in your own words, scroll down to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I know these rules. Only press it when you really have read them all — that button is your promise that you did. You will know the page is finished when the I know these rules button has been pressed and the page shows it is done. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read the first rule. 🙂

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today we do our big Unit 7 project. You are going to make your very own robot! Why do we do this? Because it shows you know the big idea of this unit. A robot is a machine with a computer inside. The computer controls it — it tells it what to do. And your robot needs an output, so it can tell people things. What I expect from you: think first, then build, then talk about it. Take your time. You can ask a grown-up to help with cutting and sticking. Here are the steps. 1. Read the Unit Project box on your screen. It tells you what to make: a robot, made from boxes and tubes. Under it you will see a list of things a good project has. Read that list slowly, or ask a grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know two things before you build: what your robot's job is, and what output it will have. 2. Now make your robot, step by step, and tick each thing on the list as you finish it. First, plan the job — say it out loud, like "my robot waters the plants." Next, find cardboard boxes, tubes and bottle caps, and stick them together to make a body, a head and arms. Then choose one output for your robot: a speaker to make sound, a screen to show pictures, or a flashing light. Then give your robot a name and colour it in. Last, tell someone — a grown-up, a friend, or your class — what your robot is called, what job it does, and what its output is. Tick each item on the list only after you really did it. 3. When every item on the list is ticked, press the button that says My project is finished. Press it yourself — that is how the page saves your good work. Do not press it early, even if you feel excited! You will know the page is done when every box on the list has a tick, and you have pressed My project is finished. Ready? Start with step 1: read the project box, and tell me what job your robot will do. 🤖

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today we finish Unit 7 with the Unit Challenge. It is a little quiz about computers that hide inside things, robots, and output. We do it to show what your brain has learned. You need a quiet spot, your eyes, and your thinking. I will not give answers, but I will always help you think. Here is the whole page, step by step. 1. There are 12 questions. Read one question all the way to the end. Then read every choice before you pick. Ask yourself, "Is this about a computer inside something, or a robot, or output?" Pick the answer that matches the words we learned. Then press Next question. I expect you to read slowly and choose on your own. 2. Do this for all 12 questions, one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. If a question feels hard, say the key word out loud, like robot or output, and think what it means. A robot is a machine that does a job by itself. Output is what a computer shows us. I expect you to try every question, even the tricky ones. 3. At the end you will see your score. You pass when more than half are right. Look at your score and tell me how you did — I would love to hear! 4. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing at all. Mistakes are how we learn. This time, go a bit slower and think about which words we learned in this unit. 5. When your score is good, press Continue. That is the last button on the page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue after a passing score. Ready? Here comes question one — read it carefully, and tell me if you want a hint. 🙂

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Tools and Setup. This page tells you what you need for Unit 8, Be a Data Collector. In this unit you will ask people questions, write the answers down, and colour a picture chart. Before we start, a good data collector gets their things ready. That is what this page is for. It will take just a few minutes. Here are the 3 steps. Do them one at a time. Step 1. Read the Tools and Setup page on your screen. Look at the list of things you need. For this unit it will be simple things, like paper, a pencil, and some colours. You can ask your grown-up to read the words with you. I expect you to look at every line, not just the first one. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Now check each thing on the list. Say it out loud, then find it. "Paper — yes, I have it." "Pencil — yes." "Colours — yes." If something is missing, ask your grown-up to help you find it. If the list says something on a computer or tablet, ask your grown-up to open it for you. I expect you to touch or hold each thing, so you really know it is there. That is how a careful data collector works. Step 3. When everything on the list is ready in front of you, press the button at the bottom that says My tools are ready. Only press it after you have checked every item. Pressing that button is how the page knows you are set up. How will you know the page is finished? When you have read the list, found every thing on it, and pressed My tools are ready. Then we can go and start collecting data! Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read the list. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like peeking at a map before a trip. It tells you what Unit 8, "Be a Data Collector", is all about. By the end of this page, you will know what you are going to learn. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here are the three things to do. Take them one at a time. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let it read to you. Listen right to the end, and try to catch these words: data, collect, tally, pictogram. I expect you to read or listen to the whole thing, not just the first line. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, or tell your grown-up. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn to ask people questions, write down their answers, and make a picture chart." You do not need big words. I expect one or two of your own sentences — your words, not the page's words. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. That is the button at the bottom. Only press it after you have done Step 1 and Step 2. I expect you to feel ready, like you know what is coming next. You will know this page is finished when you have listened to it all, said what you will learn, and pressed Continue. Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me when you have finished listening. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello, my data collector! Today we learn how to find things out and write them down. This page is called The Lesson. It has five little cards. Each card teaches one idea, like data, forms, tally marks, and pictograms. By the end, you will know what a data collector does. You need your eyes, your voice, and a pencil and paper nearby. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say things out loud, and try each example yourself. Do not rush. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Read the first card. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Follow the words with your finger while you listen. Do this for all five cards, one at a time. I expect you to stop after each card and tell yourself the idea in your own words. Step 2: Say the example out loud, then try it with your own things. For tally marks, draw one little line for each toy on your table. For data, say your own favourite fruit out loud. A good try means you used YOUR own things, not just the ones on the page. Step 3: When you have read all five cards, scroll down and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really read them all. That button tells the page you are done reading. Step 4: Under the page there is a deck of slides. It shows the same five ideas, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Read it, and use the same buttons on each slide. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 5: Keep going, one slide at a time, until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to read each slide, not just click fast. Slow eyes learn more! You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and the dots show you reached the last slide, and you pressed the finish button. Ready? Start with Step 1, and come tell me when card one is done. 🙂

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Computing Words page. This page teaches you the special words we use in Unit 8, Be a Data Collector. Words like data, tally and pictogram. When you know these words, everything else in the unit gets easier. You only need your eyes, your voice, and your fingers for typing. Ready? Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first word card. Read the word. Then read what it means. Then press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Listen carefully — that helps your ears learn the word too. 2. Now say the word out loud yourself. Say it slowly, like this: "tal-ly". Nobody is laughing — saying it out loud helps you remember it. I expect to hear your voice, not just your eyes reading. 3. Say the meaning in your OWN words. Do not copy the card. For example, for tally you might say, "a little line I make when I count something." Short is fine. Your own words are best. 4. Now type a sentence with the word in it, then press Check sentence. A good sentence shows you know the word. "I made a tally for each friend" is good. "Tally is a word" is not — it does not show what the word means. 5. Read what the checker says to you. If it says well done, smile and go on. If it asks you to try again, that is fine — change your sentence a little and press Check sentence again. Mistakes are how we learn. 6. Do steps 1 to 5 again for every word on the page: data, collect, record, form, sort, tally, pictogram, data table, paper form and computer form. One word at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. 7. When you have done every word, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the computing words. Only press it when you really did them all — that button tells your teacher you finished. 8. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 9. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning your own way, type your sentence, and press Check sentence. Same job, new slide. 10. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 11. Keep going until you reach the last slide. On that last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when two things are done: the I explored the computing words button is pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now start with step 1, and tell me when your first word is done. I am right here. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello, data collector! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and shapes that show our ideas. Looking at them helps the ideas stick in your head. You need your eyes, your finger or mouse, and your voice. Let's start. 1. Look at the first model, "What is data?". Press it, and if it moves, drag it slowly to turn it. Try any buttons on it too. I want you to look for a few seconds, not rush. Then tell me one thing you see. 2. Read the caption under that model. A caption is the little bit of writing below the picture. Then press Listen and hear it read out loud. Good listening means eyes on the words while you hear them. 3. Now the second model, "Recording data with a form". Drag it to turn it and press its buttons. Look for the questions on the form. I expect you to notice that a form has questions, and we write our answers next to them. 4. Read its caption, then press Listen again. Try saying one word out loud with the voice. The word "form" is a good one to say. 5. Next is the third model, "Sort, count, and tally". Drag it and press its buttons. Look at how the same things go into one group. I expect you to see one little tally mark for one thing. 6. Read that caption and press Listen. Then count some tally marks with your finger, one, two, three. Counting slowly is doing it well. 7. Now the fourth model, "Make a pictogram and answer questions". Drag it to turn it and press its buttons. Look at the rows of boxes. Remember: one box means one child, not the whole group. 8. Read its caption and press Listen. Then find the longest row with your finger. The longest row is the most, the favourite. 9. Last one, the fifth model, "Be a data collector: the Mini-Project". Drag it and press its buttons. This one shows the whole job: ask, tally, count, colour, answer. I expect you to see the order of those steps. 10. Read the caption and press Listen one more time. Then say to yourself what a data collector does. 11. When you have looked at all five models and heard all five captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only press it when you really did look at every one. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models and it saves your work. Ready to start with model one? Tell me what you see, and I will be right here. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. On this page you become a data collector. Data means the little bits of what we find out, like your favourite fruit. You will try six little discoveries about collecting data, writing it down, and making a picture chart. By the end you will be able to sort, tally, and read a pictogram. You need a pencil, some paper, and colours nearby. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then type your own idea in your own words. Short is fine. One sentence is plenty. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1. Read the little story, and look hard at the picture or model. Point at it with your finger and say out loud what you see. I expect you to look before you type. Step 2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it twice. Think for a moment. Then type your idea in the box and press Check my idea.
