Use words from our unit, like data, sort, tally, or pictogram, if they fit. Step 3. If the page says Look again, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it, then change one small thing in your answer and press Check my idea again. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a little tick. Well done! Step 4. Now press tab 2 and do the same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going to tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6, one at a time. Do not rush. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5. Watch your ticks. When all six tabs have a tick, the top part of the page is done. If one tab has no tick, go back to it and try again with the Hint. Step 6. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides. They show the same discoveries, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 8. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That saves your work for you — I cannot press it, only you can. You will know the page is finished when every discovery tab has a tick and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Press tab 1 now, and tell me what you see. I am right here with you. 🙂

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Code Examples page. On this page we look at a little bit of "code" — that just means lines we read one at a time. Our lines show tally marks for fruit. We do this so you can practise reading data before you make your own chart. By the end, you will be able to look at tally marks and say the number. You need your eyes, your counting finger, and a pencil if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, count out loud, and say each line in your own words. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 1. Look at the example box on the page. Read the first line: Mango, then the marks. Point at each mark with your finger and count out loud: one, two, three, four, five. Then say the line in your own words, like this: "Five friends like mango." Do the same for the banana line and the dates line. A good job means you counted every mark, one by one, and did not skip any. Step 2. Now press the button that says Copy the code. That copies the lines so you can use them. If you have paper, write the same lines out with your pencil — one mark for each friend. If you cannot write it now, that is fine, just read it again. Then press the button under the example to mark it done. I expect your marks to match: five for mango, three for banana, two for dates. Step 3. Scroll down to the slides at the bottom of the page. Press Start. One example will show on each slide. Read the code on that slide out loud, then mark it done, then press the arrow to go to the next one. Keep going until there are no more slides. Doing it well means you read every slide, not just click quickly. Step 4. When you have read every example, press Go to Build It. That takes you to the next part, where you make your own chart. You will know the page is finished when every example has been marked done, all the slides are used up, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Shall we start with step 1? Count the mango marks and tell me the number. 🥭

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello, my clever data collector! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with the answer already worked out, step by step. We look at these so we can see how a good data collector thinks. By the end, you will know how to count tallies, read a pictogram, and find the most and the fewest. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here we go, one step at a time. Step 1. Look at the first worked example on the page. Read the question out loud, slowly. Do not press anything yet! First have a little think and say your own answer out loud. I expect a guess from you, even a small one. Guessing is good thinking, not cheating. Step 2. Now press Show worked solution on that first example. Read the working line by line, from top to bottom. Point with your finger as you read. Ask yourself, "Is this the same as my answer?" If it is different, that is fine. Find the line where your idea and the solution went different ways. That line is the bit you just learned. Step 3. Do the same thing for all 6 worked examples. Read the question, guess, then press Show worked solution and compare. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It tells you how many you have opened. I want all 6 opened, none skipped. Take your time, there is no rush. Step 4. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Read that slide the same way as before: read, think, then press the same buttons you used above. Step 5. When you finish a slide, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are in the deck. One dot for each slide, just like one box for one child in a pictogram! Step 6. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On that last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to read every slide, not click straight past them. How you will know you are finished: the counter at the top shows all 6 worked examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the page is done. Now go and do Step 1, and come back and tell me your guess for the first question. I will be right here waiting. 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a recipe. On this page you will meet 5 methods for being a data collector — asking, writing down, sorting, counting and making a picture chart. We do this so the steps stay in your head when you collect your own data. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. Let's start! 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step. Then say it out loud in your own voice. When you have said it, press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to read before you press — no fast clicking! 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step, one press at a time. Say every new step out loud too. Keep going until the page tells you Method complete. That message means you finished that one method. Well done! 3. Now do the same for the next method. Read a step, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and keep going until it says Method complete. Do this for all 5 methods. I expect you to finish every method, not just the first one. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one method on it. Press Start on the first slide. Then use the same buttons on that slide, just like before, and say each step out loud. 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. Move along the dots one by one. 6. On the last slide, do the steps, then press the finish button. That is the very end of the deck. I expect you to visit every slide, not skip any. You will know the page is finished when all 5 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, then tell me when your first method says Method complete. Take your time — there's no rush.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello, my data collector! Today we are on the Guided Practice page. This is where you practise everything from our unit: what data is, what a form is, tally marks, and pictograms. We practise so the words stick in your head and you can use them all by yourself. You need a pencil, a piece of paper, and your thinking brain. Here is what I expect from you: try each question first on your own, and only press for a hint after you have had a good go. There are 7 questions on this page, and then a small deck of slides at the bottom. Let's go step by step. Step 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then work it out on paper or in your head. If the question shows tally marks, count them one by one and point with your finger. If it asks "the most" or "the fewest", remember the longest row is the most. I expect a real try from you before you type anything. Step 2. Type your answer in the box. Try to write a whole little sentence, like "A form is a list of questions." Then press Check my answer. That button tells you if you got it right. Step 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. Take the first hint and try again before you ask for the next one. If you are still stuck, press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working, so you can carry on yourself. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 4. If your answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint, fix your answer, and press Check my answer again. Keep going until it is right. Step 5. Now do the same for every question, one to seven. Read, think, type, press Check my answer. Do not skip any. The page is finished when all 7 questions are right. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. This is your practice round — try to answer without hints this time. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your answer, press Check my answer, and press Give me a hint or Show next step only if you really need them. Step 8. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the whole page is finished when all 7 questions show as right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then come back and tell me — I would love to hear which question was the trickiest one for you. Ready? Tell me question one, and let's start.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today we are on the Quick Reference page. This page is like a little treasure box. It holds all the important words and facts from Unit 8, Be a Data Collector, in one place. We read it so the words stay in your head. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up close by. There are three steps. Step 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page slowly, from the top to the bottom. When you see a little speaker picture, press Listen. Listen to the word, then say it out loud too. Look for these words: data, collect, record, form, sort, tally, pictogram, and data table. I expect you to read every box, not just the first one. Go slowly. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a moment, or look away from the page. Say out loud what data means. Say what a tally mark is. Say what a pictogram is. Your own words are perfect — you do not need to copy the page. For example, you might say, "A tally is one little line for one thing." I expect you to say at least three facts out loud. You can say them to me here, or to your grown-up. Step 3. Press Reference reviewed. This button is at the bottom of the page. Press it only when you have read the whole page and said your facts out loud. That button tells the page you are done. I cannot press it for you — that part is your job! You will know the page is finished when you have read every box, said three facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Now go and do Step 1. Read the page slowly and press Listen on each speaker. Tell me when you are done, and we will do Step 2 together. 🙂

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Build It. It is where you become a real data collector. You will ask questions, write answers down, count them with little marks, and colour a picture chart. By the end you will be able to make a pictogram and say which fruit is the favourite. Get a pencil, a sheet of paper, and some colours. Ready? Here are your steps. Step 1. Look at the first build-it activity at the top of the page. Read it slowly. Then press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listening and reading together helps the words stick. I expect you to know two things after this: what to get, and what to do. If you are not sure, press Listen one more time. Step 2. Get the things it names. Most of these need only paper, a pencil, and colours. Put them on your table before you start. A good data collector gets ready first, so nothing stops them in the middle. Step 3. Now do the activity on your paper. Take your time — there is no rush. For a tally, make one little line for one thing, never two. For a pictogram, colour one box for one child. Do it carefully, not fast. Step 4. Write in the box on the screen. Type your answer, or what you noticed. Even a few words is good, like "mango has 5" or "banana row is longest". I expect your box to show the numbers you counted, not just "done". That is how you record your data. Step 5. Press Mark complete under that activity. Only press it when you really did it on paper and wrote in the box. Pressing it is your way of saying, "Teacher, this one is finished."

Step 6. Now do the same for all 8 activities, one at a time, in order. Read, press Listen, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. Do not jump ahead. Each one helps the next one — your tally marks give you the numbers for your pictogram. Step 7. When all 8 have Mark complete pressed, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. That saves all your good work. Step 8. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 9. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, write in the box, Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Step 10. On the last slide, press Finish activities. Well done, data collector! You will know the page is finished when every activity says complete, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom of the page and on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1. Tell me when you have pressed Listen, and I will help you with the first activity. 🍋

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello, my clever data collector! Today we play "spot the mistake."

On this page, each card shows a little mix-up about collecting data. Something in it is wrong. Your job is to find it. We do this because good data collectors always check their work. By the end, you will be able to look at a chart or a tally and say, "Wait — that is not right!"

You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil. Here are your steps. Step 1. Look at the first card. Read it slowly, all the way to the end. Say it out loud if that helps. I expect you to guess the bug yourself BEFORE you press anything. Even a wrong guess is good — guessing makes your brain strong. Step 2. Now press Show the bug. It will tell you what was wrong and what it should be. Read it, then say out loud in your own words WHY it was wrong. For example: "One box means one child, not the whole group." I expect a short sentence from you, not just a nod. Step 3. Now press the button to mark that bug done. Then move to the next card and do Step 1, Step 2 and Step 3 again. Keep going until every card has been done. Step 4. Look under the cards. There is a slide deck with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. Step 5. On each slide, find the bug first with your own eyes. Then press Show the bug, say why it was wrong, and mark it done. Then press the arrow to go to the next slide. I expect you to try first every single time — no peeking early! Step 6. When you have finished all the cards and all the slides, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. You will know the page is finished when every card and every slide is marked done, and the I practised debugging button has been pressed. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you are looking at the first card, and I will help you if you get stuck. 🍋

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Let's get you ready for this page. This page is called Computing Fluency. Fluency means quick and sure — like when you say your own name without stopping to think. You will answer 7 quick questions about being a data collector. We do this so the words data, form, tally and pictogram pop into your head fast. You need nothing but your eyes and your fingers to type. Take your time to read, but answer as soon as you know. Here is what I expect from you: read each question twice, then type a short, clear answer. Try it yourself before you ask me. It is fine to be wrong — mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Before you start, whisper these four words to yourself: data, form, tally, pictogram. Data is what we find out. A form is a list of questions. A tally is one little mark for one thing. A pictogram is a picture chart, and one box means one child. This warm-up makes the sprint much easier. Step 2. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. Do not worry about it! It is just there for fun. Being right matters more than being fast. Step 3. Read question one. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check & continue. Type a short answer in your own words, like "she writes it down" — not just one letter. Step 4. Keep going, one question at a time. Read, type, press Check & continue. Do this for all 7 questions. If a question shows a pictogram or tally marks, point at each box or line with your finger and count out loud. One box, one child. Step 5. If you get stuck on one, do not sit and worry. Make your best guess, press Check & continue, and come back to that idea later with me. I am right here if you want a hint. Step 6. At the end you will see your score. You need most of them right. If you got fewer than that, press Run the sprint again. That is not a fail — it is practice, and the second sprint is nearly always better. Step 7. Run the sprint again as many times as you need. Each time, ask yourself: which question tripped me up last time? Watch for that one. Step 8. You will know the page is finished when you finish a sprint with enough right answers and the page lets you move on. Then come and tell me your score, and tell me which word was the hardest. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me how it goes. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the games on this page. This is Unit 8, Be a Data Collector. The games ask you little questions about data, tally marks and pictograms. Playing them helps the words stick in your head. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Here is our plan. Step 1: Look at the list of games. Pick one you like. Press Start game on that game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then tap the answer you think is right. Do this for every round in the game. I expect you to think before you tap — not just guess fast. Each round you get right gives you a star. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: When the game ends, look at your stars. If the game does not have all its stars yet, press Play again. Play the same game once more. This time you will remember some answers, so you should get more right. I expect you to try again with a happy heart, even if you got some wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. When a game has all its stars, it is mastered. That means you really know it! Step 3: Now do the same for the other games. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again until that game has all its stars. Keep going, one game at a time, until every game is mastered. I expect you to finish one game before starting the next one. That helps your brain hold the idea. How you will know you are done: when every game on the page has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not press anything special at the end. You will just see all the games full of stars. Now go and press Start game on your first game. Tell me when you have played one round, and tell me what the question asked. I will be right here. 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. Here is what it is. There are 4 little stories about real life — at home, at school, at the market, and in your community. Each one asks a data question, like "Which fruit is the most?" or "Which fruit has the fewest?" You will use what you learned: counting tally marks and reading a pictogram. Why do we do it? Because data collectors do not just make charts — they use them to answer questions. This page shows you that your chart is useful in real life. What I expect from you: read slowly, count carefully with your finger, and write your answer in a full sentence. Show me how you counted, not just the number. Get a pencil and paper next to you for counting. Here are all the steps. Step 1: Read the first problem out loud, slowly. Look for the question words: "how many", "the most", or "the fewest". Point at the picture or the tally marks with your finger. I expect you to be able to tell me, in your own words, what the question is asking before you answer it. Step 2: Work it out. Count one box, or one tally mark, at a time — one, two, three — and say the numbers out loud. Remember: one box means one child. The longest row is the most. The shortest row is the fewest. Step 3: Type your working and your answer in the box, then press Check answer. Good working looks like this: "I counted 4 boxes. Banana is the most." If you feel stuck, press Hint first and try again — asking for a hint is smart, not a mistake. Step 4: When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Now do the same three things for problem 2, then problem 3, then problem 4: read it, count it, type it, press Check answer. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 5: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 6: On each slide, do the same as before: read, count, type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 7: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. How will you know the page is finished? All 4 problems will say your answers are right, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your work saved. Ready? Start with problem 1 and tell me what the question is asking. 🍌

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Stay Safe Online page. This page has three safety rules for using computers and the internet. We learn them because a data collector like you will one day type answers, tap forms and look things up on a screen. Being safe is just as important as being clever. By the end, you will be able to say each rule in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and your listening ears. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say the words out loud, and think of one real example for each rule. There are three steps. Step 1. Read every rule slowly. Look at the first rule on the page and read it word by word. Where you see a little speaker, press Listen and let it read the rule to you. Then do the same for rule two and rule three. Do it well by going slowly — no racing. I expect you to read all three rules, and press Listen on every speaker you can see. Step 2. Say each rule in your own words, and give one example from your own life. So for the rule about checking before you trust, you might say, "Not everything on the internet is true, so I check with my grown-up." For the rule about telling someone, you might say, "If something on the screen scares me, I tell my mum or my teacher." For the rule about other people's work, you might say, "I do not take someone's picture and say I made it. I put my own name on my own work." I expect three short sentences from you, one for each rule, in your own voice. Step 3. Press the button that says I know these rules at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have read all three rules and said them in your own words. That button is how the page saves your work — I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when all three rules are read, you have said each one your own way, and you have pressed I know these rules. Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me when you have read the rules, and we will do Step 2 together. 🙂

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Explain Your Thinking" page. On this page you say your thinking out loud in words. You will explain what data is, how a form works, how we sort and tally, and how a pictogram shows the most and the fewest. Doing this helps the ideas stick in your head. All you need is this page and your thinking brain. A grown-up can help you type. Here is what I expect from you: not one tiny word. I want a little answer with the idea in it, using our unit words like data, form, tally, pictogram, most and fewest. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 4 things to do. Here they all are. 1. There are 4 prompts on the page. A prompt is a question that asks you to explain. Read the prompt slowly. Under it you will see key ideas — these are the words I want to hear in your answer. Read them too, and say them out loud once. I expect you to read before you write, every time. 2. Now write in the box. Say what you know, say the rule you used, and say why your answer makes sense. Like this: "A pictogram is a picture chart. One box means one child. So if 5 like mango, we colour 5 boxes." Then press Check your reasoning. If it asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check your reasoning again. I expect you to try your own words first, before you look at any answer. 3. Next, press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Ask yourself: did I use the key ideas? Did I say why? If you missed an idea, go back and add it to your box. Do this for all 4 prompts. I expect you to compare, not copy. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Do the same things again: read, write, press Check your reasoning, then Show model explanation. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? When all 4 explanations use the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Ready? Start with prompt one, and tell me what it says. I am right here with you. 🙂

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Welcome to your Unit Project, my clever data collector! In this project you will be a real data collector. You will ask your friends one question, write down every answer, and make a colourful picture chart called a pictogram. We do this so you can see your data with your own eyes, and say which fruit is the favourite. You need a pencil, some colours, a sheet of paper, and about five friends or family members to ask. A grown-up can sit with you. Here is what I expect from you: ask kindly, write down every answer straight away, count carefully, and colour neatly. Do your own work, and take your time. 1. Read the Unit Project first. Look at the top of the page. Read what you will make: a tally, a pictogram, and the answer to "which fruit wins?" Then read the list of things a good project has. That list is your helper. It says: I asked my friends the question, I made a tally mark for each answer, I counted the marks and wrote the number, I coloured my pictogram, and I found the favourite fruit. Read the list out loud once. I expect you to know what you are making before you start. 2. Now make your project, one bit at a time, ticking the list as you go. 2a. Draw three rows on your paper: Mango, Banana, Dates. Ask your friends, "What is your favourite fruit — mango, banana, or dates?" About five people is plenty. Tick the first thing on the list when you have asked them. 2b. For every answer, make one little mark in the right row. One mark for one friend, like this: | | |. Do it straight away, or you will forget. Tick the second thing on your list. 2c. Now count the marks in each row. Write the number at the end of each row. Count slowly, and point at each mark with your finger. Tick the third thing. 2d. Make your pictogram. Draw a row of boxes for each fruit and colour one box for each friend. Remember: one box means one child, not the whole group. If four friends said mango, you colour four boxes. Tick the fourth thing. 2e. Look at your pictogram. The longest coloured row is the most — that is the favourite. The shortest row is the fewest. Say out loud: "The favourite fruit is ______." Tick the last thing. 3. Finish the page. Look at your list again. Is every single thing ticked? If one is missing, go back and do that bit. When all of them are ticked, press the button that says "My project is finished". You will know the page is done when every item on the list has a tick and you have pressed "My project is finished". Now start with step 1, and tell me when you have read the list. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today we finish Unit 8 with the Unit Challenge. The Unit Challenge is a little quiz about being a data collector. You have already learned a lot: data, forms, tally marks, and pictograms. This quiz lets you show what you know. There are 12 questions. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and no rush. I will not tell you any answers — but I will help you think. Ready? Here is the whole plan. 1. Get ready. Sit comfy and have a pencil and paper near you, in case you want to draw tally marks to help you count. Take a slow breath. I expect you to try every question by yourself, even the hard ones. Mistakes are how we learn. 2. Read question one. Read the question twice before you answer. Slowly. Look for the important word: is it about data, a form, a tally, or a pictogram? That word tells you what the question is really asking. 3. Look at all the answer choices before you pick. Do not grab the first one. Read each choice, then ask yourself, "Does this match what we learned?" I expect you to think about every choice, not just one. 4. Choose your answer, then press Next question. Only press it when you are happy with your choice. If a question is about "the most" or "the favourite", remember the longest row wins. If it is about "the fewest", the shortest row wins. 5. Keep going, one question at a time, until you reach question 12. After each answer, press Next question. Take your time — there's no rush. Nobody is timing you. 6. Little helper for counting questions. If a question shows tally marks, touch each mark and count out loud: one, two, three. One mark means one thing. One box in a pictogram means one child. That is the rule that helps you most. 7. At the end you will see your score. This tells you how many you got right out of 12. I expect you to look at it kindly, whatever it says. It is telling us what to practise next. 8. You pass with more than half right. That means 7 or more out of 12. If your score is high enough, well done — you are a real data collector! 9. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing! It just means one or two ideas need a little more practice. Come and tell me which question felt tricky, and we will look at that together before you try again. 10. When you have passed, press Continue. That moves you on and finishes the page. You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Now go and read question one. When you have answered it, come and tell me how it felt — I am right here. 🙂

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text:
Hello, my games developer! Today we get ready to make games. This page is called Tools and Setup. It tells us what we need before we build. We do this first so nothing stops us later. By the end, you will have your tablet and your paper ready, and you will know how to open ScratchJr. What I want from you is simple: look carefully, check each thing, and ask your grown-up if you need help. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1: Read Tools and Setup. Look at the page on your screen and read the list of things you need. For this unit it is ScratchJr, a free app where you join picture blocks to make a game. You also need paper, a pencil and colours for planning. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to be able to name the app we will use — ScratchJr. Step 2: Check each tool. Now check them one by one, like a helper doing a job. Is ScratchJr on your tablet? Tap it and see if it opens. Do you have paper, a pencil and some colours next to you? If something is missing, ask your grown-up to help you get it. I expect every tool on the list to be checked, not just looked at. Step 3: Press My tools are ready. When everything is there and ScratchJr opens, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says My tools are ready. Only press it when it is true. That button is how the page saves your work, so I cannot press it for you — you must do it yourself. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed My tools are ready and it shows you are done. Then we can go and make a frog hop! 🐸

Tell me when you have finished Step 1, and I will check it with you.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 9: Be a Games Developer. A games developer is a person who makes computer games. In this unit you will make a tiny game, try it, and fix it when it goes wrong. This first page is small and easy — it just shows you what is coming. There are 3 steps. I will be right here with you. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen and read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let it read to you. You can press Listen twice if you want. I expect you to look for three big words: test, error, and debug. Test means trying your game to see if it works. Error means a mistake. Debug means finding the mistake and fixing it. Step 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the screen. Just say it out loud, like you are telling a friend. Something like, "I will make a little game and fix it when it goes wrong." One good sentence is plenty. You can say it to me here, or to your grown-up. I expect your own words, not perfect words. Step 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Only press it after you have read the page and said your sentence. Continue is the button that takes you to the next part, where the real teaching starts. Take your time — there's no rush. How will you know the page is finished? You have read the overview, you have said one sentence about what you will learn, and you have pressed Continue. When the next page opens, this page is done. Ready? Start with Step 1, then tell me your own sentence for Step 2. I can't wait to hear it! 🐸

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello, my games developer! Today we learn how to make a little game and fix it when it goes wrong. This page is called The Lesson. It has 5 short ideas, called concepts. They teach you what a games developer is, how to make a frog hop when you tap it, what testing means, what an error is, and what debugging means. By the end, you will be able to make a tiny game, try it, and fix one wrong block. What I expect from you: read slowly, listen, and say things out loud. Talking helps your brain remember. You can ask your grown-up to help you press the buttons. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first concept box on the page. It is called "We are games developers!" Read it slowly with your finger under the words. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. I expect you to hear one big idea: a games developer is a person who makes computer games. Step 2. Each concept has an example under it. Say the example out loud, like a teacher. Then make it your own. For example, say: "My character is a cat, and my cat will hop when I tap it." Your own example is the best kind. Step 3. Now go to the second concept, "Make a tap game and test it." Read it, press Listen, and say the star word out loud: testing. Testing means trying your program to see if it works. Say it three times so it sticks. Step 4. Read the third concept, "Find the error." Press Listen. An error is a mistake — the game does the wrong thing. Say out loud what happened to Maya's cat: she wanted 1 step, but it went 3 steps. That is an error. Step 5. Read the fourth concept, "Debug it: fix the mistake." Press Listen. Debug means to find the mistake and fix it. Say this out loud with me: "Mistakes are okay. I can fix them." Every games developer does this all day. Step 6. Read the fifth concept, "Make your own tap game." Press Listen. Then say your plan out loud: your character, and what it will do when you tap it — hop, move, or say a word. I expect one clear plan, not five. Step 7. When you have read all five concepts, scroll to the bottom and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after you have really read them all. That button tells the page you are done reading. Step 8. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same five ideas, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Step 9. On each slide, use the same buttons as before, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Go slowly. Before you move on, say one thing you remember from that slide out loud. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That closes the deck nicely. How will you know the page is finished? You will have pressed I studied the concepts, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the page is complete. Now go and do Step 1, and tell me when it is done. Take your time — there's no rush.

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today we learn our Unit 9 words together. These are the words a games developer uses. A games developer is a person who makes computer games — that is you today! When you know these words, you can talk about your game like a real developer. You need your voice, your eyes, and your fingers for typing. Here is our plan, step by step. 1. Look at the first word card. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to look at the word while you listen — that helps your eyes and ears learn together. 2. Now say the word out loud. Say it slowly, like the Listen voice did. Then say the meaning in your own words — not the same words on the page, YOUR words. For example, for "character" you might say, "it is the frog in my game." I expect a try, even a wobbly one. Wobbly tries are how we learn. 3. Now type a sentence with the word in it. Make it about your own life or your own game, like "My character is a cat." Then press Check sentence. Read what the checker tells you. If it says to add something, fix your sentence and press Check sentence again. 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for every word on the page. Our words are games developer, character, block, test, error, debug, and ScratchJr. Take your time — there is no rush. I expect every word to get a Listen, a say-out-loud, and a sentence. 5. When every word is done, go to the bottom and press I explored the computing words. Only press it when you really have done them all. That button tells the page you finished this part. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is like practice — the same words again, so they stick in your head. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, say it out loud, type your sentence, press Check sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. 8. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the whole page! You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the computing words, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with word one, press Listen, and tell me which word you are on. 🐸

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Visual Models. Visual models are pictures and shapes that show our big ideas. There are 5 of them, one for each idea in Unit 9. Looking at them helps the words stick in your head, like a picture in a story book. By the end you will be able to say what testing, error and debug mean. You need your eyes, your finger, and your listening ears. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: look slowly, touch every model, and say each caption out loud. Slow looking is good looking! Step 1. Look at the first model, "We are games developers!". Put your finger on it and drag it slowly to turn it around. If it has buttons, press them one at a time and watch what changes. Good work here means you can tell me one thing you noticed. Step 2. Under that model there is a caption, which is the little bit of writing. Press Listen and hear it read to you. Then say it out loud with me, slowly. Step 3. Now go to model 2, "Make a tap game and test it". Drag it to turn it, press its buttons, then press Listen for its caption. I want you to spot the star word: testing means trying your program to see if it works. Step 4. Go to model 3, "Find the error". Turn it with your finger and press its buttons. Press Listen for the caption. Remember, an error is a mistake, when the game does the wrong thing. Step 5. Go to model 4, "Debug it: fix the mistake". Drag it, press its buttons, then press Listen. Debug means to find the mistake and fix it. Mistakes are okay, they are just little puzzles. Step 6. Go to model 5, "Make your own tap game: the Mini-Project". Turn it and press its buttons, then press Listen for the caption. This one shows the games developer plan: plan it, build it, test it, fix it. Step 7. Check yourself. Did you touch all 5 models? Did you press Listen under each one? If you missed one, go back and do it now. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 8. When you have looked at all 5, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. I cannot press it for you, so it must be you. When you press it, the page is finished and your work is saved. Now go and do Step 1, then come back and tell me one thing you noticed. 🐸

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello, my games developer! Today we are on the Explore the Concept page. This page has six little discoveries about making games. You will try things, guess what happens, and type your own idea. By the end you will know three big words: testing, error and debug. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. Grown-up nearby? Great. Let's start. Here is our whole plan. There are four parts. 1. Open a discovery. At the top you will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press tab 1 first. Read the little story on it, and look at the picture or the blocks. Take your time. I expect you to look carefully and say to yourself, "What is happening here?" Do not rush to the box yet. 2. Type your idea. Under the picture there is a question and a box. Think first, then type what you think in the box. Then press Check my idea. Write your own words, even short ones like "the frog hops when I tap it". That is a good answer. If it says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint, read it, and try once more. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a tick. Well done! 3. Do all six. Now press tab 2 and do the same thing: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Then tab 3, then 4, then 5, then 6. One tab at a time, please. I expect a tick on every tab. Remember, a wrong try is not a fail. Mistakes are how we learn. 4. Do the slides at the bottom. Scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All six tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is the page complete! Now go and press tab 1. Read it, then tell me what you see, and I will help you with the rest. 🐸

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello, games developer! Today we are on the Code Examples page. Here you look at little bits of code — the blocks that tell your character what to do. Reading code is like reading a plan: you say what each block does, one at a time. By the end you will be able to look at a set of blocks and know what will happen before you even tap. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want to try it on a tablet. Here is what I expect from you today. Say each line out loud in your own words. Go slowly. It is fine to be unsure — just have a good guess. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read each code example. Look at the first example on the page. Put your finger on the top block and say what it does, like "this one starts when I tap." Then move your finger down to the next block and say that one too. Do this until you reach the last block. A good job sounds like a little story: "Tap the frog... it hops... then it stops." I expect you to talk out loud, not just look. Step 2: Press Copy the code. This copies the code so you can try it yourself. If you have ScratchJr on a tablet, build the same blocks and tap your character to test it. Testing means trying it to see if it works. When you have read it and tried it, press the button under the example to mark it done. Only press it after you really read it — that is how a good developer works. Step 3: Do the slides at the bottom. Under the examples there is a deck of cards, with one example on each slide. Press Start. Read the code on that slide the same way — finger on each line, say what it does. Then mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next one. Keep going until there are no more slides. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 4: Press Go to Build It. Do this only when you have read every single example. That button takes you to the next part, where you build your own game. Do not press it early, or you will miss something fun. You will know the page is finished when every example is marked done, all the slides are read, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me what the first block does. 🐸

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello, my games developer! Today we are on the Learn the Method page. A method is a way to do something, step by step, like a recipe. This page has 5 methods about making games, testing them, and fixing bugs. By the end, you will know how a real games developer works: make it, try it, fix it. Here is what I expect from you: press the buttons yourself, read each step, and say it out loud. Slow is good. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the very first step. Then press the button that says "Show me the next step". A new step will pop up. I expect you to read each step out loud before you press again. Step 2. Keep pressing "Show me the next step" again and again. Each time, say the step out loud, like you are teaching a little brother or a toy. Stop pressing when the page says "Method complete". That means you finished that one method. Well done! Step 3. Now do the same thing for every method. There are 5 methods in all. For each one: read a step, say it out loud, press "Show me the next step", and keep going until it says "Method complete". Five methods, five times "Method complete". Step 4. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. Each slide has one method on it, the same as before. On the first slide, press "Start". Step 5. On each slide, use the same buttons to move through the steps, one at a time. Say each step out loud again. Saying it helps your brain remember it. Step 6. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many slides are left. Step 7. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you know you are finished: all 5 methods say "Method complete", and the last slide has had its finish button pressed. That is the whole page done! Ready? Go and press "Show me the next step" on method one, then come back and tell me what the step said. I'll be right here. 🐸

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello, games developer! Today we work on the Worked Examples page together. A worked example is a question with the answer shown, step by step. It is like watching me solve one, then trying it yourself. This helps you learn how to test a game and how to find and fix a mistake. All you need is your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil. Here is what I expect from you: try each question in your head FIRST, before you peek. Guessing and being wrong is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. Find the first worked example. Read the question slowly. If a word is hard, ask your grown-up or ask me. Step 2. Now think of your own answer before you look. Say it out loud, or whisper it. Even a small guess counts. This is the most important part. Step 3. Press the button that says Show worked solution. Now read the answer line by line, from the top to the bottom. Point with your finger as you read. Step 4. Compare. Ask yourself: was my answer the same? If yes, say "I got it!" If not, that is okay — find the one part where your idea was different. That is the bit you just learned. Step 5. Do the same thing for every worked example. There are six of them. Read, think, press Show worked solution, compare. One at a time, no rushing. Step 6. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It counts how many examples you have opened. Keep going until it shows all six are open. That means the top part of the page is done. Step 7. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. It has the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons — read the question, think first, then press the button to see the solution. Step 9. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all six examples opened, AND you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me when you have read the first question. Take your time — there's no rush.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello, my Games Developer! Today we are on the Guided Practice page. This is where you practise the big ideas of Unit 9: testing, finding an error, and debugging. Practice makes these words stick in your head. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is our plan, step by step. 1. Look at the first practice question on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Then work it out in your head, or write it on paper. I expect you to think first, before you type anything. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Now type your answer in the box. Use words from our unit, like testing, error, debug, or Start on Tap. Then press Check my answer. A short, clear answer is a good answer. 3. If your brain feels stuck, that is okay! Press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint helps a little more. Try again after each hint before you press it again. 4. Still stuck after the hints? Press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working. Read it, then finish the rest yourself. I expect you to keep trying — mistakes are how we learn. 5. Do this for every question. There are 6 questions in all. Keep going until each one is right. When all six are right, that part of the page is done. Brilliant work! 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your answer, press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Same job, new place. 8. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. 🌟

Ready? Tell me your answer to question one, and I will check it with you.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Quick Reference. It is like a little card that holds all the important words of Unit 9, Be a Games Developer, in one place. We read it so the big words stay in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what testing, error and debug mean, all by yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here are the three steps. 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page slowly, from the top to the bottom. Read each word and its meaning: games developer, character, block, test, error, debug, ScratchJr. Where you see a little speaker, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Say it back after the voice. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to read every word, not just look at the page. 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a second, then say them out loud. Try these three: testing means trying my game to see if it works. An error means my game did the wrong thing. Debug means I find the mistake and fix it. Say each one in a full sentence, in your own words — not word for word from the page. If one word slips away, peek at the page, then say it again without looking. I expect three good sentences from you, said out loud. 3. Press Reference reviewed. When you have read the page and said the words, look at the bottom of the page and press the button that says Reference reviewed. That button is yours to press — it tells the page that you did the work. I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when you have read every word, said the three key facts out loud in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Ready? Start with step 1 and tell me when you have read it all. 🐸

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello, games developer! Today we build. On this page you make your very own tap game, little bit by little bit. You will choose a character, put blocks in order, test your game, and fix a bug. Testing means trying your game to see if it works. All you need is your tablet with ScratchJr, a pencil, some paper, and your happy trying-again face. Here we go, step by step. 1. Look at the first activity box on the page. Press Listen. My voice will read it to you. Listen all the way to the end. Then get the things it names, like your tablet or your pencil. I expect you to have everything ready before you start. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Now do that first activity. It asks you to choose your character. Circle one — frog, cat, dog or bird — or draw your own. Then in the answer box, type or write which one you picked. A good answer names your character, like "I picked a frog."

3. When you have done it, press Mark complete under that activity. Only press it when you really did the activity. That button tells the page, "I finished this one!"

4. Next activity: Put the Blocks in Order. Press Listen first. Then write 1, 2 and 3 next to the blocks Hop, Start on Tap and End. Think: which block must come first, so the game knows when to start? Which one comes last? Write your order in the box, then press Mark complete. 5. Next: Make It Hop When You Tap. Open ScratchJr. Add a frog. Join the blocks and then tap the frog to test it. Did it hop? Then change the number 4 to a bigger number and tap again. In the box write what happened, like "It hopped higher." Then press Mark complete. 6. Next: Find the Error. Press Listen. Maya wanted her cat to move 1 step, but it went too far. Circle the block that does not match her plan, and write the number it should be. I expect you to point at one block only — usually just one block is wrong. Then press Mark complete. 7. Next: Fix the Bug. Sami tapped his frog and nothing happened. Circle the block that is wrong, and write which start block it should be instead. Then, if you can, fix it in ScratchJr and test it again. Write in the box what you fixed. Press Mark complete. 8. Next: Draw. Draw your character doing something fun in the box. Make it big and colourful. Then write one sentence about it, like "My dog jumps when I tap it." Press Mark complete. 9. Next: Choose and Plan. Circle your character, then circle what it will do when tapped — hop, move, or say a word. That is your plan. A good plan says one clear thing your character will do. Write it in the box and press Mark complete. 10. Last one: Build It and Test It. In ScratchJr, press the big plus for a new project, pick a Background, press the blue plus to add your character, join your blocks, then tap your character to test it. Write in the box whether it worked, or what you changed. Press Mark complete. 11. When every activity has Mark complete pressed, go to the bottom and press Finish activities. That saves all your good work. 12. Under the page there is a deck of slides. They have the same build-it activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the activity, use the same buttons on the slide, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 13. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity says complete, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom and on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1 and press Listen. Tell me when you have chosen your character, and I will check it with you. 🐸

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text: Hello, my Grade 1 games developer! Today we are on the Debug It page. A bug is a mistake in a program. Debug means find the mistake and fix it. Real games developers do this every single day. By the end, you will be a bug-finder too! You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a happy heart. Mistakes are okay. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Look at the first card. Each card shows a small program with blocks. Read the plan first — what should the character do? Then look at each block, one at a time. Point with your finger. Ask yourself: does this block match the plan? Try to find the bug yourself before you press anything. I expect you to really look, and to guess. A guess is not a fail. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Now press Show the bug. It will show you which block is wrong and what it should be instead. Say out loud why it was wrong. For example: "The block said Start on Green Flag, but we tap the frog, so it needs Start on Tap." Then press the button on the card to mark that bug done. I expect you to say the why in your own words, not just press the button. Step 3. Do the same for every card on the page. One card at a time. Look, guess, press Show the bug, say why, mark it done. Remember: usually only ONE block is wrong. Change one thing, then test. Step 4. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. There is a little deck with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. Step 5. On each slide, find the bug with your eyes first. Then press Show the bug. Say why that block was wrong. Then mark it done. I expect a guess from you before you press! Step 6. Press the arrow to go to the next slide. Do the same thing again: find, Show the bug, say why, mark done, arrow. Keep going until the slides are finished. Step 7. When all the cards and all the slides are done, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. That button is yours to press — it saves your good work. You will know the page is finished when every card is marked done, every slide is marked done, and you have pressed I practised debugging. Ready? Start with card one. Tell me which block you think is the bug, and I will be right here. 🐸

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for the Games page. This page is where we play little games about Unit 9, Be a Games Developer. Each game asks you questions about words like testing, error and debug. Playing them helps the words stick in your head. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a happy face for mistakes. Mistakes are how we learn. Here is what I expect from you: read each question slowly, think before you tap, and keep trying if you get one wrong. Take your time — there's no rush. There are three steps. Here they all are. 1. Pick a game and press Start game. Look at the list of games on the page. Choose any one you like. Press the button that says Start game. Now a question comes up with some answers to choose from. Read the question, then read every answer before you tap one. Tap the answer you think is right. If you get it right, you earn a star. If you get it wrong, that is okay — read the little explanation, because it tells you why. I expect you to answer every round in that game, one at a time, and to look at the explanation each time. 2. Press Play again to collect more stars. When the game ends, you will see how many stars you got. To get more stars, press the button that says Play again. The same game runs again, so this time you already know some answers. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. That means you filled up every star for that game. I expect you to keep pressing Play again until that one game has all its stars before you move on. 3. Master every game on the page. Go back to the game list and choose the next game. Do the same thing: press Start game, answer the rounds, then press Play again until all its stars are full. Keep going, one game at a time, until every game on the page is mastered. Do not rush to the next game before the one you are on is full of stars. I expect you to finish games one by one, not jump around. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not have to press anything special at the end. Every game will show its full stars, and that is your finish line. Now go on — press Start game on your first game, and tell me how the first question goes. I am right here with you. 🌟

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's get ready for the Computing Fluency page. This page is a little speed game. You answer six quick questions about being a games developer. It helps the words stick in your head, like practising a song until you know it. By the end, you will say words like testing, error and debug fast and easily. You need your eyes, your fingers for typing, and a happy brain. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: try your best on every question, answer quickly but carefully, and stay smiling if one is wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just for fun — it shows how fast you go. Do not worry about it. Take your time if you need to. 2. Read question one slowly. Think about what it is really asking. If it says "What does testing mean?", picture yourself tapping the frog to see if it hops. 3. Type your answer in the box. Use short, clear words. A full sentence is lovely, like "Testing means trying your program to see if it works."

4. Press Check & continue. The page will tell you if you were right, and then question two comes up. Keep going the same way for all six questions. 5. If a question is tricky, remember our four star words: testing means trying your program to see if it works, an error is a mistake, debug means find the mistake and fix it, and Start on Tap is the block that waits for a tap. I will not tell you the answers — you know these! 6. Keep going until you finish all six. That is the whole sprint. Well done for finishing it! 7. Now look at your score. You need most of them right. If you got fewer than that, press Run the sprint again and try the whole six once more. That is not failing — that is practice, just like a real games developer testing again. 8. You will know the page is finished when you get enough right in one sprint. The page will show you it is done. Then come back and tell me how you did! Ready? Go and read question one, then tell me what you typed. 🐸

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today we are learning how to stay safe online. This page has some safety rules. We read them, we say them in our own words, and then we press a button to show we know them. This matters because you are a games developer now, and games developers use computers and the internet. By the end you will be able to say three safety rules by yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and a quiet moment to think. Here are the three things to do on this page, one at a time. 1. Read every rule slowly. Look at the rules on your screen. Read them one by one, not all in a rush. Where you see a little speaker, press Listen and hear the words read out loud. That helps if a word looks tricky. I expect you to read all the rules, top to bottom, before you move on. If a word is hard, ask me or ask your grown-up. 2. Say each rule in your own words. Now close your mouth for a second, think, then say the rule out loud like you are telling a friend. For example, one rule says to check before you trust — you might say, "Not everything on the internet is true, so I check with a grown-up." Then give an example from your own life, like a time you saw something online at home. I expect one short sentence for each rule, in your own words, plus one small example. It does not have to be perfect. Your own words are what make it stick. 3. Press "I know these rules" at the bottom. Only press it after you have read every rule and said them in your own words. That button is your promise that you know the rules. I expect you to be honest with yourself — if one rule still feels fuzzy, go back and read it again first, then press the button. You will know the page is finished when you have read every rule, said each one your own way with an example, and pressed "I know these rules" at the bottom. That button is what saves your work, so do not forget it! One last thing to remember, and it is the most important rule of all: if anything online ever worries you or makes you feel funny inside, tell your parent or your teacher straight away. That is exactly what grown-ups are for. When you have done step 1, tell me, and we will do step 2 together. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's get started. 🐸

This page is called Solve Real Problems. It has four little problems about making games. Each one is a real "oops!" moment, like when you tap a frog and nothing happens. You will use our unit words: testing, error, debug, and block. By the end, you will be able to spot the wrong block and say how to fix it — just like a real games developer. What you need: your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. What I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then answer in your own words. Do not rush. Mistakes are fine here — mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first problem on the page. Read it slowly, all the way to the end. Then read it one more time. Ask yourself: what is this problem asking me? Is it asking what a word means, or is it asking me to find the wrong block? I expect you to know what the question wants before you write anything. Step 2. Now think of your answer. Say it out loud first, in a full sentence. Then type it in the box and press Check answer. If your brain goes blank, press Hint — the hint gives you a little push, not the answer. A good answer uses our unit words, like "Start on Tap" or "testing" or "error". I expect a full sentence, not just one word. Step 3. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little clap! Then move to the next problem and do the same thing: read it twice, think, type, press Check answer. Keep going until all four problems say you are right. If one says "not quite", that is okay — read it again, press Hint, and try once more. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then answer that slide the same way as before, using the same buttons — Check answer, and Hint if you are stuck. Step 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are, like footprints. Do every slide, one at a time. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All four problems will show that you are right, and the slide deck will be finished after you press the finish button on the last slide. That means you have done the whole page. 🎉

Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me when you have read the first problem. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Explain Your Thinking" page. On this page you say WHY, not just what. You will use our unit words: character, block, test, error and debug. This helps your ideas stick in your head, like glue. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your typing finger. Let's start with something small. Here is what to do, step by step. Step 1. Look at the page. There are 4 prompts. A prompt is a question that asks you to explain. Read the first prompt slowly. Then read the key ideas printed under it. Those key ideas are your helper words. I expect you to read the prompt twice before you type anything. Step 2. Now click inside the writing box and type your explanation. Say three things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. Try to use the key ideas words in your sentences. For example you might start with "I know that..." and then "so...". Even one or two sentences is good work in Grade 1. Step 3. Press the button that says Check your reasoning. If the page asks you for more, do not worry. That is normal. Just add one more sentence, then press Check your reasoning again. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4. Now press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare. Read it and ask yourself: did I say the same big idea? Did I use the key words? You do not have to copy it word for word. Your own words are best. Step 5. Do steps 1 to 4 again for prompt 2, then prompt 3, then prompt 4. One prompt at a time, no rushing. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your explanation, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 8. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How you will know the page is finished: all 4 explanations are written and checked, each one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1. Read prompt one, and tell me when you are ready. 🙂

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today you are a games developer. That means a person who makes computer games. This page is your Unit Project. You will make your very own tap game in ScratchJr, test it, and fix a bug. I expect you to try, to test, and to smile when something goes wrong — because fixing mistakes is what games developers do all day! Let's go, one step at a time. 1. Read the Unit Project first. Look at the top of the page and read what you will make. Under it there is a list of things a good project has: I chose my character, I built my tap game in ScratchJr, I tapped my character to test it, I found and fixed the bug, and I added one thing to make it better. Read that list slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know what you are making before you start. 2. Choose your character. A character is the thing in your game — a frog, a cat, a dog or a bird. Say out loud what it will do when you tap it: hop, move, or say a word. That is your plan. Then tick the first thing on the list: I chose my character. 3. Open ScratchJr and start a new project. Tap the big plus. Then tap the picture button and pick a Background. Then tap the blue plus and add your character. I expect one character on your screen, ready to go. 4. Join your blocks. Drag Start on Tap first. Then drag Hop (or Move) next to it. Then put End at the finish. Start on Tap is the block that waits for you to tap the character — that is the right start block for a tap game. Now tick: I built my tap game in ScratchJr. 5. Test it! Testing means trying your program to see if it works. Tap your character. Did it do what you planned? If yes, brilliant! If not, that is fine — you have found an error. Tick: I tapped my character to test it. 6. Find and fix the bug. Look at your plan, then look at your blocks. Where do they not match? Maybe the number is too big, or the start block is the wrong one. Change just one block, then tap and test again. Fixing a mistake is called debugging. Tick: I found and fixed the bug. 7. Make it better. Add one small thing — a bigger hop number, a sound, or a second block. Test it again after your change. Tick: I added one thing to make it better. 8. Check your list. Look at every item on the list. Is each one ticked? If one is empty, go back and do that bit. I expect all of them ticked before you finish. 9. Press My project is finished. When every item on the list is ticked, press the button that says My project is finished. Only you can press it — that is how the page saves your good work. You will know the page is done when the whole list is ticked and you have pressed My project is finished. Ready? Start with step 1, then tell me when you have chosen your character. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is our Unit Challenge. The Unit Challenge is the last part of Unit 9. It is 12 little questions about being a games developer. It shows you how much you know about testing, errors, and debugging. You do not need a tablet — just your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. I will not tell you answers, but I will help you think. Ready? Here are the steps. 1. Look at the first question on the screen. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Then read it one more time. Reading twice helps your brain hear it properly. I expect you to read before you tap — not tap quickly and hope. 2. Look at all the answer choices before you pick one. Some choices look a bit the same, so take your time. Think: which one matches what we learned? Remember our unit words — testing means trying your program to see if it works, an error is a mistake, and debug means finding the mistake and fixing it. 3. Tap the answer you think is right, then press Next question. Do this for every question, all the way to number 12. Take your time — there's no rush. If one question feels hard, do your best and keep going. 4. Some questions ask about mix-ups, like "Start on Tap and Start on Green Flag are the same." Think about our frog game. Which block waits for a tap? That memory will help you choose. 5. When you finish the last question, the page shows your score. This tells you how many you got right. More than half right means you passed. Well done for finishing all 12! 6. If your score is not high enough, that is okay. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Try again and do the questions once more. This time you will know more, so you will do better. 7. When your score is good, press Continue. That finishes the page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed Continue after a good score. Then come and tell me your score — I would love to hear it! 🐸

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Welcome to Unit 10: We Are Connected. This page is the Unit Overview. It is like a map. It shows you where we are going before we start walking. In this unit you will learn what a network is, how things join with a wire and with no wire, and what the internet is. By the end of this page, you will know what you are going to learn. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words at the top of the page. Read them slowly. If you see a speaker picture, press Listen and let it read to you. Listen right to the end. I expect you to spot two or three words that sound new, like network, wire, online or offline. It is fine if you do not know them yet — that is why we are here! Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, to me or to your grown-up. You do not need long words. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn how computers join together and share." One or two sentences is perfect. I expect you to use at least one new word from Step 1. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. This button takes you to the next part. Only press it when you have read the overview and said your sentence. I expect you to press it yourself, and to come to the lesson ready to think. You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, said your own sentence out loud, and pressed Continue. Then the lesson will open. Off you go with Step 1, and tell me when it is done. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for this page. It is called The Lesson, and it teaches us how computers join up and share.
