By the end you will be able to say what a network is, tell wires from no wires, and say what online and offline mean. You need your eyes, your ears, your voice, and maybe a pencil. Let's start with something small. 1. Read the five concepts, one at a time. The five are: what is a network, connect with a wire, connect without a wire, the internet, and online and offline. Read each one slowly, then press Listen to hear it read to you. I expect you to read and listen to all five, not to rush. If a word feels hard, listen again. 2. Say each example out loud, then try it yourself. For example, hold up two fingers as two computers, then join them with your other hand to make a network. For the wire one, point to a real wire in your home. For the no-wire one, name a phone or a tablet. I expect to hear your own voice saying it, and to see you use real things around you. 3. When you have read all five concepts, press I studied the concepts at the bottom. Only press it after you have truly read every one. I expect you to be able to tell me, in your own words, what a network is before you press it. 4. Now look under the page for the deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same concepts. Press Start on the first slide, then use the same buttons on each slide, just like you did above. I expect you to take your time on every slide. 5. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Count the dots with me — they help you see how many slides are left. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done all the slides. I expect all five slides to be done, not skipped. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. 🌟

Now tell me when step 1 is done, and I will check you before we go on. Take your time — there's no rush.

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Tools and Setup. It tells you what things you need for Unit 10, We Are Connected. We do this first so that when we start drawing and learning, nothing stops us. It is a bit like putting on your shoes before you go outside. Here is what I expect from you: look at each thing on the list, find it, and put it near you. If you need help, ask your grown-up. There are three steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Read the Tools and Setup page. Look at the words on your screen from the top to the bottom. Read them slowly, or ask your grown-up to read them with you. This page tells you what you need for this unit. For Unit 10, most of our work is on paper, so look out for things like paper, a pencil and colours. I expect you to read every line, not just the first one. Step 2. Check each tool on the list, one at a time. Go down the list and find each thing in real life. Put a sheet of paper on your table. Put a pencil next to it. Put your colours next to that. If the page names something on the computer, ask your grown-up to help you open it. I expect you to touch each thing and say to yourself, "Yes, I have this." If something is missing, tell your grown-up now, not later. Step 3. Press the button that says My tools are ready. It is at the bottom of the page. Only press it when everything on the list is really beside you. Pressing it tells the page that you are set up and ready to start learning. I expect you to be honest — if one thing is still missing, find it first, then press. How will you know the page is finished? When you have read the page, put every tool next to you, and pressed My tools are ready. Then the page will let you move on to the first lesson about networks. When you have pressed it, come back and tell me — and tell me one thing you put on your table. 😊

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Computing Words. On this page we meet the special words for our unit, We Are Connected. Words like network, wire, online and offline. We do this so the words feel easy when we talk about computers joining together. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, your eyes and your fingers for typing. Take your time — there is no rush. Here is what to do, step by step. 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read the little line that tells you what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to listen right to the end, not press and rush away. 2. Now say the word out loud, all by yourself. Say it slowly and clearly. Then say the meaning in YOUR own words — not the same words as the page. For example, for "wire" you might say, "a cord that joins two things so they can share." That is a great answer. 3. Now type a sentence with that word in it, and press Check sentence. A good sentence has the word in it and shows you know what it means, like "The tablet is online, so the video plays." Then read what the checker says to you. If it asks you to try again, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. 4. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for every word on the page: connect, network, device, wire, internet, online, offline and animation. One word at a time. I expect you to finish one word properly before you start the next one. 5. When you have done every single word, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the computing words. Only press it when all the words are done — that button tells the page you finished. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning, type your sentence and press Check sentence. You are practising the same words again, and that is how they stick in your head. 8. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many slides are left. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is the end of the slides. You will know the page is finished when every word has your own sentence, the button I explored the computing words is pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Off you go with step 1. Tell me the word you are on, and tell me the meaning in your own words — I will listen. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here is what it is. There are 6 little discoveries about how computers join together. You will look, think, and type your own idea. By the end you will be able to say what a network is, which things join with a wire, which join with no wire, and what online and offline mean. What I expect from you: try your own idea first, in your own words. A short sentence is perfect. Mistakes are how we learn, so a wrong try is still a good try. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Here are all the steps. Do them one at a time. 1. Look for the numbered tabs at the top. Press tab 1. Now read the little story and look at the picture or model. Take your time and look carefully. I expect you to notice what is joined and what is not joined. 2. Under the picture is the discovery question. Read it, then think for a moment. Now type your idea in the box and press Check my idea. Write what YOU think, even if it is short — like "they are joined so they can share". 3. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint, read it, and try once more. Change one word or add one word to your answer. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a little tick. Well done! 4. Now press tab 2 and do the same three things: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tabs 3, 4, 5 and 6. One tab at a time, no rushing. The page is finished when every tab has a tick. 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one slide each. Press Start on the first slide. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your idea and press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? All 6 tabs have ticks, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is the whole page complete! Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of our big ideas. Looking at a picture helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, and how devices join with a wire or with no wire. You need your eyes, your finger or mouse, and your voice for saying words out loud. Let's start. 1. Find the first model, "What is a network?" Look at it carefully. If it moves, drag it slowly with your finger or mouse to turn it around. If it has buttons, press them one at a time and watch what changes. I expect you to see two computers joined together. That joining is the network! 2. Under that model, read the caption. The caption is the little bit of writing that tells you about the picture. Then press Listen to hear it read to you. Good listening means you sit still and hear the whole thing. Then say one word from it out loud, like "network". 3. Now go to model 2, "Connect with a wire". Drag it to turn it, and press its buttons. Look for the wire — the cord that joins two things so they can share. I expect you to point at the wire with your finger and say, "This is a wire."

4. Read the caption under model 2, then press Listen. Now a little challenge for you: think of one thing at home that joins with a wire. A printer is a good one. 5. Go to model 3, "Connect without a wire". Turn it and press its buttons. This one has no cord at all. It joins through the air! I expect you to name one device with no wire — like a tablet or a phone. 6. Read the caption under model 3 and press Listen. Say this out loud with me: "Some devices join through the air."

7. Go to model 4, "The internet: computers all around the world". Drag it slowly all the way round. Look at all the little computers joined by lines. I expect you to notice that there are lots and lots of them, everywhere. 8. Read the caption under model 4 and press Listen. Then think of one person far away you would like to video-call. That is the internet helping you! 9. Go to model 5, "Online and offline". Press its buttons and watch. When we are online, the video plays. When we are offline, we see a spinning circle going round and round. I expect you to say which one has no internet. 10. Read the caption under model 5 and press Listen. This is the last caption, so listen right to the end. 11. Now check yourself. Have you looked at all five models? Have you pressed Listen under every one? If you missed one, go back and do it now. 12. Last step! Press the button at the bottom that says "I explored the models". Only press it when you really have seen all five. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed "I explored the models" at the bottom. That saves your work — I cannot press it for you, so it must be you. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have looked at the first model. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Learn the Method" page. 🙂

A method is just a way to do something, step by step — like the steps for washing your hands. On this page there are 5 methods about networks, wires and the internet. We do this so your brain learns the order of the steps, not just the words. All you need is your eyes, your voice, and a finger to press the buttons. Let's start! 1. Look at the top of the page and find the first method. Read its first step. Read it out loud, slowly, with your reading voice. I expect you to say the words out loud, not just in your head — saying it helps you remember it. 2. Now press the button that says "Show me the next step". A new step will pop up. Read that one out loud too. Take your time — there's no rush. 3. Keep pressing "Show me the next step" and reading each new step out loud. Do this again and again until the page tells you "Method complete". That message means you finished that method. Well done — one down! 4. Now do the very same thing for the next method: read step one out loud, press "Show me the next step", read, press, read — until it says "Method complete" again. I expect you to say every step out loud, even the short ones. 5. Keep going like this for all 5 methods. Every single one must say "Method complete" at the end. If a step feels tricky, that's okay — tell me and I will help you say it in easier words. 6. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. It has the same methods, but only one method on each slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. 7. On the first slide, press "Start". Then use the same buttons as before: press "Show me the next step" and say each step out loud, until that slide is done. 8. Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Do the same again: press "Start", then step through and say each step out loud. 9. Keep going slide by slide, using the right arrow each time. Watch the dots move along — that tells you how many slides are left. 10. On the last slide, step through to the end, then press the finish button. That is the very last press! You will know the page is finished when all 5 methods have said "Method complete", and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Off you go — start with step 1, and tell me when your first method says "Method complete". I'll be right here. 🌟

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Code Examples page. On this page we look at little bits of "code" — that means words and pictures that tell a computer what to do. Our code shows one computer, and then two computers joined together. We do this so you can SEE what a network looks like. All you need is your eyes, your reading voice, and a pencil if you want to draw. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Read the code example on the page. Read it slowly, one line at a time, out loud if you can. The first line says "One computer" and shows one computer box. The second line says "A network" and shows two computer boxes with a little line between them. I expect you to point at each line and tell me what it shows. Good reading sounds like this: "This line has one computer. This line has two computers joined by a line, so it is a network."

Step 2. Press the button that says Copy the code. That copies the code so you can keep it. If you have a computer or paper, try it yourself — copy the two lines, or draw them with your pencil. Then press the button under the example to mark it done. I expect your drawing to have two computer boxes and a line joining them. Step 3. Look under the examples. There is a slide deck — that means cards you flip, one example on each card. Press Start. Read the code on the card, just like you did before. Then mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next card. Do this for every card. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 4. When you have read every example, press Go to Build It. That takes you to the next part, where you get to make your own network. You will know the page is finished when every example has been marked done, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me what you see in the two lines. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. Worked examples are questions with the answer already shown, step by step. We read them to learn how a good answer looks. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, and talk about wires, no wires, the internet, online and offline. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here we go. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question by yourself, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Say your own answer out loud first, before you look at any solution. Even a small guess counts — trying first is what makes your brain grow. 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read it slowly, line by line, and compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: what did I get right, and what did I miss? I expect you to notice one thing that was the same and one thing that was new. 3. Do the same for all 6 worked examples: read, say your answer, then press Show worked solution. Take your time — there's no rush. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It tells you how many you have opened. When every one is open, this part is done. 4. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one slide each. On the first slide, press Start. 5. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read the question, think of your answer, then press Show worked solution. Say your answer out loud each time, like you are teaching a friend. 6. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show where you are in the deck. Each dot is one slide. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done all the slides. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 6 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with worked example 1 and tell me your own answer before you press the button. I'm right here. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. This is our practice page for Unit 10, "We Are Connected". You will answer six little questions about networks, wires, and the internet. Practice helps the words stick in your head, like learning a song. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first question and read it slowly. You can read it twice — that is a smart thing to do. Think of the answer in your head, or write it on your paper first. I expect you to try, even if you feel unsure. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Now type your answer in the box. Use one word or a few words, like "network" or "wire". Then press Check my answer. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint — you can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try a hint before you ask for the whole step. 3. Keep going question by question, until every question is right. If one is wrong, that is okay — mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint, fix your answer, and press Check my answer again. I expect you to finish all six, one at a time, not rushing. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it and use the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints. 5. Keep going through the slides, one at a time, the same way. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to say each answer out loud too — that helps your brain remember it. You will know the page is finished when all six questions are right and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me when you have read question one, and we will look at it together.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Build It page. This page is where we make our learning with our hands. You will draw computers, join them with lines, and circle the right pictures. By the end you will be able to say what a network is, name things that use a wire, name things that need no wire, and show what online and offline mean. You will need a pencil, some paper, and colours if you have them. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. What I expect from you: try each one yourself first, write something in every box, and use our words — network, wire, device, internet, online, offline. Even one short line is good work. Neat drawing and a real try matter more than being perfect. Here we go, step by step. 1. Look at the first build-it activity. Read the words at the top. Then press Listen to hear them read out loud. Listening helps if a word looks tricky. Now go and get the things it names — usually just paper and a pencil. I expect you to have your pencil in your hand before you start. 2. Now do the activity. Draw it or circle it on your paper. Take your time — there's no rush. Then find the box and write your answer, or write what you noticed. A good answer uses a unit word, like "Two computers joined together make a network."

3. When that one is done, press Mark complete under that activity. Only press it after you have really drawn it and written in the box. That button tells the page, "I finished this one!"

4. Now do the same for all 8 activities, one at a time. Read, press Listen, get your things, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. One activity per go. Do not skip ahead — each one teaches a new little thing. 5. Here is what the 8 are about, so you know what is coming: joining two computers to make a network; circling things that use a wire (desktop computer, printer, games console); circling things that need no wire (smartphone, tablet, camera); joining Imani to her grandma far away with the internet; circling the screen with no internet (the spinning circle); drawing your family on a video-call; drawing two computers and a printer joined with wires; and drawing three devices that need no wire. I expect you to say out loud why you chose each one. 6. When all 8 have Mark complete pressed, scroll to the bottom and press Finish activities. Check first that no box is empty. That button finishes the top part of the page. 7. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same build-it activities, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is just another way to practise — the same work, one big card at a time. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, then do it, then write in the box, then Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — count them to see how many are left. 9. On the last slide, press Finish activities. That is the end of the deck. How you will know the page is finished: every activity has Mark complete pressed, every box has your words in it, and you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom and on the last slide. Ready? Start with number 1 — press Listen, then tell me when you have your pencil and paper. 🙂

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today we are on the Quick Reference page for Unit 10, We Are Connected. This page is like a little pocket of all our big ideas: network, wire, internet, online and offline. We read it to make the words stick in our heads. You will need your eyes, your voice, and your ears. Here are the three steps. 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page slowly, from the top to the bottom. It has the key words and the key facts of this unit. Where you see a speaker button, press Listen and hear the words read out loud. I expect you to read it slowly, not fast, and to say each new word out loud once. If a word feels tricky, say it with me, slowly. 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now cover the page with your hand, or look away, and tell me what you remember. Try to say three things: what a network is, one thing that joins with a wire, and what online means. Do not copy the exact words on the page. Your own words are best, even short ones like "a network is computers joined so they can share." I expect you to try at least three facts, and I will help if one gets stuck. 3. Press Reference reviewed. When you have read the whole page and said your facts, scroll to the bottom and press the Reference reviewed button. Press it only after you really read it, because that button is your promise that you did the work. I expect you to press it yourself, not your grown-up. You will know this page is finished when you have read every part, said the key facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed at the bottom. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when you have read it. Take your time — there's no rush.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! Today we are debug detectives. A bug is a small mistake. On this page, each card shows a mistake about networks. Your job is to spot it and say the right idea instead. We do this because finding mistakes helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, and how devices join with a wire or through the air. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: try to find the bug BEFORE you press any button. Even a guess is good. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1: Look at the first card. Read the little idea on it slowly. Ask yourself, "Is that true?" Say out loud what you think the bug is. A good try sounds like this: "That is wrong, because a network is computers joined together, not one computer."

Step 2: Now press Show the bug. It will tell you where the mistake is and what it should say. Read it. Then tell me, or tell your grown-up, WHY it was wrong. Saying the why is the important part. Then press the button on the card to mark that bug done. Step 3: Do the same for every card on the page. Look, guess, press Show the bug, say why, mark it done. Take your time — there is no rush. Step 4: Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. This is a deck of cards, with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. Step 5: On the slide, find the bug first, all by yourself. Then press Show the bug and check. Say why it was wrong, and mark it done. Then press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going until the slides run out. Step 6: When every card and every slide is done, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. You will know the page is finished when all the cards are marked done, all the slides are done, and the I practised debugging button has been pressed. Ready? Start with the first card, and tell me what bug you spot!

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Computing Fluency page. Let's look at that together. This page is a sprint. A sprint means quick, quick, quick! You get six short questions about our unit, We Are Connected. They are all about words like network, wire, internet, online and offline. We do this so those words pop into your head fast, without you having to stop and think hard. What I expect from you: try your best on every question, type your answer, and don't worry about being perfect. Mistakes are how we learn. You need paper and a pencil? No — just your thinking brain and your fingers for typing. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just there to make it feel like a race. Take your time — there's no rush. Being right matters more than being fast. 2. Read question one. Most questions finish a sentence, like "Two or more computers joined together is a..." You type the missing word in the answer box. One or two words is enough. Then press Check & continue. 3. Here is how to answer well. Think of our unit words: connect, network, device, wire, internet, online, offline. Ask yourself, which word fits this sentence? For example, if I asked "A cord that joins two things so they can share is a..." you would type wire. That is the kind of answer I expect from you. 4. Keep going the same way for questions two, three, four, five and six. Read, type, press Check & continue. One question at a time. Do not skip ahead in your head — finish each one first. 5. Some questions ask you to pick a thing, not a word. Like, which one can join with no wire? Then think: does it need a cord, or does it join through the air? A phone in the park needs no cord. That is your clue. 6. At the end, the page shows how you did. You need most of them right to pass. If you got enough right, brilliant work — you are finished! 7. If you got fewer than that, do not feel sad. Press Run the sprint again. Before you start, say the words out loud once: network, wire, internet, online, offline. Then try again. You can run it as many times as you need. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers and the page tells you so. Then you have done it! Ready? Go and read question one, then come back and tell me how you did. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the games on this page. The games are little quizzes about Unit 10, "We Are Connected". We play them so the big words stick in your head: network, wire, internet, online and offline. All you need is your eyes, your thinking, and your finger to tap. Here is what we will do. 1. Look at the games on your screen and pick one. Press the button that says Start game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read it slowly, then tap the answer you think is right. If you get it right, you earn a star! I expect you to think first and tap second — no fast guessing. If a question is tricky, look for the words you know, like "wire" or "internet". 2. When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you more questions and more stars. Keep playing that same game until it has all its stars. Then it is mastered — that means you really know it! I expect you to try again even if you get one wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Every programmer's code fails the first time, and every learner gets some answers wrong first. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again, and fill up the stars. Go one game at a time, from the top. I expect you to finish one game before you start the next, so your brain stays calm and focused. You will know the page is finished when every game has all of its stars. The page finishes by itself then — you do not need to press anything extra. Ready? Go and press Start game on the first game, then come back and tell me how it went. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Solve Real Problems" page. On this page you use what you know about networks and the internet to solve real-life problems. It is like being a helper at home, at school, at the market and in your town. By the end, you will be able to say when we are online, when a video will not play, and what a network is. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your typing finger. A grown-up can sit with you to help you type. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then type your answer in a full sentence. Guessing fast is not the goal — thinking is. Step 1. There are 4 real problems on the page. Read the first one out loud, slowly. Ask yourself, "What is this question really asking me?" A good reader reads it twice before answering. I expect you to know the question in your own words before you type anything. Step 2. Now work it out in your head. Then type your working and your answer in the box, and press Check answer. Try to write a full sentence, like "The answer is ..., because ...". If you feel stuck, press Hint first, read it, and try again. Do not press Check answer before you have thought — thinking comes first, pressing comes second. Step 3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done! Then move to the next problem and do the same thing: read it twice, think, type, press Check answer. Keep going until all 4 problems say you are right. If one is wrong, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint and try once more. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, using the same buttons. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 4 problems show that your answers are right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Remember, I do not tick it for you — you press the buttons, so the page can save your good work. Ready? Read problem one to me, and tell me what you think it is asking. 🙂

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Stay Safe Online page. This page has four safety rules for using the internet. We do this because the internet joins us to lots of computers all around the world — and when we are online, we need to stay safe. By the end, you will be able to say each rule in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 3 steps. Step 1: Read every rule slowly. Start at the top of the page. Read the first rule, then stop and think about it. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen and hear the rule read out loud. Do this for all four rules, one at a time. Do not rush — reading slowly is doing it well. What I expect: you read every rule, top to bottom, and you press Listen wherever there is a speaker. Step 2: Say each rule in your own words, with an example from your life. Go back to rule one. Say it out loud in your own words, like you are telling a friend. Then give one example from your own day. For example, for keeping things private you might say, "I will not type my address into a game." Do this for all four rules. What I expect: four rules said in your own words, and four examples from your own life. Short is fine — one sentence each is perfect. Step 3: Press I know these rules. When you have read all four rules and said them in your own words, scroll to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I know these rules. Only press it when you really have read them all — that button is your promise. What I expect: you press it yourself, not your grown-up. How you will know the page is finished: you have read all four rules, said each one in your own words with an example, and pressed I know these rules at the bottom. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have read all the rules. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's do this page together. What this page is: it is called Explain Your Thinking. You will not just tick a box. You will use your own words to say WHY. That is the fun part! Why we do it: saying why makes the idea stick in your head. Grown-up computer people do this too. By the end, you will be able to explain networks and the internet all by yourself. What you need: your eyes to read, your fingers to type, and your best thinking. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. What I expect from you: use the unit words in your writing. Words like connect, network, device, wire, internet, online and offline. Try a whole sentence, not one word. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Under the prompt you will see some key ideas — little words like network or wire. Those are your helper words. Say the prompt out loud if that helps you think. I expect you to know what the question is asking before you write anything. 2. Now write in the box. Say three things: what you know, which rule from our unit you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example, you might start "I know that..." and then "so..." Try to use two of the key words. Then press Check your reasoning. If the page asks for more, add another sentence and press Check your reasoning again. That is not a mistake — it just wants more of your good thinking! 3. Next, press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare. Look for two things: did I use the key words? Did I say why? If your words are different but your idea is the same, that is still great. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for prompt 2, then prompt 3, then prompt 4. There are 4 prompts in all. 4. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom of the page. They have the same prompts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Do the same as before: write your explanation, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — they help you see how many are left. 5. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that tells the page you are done! How you will know the page is finished: every one of the 4 prompts has your own explanation, each one used the key ideas, and you pressed the finish button on the last slide. I do not tick it for you — you press the buttons, because it is your work. Ready? Start with prompt 1 and tell me when you have written your first explanation. I will be right here. 🙂

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today you are the maker. This is our Unit 10 project, called "We Are Connected". You will draw your own network and show what you have learned about wires, no wires, and the internet. We do this so you can show your ideas, not just say them. You need paper, a pencil, and colours if you have them. A grown-up or a partner can sit near you to listen. Here is what I expect from you: draw carefully, use our words (network, wire, device, online, offline), and tick each thing on the list when you finish it. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are your steps. Step 1. Read the Unit Project box on your screen. It tells you what you will make. Under it is a list of things a good project has. Read that list slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to know one thing from the list before you start drawing. Step 2. Draw two computers and one printer on your paper. Now draw lines to join them. Those lines are the wires. I expect three things joined up, with no thing left alone. This is your network! Step 3. Look at your drawing and tick that item on the list. Tick means "I did it". Only tick when it is really done. Step 4. Now draw three devices that need no wire. Think of a tablet, a phone, or a camera. I expect three different ones, not the same one three times. Then tick that item. Step 5. Tell your partner or your grown-up why you chose those three. Try to say, "This one joins through the air, so it needs no wire." Then tick that item. Step 6. Answer the online or offline question on your page. Remember: online means joined to the internet, offline means not joined. I expect you to say which one your picture shows and why. Then tick that item. Step 7. Add one small thing to make your project better. Maybe colour it in, or add a title, or draw yourself using a tablet. Then tick that last item. Step 8. Check your list. Is every single thing ticked? If one is empty, go back and finish it first. Step 9. When every item is ticked, press the button that says "My project is finished". You will know the page is done when the whole list is ticked and you have pressed "My project is finished". Then come and tell me — I would love to hear what you drew! Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me when you have read the list.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Let's do your Unit Challenge together. This page is the last part of Unit 10, We Are Connected. It is a set of 12 questions about networks, wires, the internet, and being online or offline. We do it to see what your brain has kept. It is not scary — it is like a game to show what you know. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a quiet minute. I will not tell you answers, but I will help you think. Step 1: Press the first question and read it slowly. Read it twice. Then look at all the choices before you pick. Think, "Which one sounds like what I learned?" Remember the big ideas: a network is computers joined together, a wire is a cord that joins things, and the internet is lots of computers all around the world. When you have picked one, press Next question. I expect you to try every question by yourself, even the hard ones. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Keep going the same way for all 12 questions. Read, think, choose, then press Next question. If a question feels tricky, pick the answer that sounds most like your lesson, not the silly one. I expect you to answer all 12, not skip any. Step 3: At the end, the page shows your score. You pass if you get more than half of them right. Look at your score and be proud of what you got right. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4: If your score is not high enough, press Try again. That is not a bad thing! It just means one more go. Before you try again, think about the words online, offline, wire and network. I expect you to try again calmly, reading each question twice. Step 5: When your score is good enough, press Continue. That tells the page you are finished. You will know the page is done when you have pressed Continue and it moves you on. Ready? Tell me when you have finished question one, and I will cheer you on. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Unit Overview. It is the front door of Unit 11, "Be an Artist". Here you will see what we will learn: arrows, directions, and how to draw shapes by following steps. It takes only a few minutes. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Let's start! 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen. Then the words are read to you. Listen all the way to the end. Try to find these little words: direction, arrow, step, shape. I expect you to look and listen carefully, not rush. That's all — just read and listen. 2. Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, like you are telling a friend. A good answer sounds like this: "I think I will learn about arrows. I will use up, down, left and right. I will draw a square." One or two sentences is plenty. You can also tell your grown-up, or type it to me here. I expect your own words, not the same words as the page. 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have looked, listened and said your idea, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to the next part, called The Lesson. Do not press it too early — finish steps 1 and 2 first. How will you know this page is finished? You will know because you listened to the whole overview, you said in your own words what you will learn, and you pressed Continue. Then the screen will show The Lesson. Now go and do step 1. Press Listen, and come back and tell me when you are done. Take your time — there's no rush. 🙂

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello, artist! Today we get ready for Unit 11: Be an Artist. This page is called Tools and Setup. It tells you what things you need for this unit, and how to get them ready. We do this first so that later, when we draw shapes and move a bee, nothing stops us. By the end of this page you will have everything on your desk and ready to go. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, check each thing one by one, and ask your grown-up if you need help. There are three steps. Step 1. Read the Tools and Setup page. Look at the page on your screen and read it from the top to the bottom. Read it out loud if you like. It will tell you the things we need. For this unit you need a tablet with the ScratchJr app, some paper (squared or dotted paper is best), a pencil, and some colours. I expect you to point at each thing on the list as you read it. Step 2. Check each tool, with your grown-up if you need help. Now go and find each thing. Put your paper, pencil and colours on your desk. Then ask your grown-up to open ScratchJr on the tablet. Tap the little house, then tap the plus sign to start a new project. If a green flag is on the screen, you are ready! ScratchJr is free and needs no account. I expect you to check every single thing on the list, not just some. Step 3. Press My tools are ready. When everything is on your desk and ScratchJr is open, scroll to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says My tools are ready. Only press it when it is true — that is how the page knows you are set up. How will you know the page is finished? When you have read the page, found every tool, and pressed My tools are ready, this page is done. Then we can go and be artists! Now do Step 1, and tell me when you have read the page. Take your time — there's no rush.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello, artist! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. This lesson has five little ideas. They are all about giving directions: up, down, left and right. By the end you will know how a list of steps can draw a shape, like a square window. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your reading voice. Let's start with something small. Here are your steps, one at a time. 1. Look at the first concept box at the top of the page. Read it slowly with your eyes. Then press the Listen button so you hear the words too. Reading and listening together helps the words stick. I expect you to read all the way to the end of the box, not just the first line. 2. Now find the example inside that box. Say the example out loud in your own voice. Then try it for real: point your arm up, down, left and right, or draw one arrow on your paper. I expect you to move or draw, not just look. Doing it with your body is how your brain remembers it. 3. Do the same two things for every concept box: read it, press Listen, then say the example out loud and try it. There are five boxes. Take them one by one, and do not rush. Take your time — there's no rush. 4. As you go, tell me one thing from each box in your own words. For example, "an algorithm is a list of steps in the right order." I expect a short sentence, not a long one. Can you explain that back to me in your own words? That is how I know it is really in your head. 5. When you have read all five boxes, scroll to the bottom of the page and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after you have read every box. That button is your promise that you did the work. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. The slides show the same five ideas again, one idea on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read the slide, press Listen if it is there, and say the idea out loud. I expect you to say the direction words with me: up, down, left, right. 8. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right side. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many slides are left. 9. Keep going, one slide at a time, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when two things are done: the I studied the concepts button is pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Do step 1 now, then come back and tell me what the first box said. I'll be right here. 🙂

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello, my artist friend! Today we learn our Computing Words for Unit 11, Be an Artist. These are the special words we use when we give directions and draw shapes, like direction, arrow, step and algorithm. We do this so the words feel easy when you draw and when you use ScratchJr. You need your voice, your eyes, and your hands for typing. Take your time — there's no rush. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, tell me the meaning in YOUR own words, and write one sentence that shows you really know the word. Step 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Press Listen to hear it said properly. Listen once, then listen again if you want. Good work looks like this: you can say the word clearly, all by yourself. Step 2. Now say the word out loud. Then say the meaning in your own words — not the same words as the page. For example, for "step" you might say, "one little move." I expect your own words, even if they are simple. Step 3. Type a sentence with that word in the box. Make it about YOUR life — your toys, your house, your school. A good sentence has the word in it and makes sense, like "I move one step to the right." Then press Check sentence and read what the checker tells you. If it says to fix something, change it and press Check sentence again. Step 4. Do Steps 1, 2 and 3 again for every word on the page. The words are direction, arrow, step, instructions, algorithm, shape, square, rectangle and ScratchJr. One word at a time, please — finish one before you start the next. Step 5. When every word has a green tick or a good sentence, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the computing words. Only press it after ALL the words are done. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. This is like a little game to help the words stick. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning, then type your sentence and press Check sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. Step 8. Keep going until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are all done. You will know the page is finished when every word has your sentence, the I explored the computing words button is pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have listened to your first word. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello, artist! Today we are on the Explore the Concept page. This page has six little discoveries about directions. A direction is which way something moves: up, down, left and right. By the end you will be able to follow arrows, put steps in order, and draw a square like a real artist. You will need your pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. Here we go, step by step. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Press the tab that says 1. A picture or a little model will open with a short story. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. I expect you to look at the picture carefully before you type anything. Step 2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it twice. Point at the picture with your finger while you think. Say your idea out loud first — that helps a lot. Step 3. Now type your idea in the box. Use your own words. Even a few words are fine, like "the arrow points up" or "4 corners". Then press Check my idea. I expect you to try your own idea first, not to guess quickly. Step 4. Look at what the page says back to you. If it says Look again, that is okay — mistakes are how we learn. Press Hint, read it, change one small thing in your answer, and press Check my idea one more time. When it says Exactly!, your tab gets a tick. Well done! Step 5. Now press tab 2 and do the same three things: read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going like this for tab 3, tab 4, tab 5 and tab 6. One tab at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 6. Here is what each discovery is about, so you know what to look for. One is about the four arrows: up, down, left and right. One is about helping Maya walk to the garden. One is about putting steps in the right order, with a start and a stop. One is about drawing a square window with arrows: right, down, left, up. One is about moving the bee to the flower in ScratchJr. And one is about shapes around you, like square windows and rectangle doors. Step 7. When all six tabs have a tick, scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. It has the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. Step 9. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? All six tabs will have a tick, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your work saved — I cannot tick it for you, only you can. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. I'm right here with you. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello, artist! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of our big ideas. They help you SEE what arrows and steps do. By the end, you will be able to point at each picture and say what it shows. You need your eyes, your finger to drag, and your voice to say the words out loud. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 things to do. Here they all are. 1. Look at the 5 models, one at a time. Press or tap the first model to open it. If it moves, hold it with your finger and drag it slowly to turn it around. Press its buttons to make it change. Do not rush — look at the arrows and the shape. The 5 models are: The four directions, Follow a path, Be an artist: draw a shape, Directions in ScratchJr, and Be an artist: the Mini-Project. I expect you to open every one, and to point your arm up, down, left and right when you see the arrows. 2. Read the caption under each model, then press Listen. The caption is the little bit of writing under the picture. Read it with your finger under the words. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Say one word back to me, like "arrow" or "algorithm". I expect you to press Listen on all 5 models, not just one. 3. Press I explored the models at the bottom. Do this only after you have looked at all 5 and pressed Listen on all 5. This button tells the page you are done. I cannot press it for you — the work must come from you. You will know the page is finished when all 5 models have been opened, you have heard all 5 captions, and you have pressed I explored the models at the bottom. Now start with step 1. Open the first model, "The four directions", and tell me what you see. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello, my artist! Today we learn the method. A method is a way to do a job step by step. On this page there are 5 methods about directions, paths and drawing shapes. We do this so your brain learns the right order: read a step, say it, then see the next one. You need your eyes, your voice, and a pencil and paper if you want to try drawing. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step slowly. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to read before you press, not press first. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step, one press at a time. Say each step out loud with your voice, like "move right", "move down". Keep going until the page says Method complete. That means this method is finished. 3. Now do the same for the next method. Read, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, until it says Method complete. Take your time — there's no rush. 4. Do this for all 5 methods. Finish one method fully before you start the next one. I expect you to reach Method complete five times, one for each method. 5. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one method on it. Press Start on the first slide. 6. On the slide, use the same buttons as before. Press to see the next step, and say each step out loud, until that slide's method is done. 7. Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. More dots left means more slides to go. 8. Do every slide the same way: press Start, step through it, then press the arrow on the right. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 5 methods say Method complete, and the last slide's finish button has been pressed. Then come and tell me — I would love to hear which method was your favourite. Ready? Start with method one now. 🌟

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello, artist! Today we are on the Code Examples page. Code examples are little lists of arrow steps. Each list tells a character or a pencil where to go. We read them so we can see how a picture gets made from small steps. By the end, you will be able to read a list of arrows and say what it does. You need your eyes, your reading voice, and a pencil and paper if you have one. There are four things to do. Here they all are. 1. Read each code example. Look at the first box on the page. Read it one line at a time, out loud. Say what each line does, like this: "Move right — the pencil goes right one step." Then say what the whole list draws. I expect you to read every line, not just look at it. Slow reading is good reading. 2. Press "Copy the code", then mark it done. The button called Copy the code puts the steps somewhere you can use them. If you have paper, draw the arrows and follow them with your pencil. If you have ScratchJr, you can join the same blue Move blocks. Then press the button under the example to mark it done. I expect you to try the arrows yourself before you press it. 3. Do the slides at the bottom. Under the examples there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one code example. Press "Start". Read the code on the slide out loud, the same way as before. Then mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going until there are no more slides. I expect you to read every slide, even the short ones. 4. Press "Go to Build It". When you have read every example and every slide, press Go to Build It. That takes you to the next part, where you make your own arrows. You will know the page is finished when every example has been marked done, every slide has been read, and you have pressed Go to Build It. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me what the first code example says. I am right here. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello, artist! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with the answer already shown, step by step. It is like watching me draw a square first, so you can draw one too. We do this so you learn how to think in steps — up, down, left, right. By the end, you will know how to follow directions and draw a shape. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. Here is what I expect: try each one yourself FIRST, then look. That is the secret of learning. Here are your steps. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question out loud, slowly. Then try it on your paper before you look at any answer. It is okay if you are not sure — a good try is enough. I expect a real try, not a perfect one. 2. Now press the button that says Show worked solution. Read the solution line by line with your finger. Compare it with your paper. Ask yourself: did I do the same thing? What was different? If something is different, that is a happy discovery, not a mistake. 3. Do the same for all 6 worked examples: read, try, then press Show worked solution. Take your time — there is no rush. 4. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It counts how many examples you have opened. Keep going until every single one is open. The page is finished when all 6 are open. 5. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. This is a little deck of cards with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons: read the question, try it, then press the button to see the solution. Say the directions out loud as you read them — up, down, left, right. 7. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. 8. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you will know you are done: the counter at the top shows all 6 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with worked example number one, and tell me when you have tried it. Take your time — there's no rush.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello, artist! Today we are on the Guided Practice page. This is where you practise the big ideas of our unit: arrows, directions, and putting steps in order. Doing it yourself helps the ideas stick in your head. You need your eyes, your brain, and a pencil and paper if you like. There are 4 practice questions, and then some slides at the bottom. Here we go, one step at a time. 1. Look at the first question and read it slowly. Read it twice. Some questions ask about arrows, like which arrow points up. Some ask about shapes, like how many corners a square has. Some ask you to put steps in the right order. Work it out on paper or in your head first. I expect you to think before you type — even a little think is good. 2. Now type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. Type your best answer, not a guess. If you are stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step, and it shows you one line of the working. That is not cheating — that is learning! I expect you to try a hint before you look at the next step. 3. Do this for every question, one by one, until each one is right. If an answer is not right, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, look at what it is really asking, and try once more. When all 4 questions are right, that part of the page is done. I expect you to keep going with a smile, even on the tricky one. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, with the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going until the last slide, then press the finish button. I expect you to say each answer out loud before you type it — that helps it stay in your memory. You will know the page is finished when all 4 questions show as right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me your answer. Take your time — there's no rush.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Quick Reference. It is like a little poster of everything in Unit 11, Be an Artist. It has our four directions, our special words, and our shapes, all on one page. We read it so the words stay in your head, ready for your project. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe your finger to point. There are three steps. Step 1. Read the Quick Reference slowly. Look at the words like direction, arrow, step, algorithm, square and rectangle. Read each word, then read what it means. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Do it well by going slowly, one word at a time, and pointing with your finger. I expect you to read every word on the page, not just the first ones. Step 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Close your eyes for a second and try it out loud, like you are telling a friend. For example you might say, "A direction is which way something goes. Up, down, left, right." Then say what an algorithm is: a list of steps in the right order. Do it well by using your own easy words, not copying the page word for word. I expect you to say at least three of the words out loud, all by yourself. Step 3. Press Reference reviewed at the bottom. This is the button that tells the page you have finished reading. Only press it after you have read every part and said the facts out loud. Do it well by checking first: did I press Listen? Did I say the words? I expect you to be honest with yourself before you press. You will know the page is finished when you have read the whole Quick Reference, said the facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed at the bottom. Now start with Step 1. Read slowly and press Listen where you see a speaker. Tell me when you are done! 😊

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Build It page. On this page you do the fun part: you make things. You will point arrows, walk a path, put steps in order, and draw a square window like a real artist. Why? Because in this unit we learn that a picture can be made from a list of steps — up, down, left and right. Doing it with your own hands is how it sticks. What I expect from you: try each one yourself, say the direction words out loud, and write something in the box every time. Neat is nice, but trying is what counts. Get ready a pencil, some paper, colours, and a tablet with ScratchJr if you have one. A grown-up can sit with you. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first activity box. Press Listen to hear it read to you. Read along with the words. Each activity tells you what to use and what to do — so go and fetch those things first, like your pencil and paper. I expect you to have your things ready before you start moving your pencil. Step 2. Now do the activity with your hands. Point your arm up, down, left and right. Trace the arrows. Follow Maya's path with your finger, then draw it. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3. Write your answer in the box. It can be short! You can write the arrow words, or a number, or what you noticed. For "How many corners does a square have?" you would write a number. For the bee, you could write "Yes, the bee reached the flower." I expect one true thing from you in every box. Step 4. Press Mark complete under that activity. Only press it after you really did it. That button is your little tick that says "I did this one."

Step 5. Now do the same for all 8 activities, one at a time. Read, press Listen, get your things, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. Do not skip one — each activity teaches a new little piece. Step 6. When every activity has its tick, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. This tells the page you have finished them all. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same activities, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. This is your chance to practise them again, nice and slowly. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: Listen, then do it, write your answer, then Mark complete. Same as before — you know how to do this now. Step 9. Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. Step 10. On the last slide, press Finish activities. That is the end of the deck. How you will know the page is finished: every activity has Mark complete pressed, every box has your writing in it, you pressed Finish activities on the page, and you pressed Finish activities on the last slide too. Ready? Start with activity one — press Listen, then tell me when you have your pencil and paper. I will be right here.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello, artist! Today we are bug hunters. 🐛

A bug is a little mistake in a list of steps. On this page you will look at small programs — lists of arrow steps — and find the mistake. We do this because every programmer's code fails the first time. Finding the bug and fixing it is a real computing skill, and you can do it. You need your eyes, your finger to point, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the first card. Read the steps slowly, one at a time, with your finger. Ask yourself: is there a start? Is there a stop? Is one arrow pointing the wrong way? Are the steps in the right order? I expect you to guess the bug in your own head BEFORE you press anything. Guessing first is the whole game. Step 2. Now press Show the bug. The card will show you where the bug is and what it should be. Check your guess. Then say out loud why that step was wrong, like this: "It should be Move left, because we need to go back to the other side." Then press the button on the card to mark that bug done. I expect a reason, not just "it's wrong."

Step 3. Do the same for every card on the page. Read, guess, press Show the bug, say why, mark it done. Take your time — there's no rush. If a card feels hard, look for a missing start or stop first. That is the most common bug of all. Step 4. Scroll down to the slides at the bottom. This is a deck with one bug on each slide. Press Start to begin. Step 5. On each slide, find the bug with your eyes first. Then press Show the bug. Say why it was wrong, mark it done, and press the arrow to go to the next slide. Keep going until the slides run out. I expect the same careful looking every time — even when you feel fast. Step 6. When all the cards and all the slides are done, press I practised debugging at the bottom of the page. Only press it when you really have done them all. That button is your record of your work, so it must come from you. You will know the page is finished when every card and every slide is marked done, and the I practised debugging button has been pressed. Ready? Start with card one, read it slowly, and tell me what bug you think you see. 🕵️

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Games. It is where we play little games about arrows and shapes. You will pick the right answer, and you will earn stars. Why do we do this? Because playing helps the words stick in your brain. By the end, you will know up, down, left and right. You will know a square has 4 corners. And you will know that steps must go in the right order. What you need: your eyes, your finger to tap, and a happy try-again heart. It is okay to get one wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. What I expect from you: read each question, think first, then tap. Not too fast! Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the games on the page. Pick one. Press Start game. A question will come up with some answers under it. Read it, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Think about our unit words: direction, arrow, step, algorithm, square, rectangle. Then tap the answer you think is right. Do this for every round. You earn a star for every round you get right. I expect you to think before you tap — that is the most important part. Step 2. When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you another go, so you can earn more stars. Try to remember the ones you got wrong last time. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. Mastered means you got it! I expect you to press Play again until that game has all its stars. Keep going with a smile. Step 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game on the next one, answer the rounds, then press Play again until it has all its stars too. Do this game by game until they are all mastered. I expect you to try every single game, even the tricky ones. Look how far you've already come today. How will you know the page is finished? You do not have to press anything special at the end. When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. That means you did it! One little hint for the games: an arrow always points the same way on the page. It does not change when you turn your head. Go and press Start game now. Come back and tell me how many stars you got — I want to hear!

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Computing Fluency page. 🎨

This page is a little sprint. A sprint means going fast! You answer four quick questions about arrows, steps and shapes. We do it so the words from "Be an Artist" pop into your head quickly, without you having to think hard. What I expect from you: try your best, answer fast, and don't worry if one is tricky. Get a pencil and paper near you. You can draw with your finger in the air too! Here are the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time. It starts counting when you begin. Don't be scared of it — it is just a friendly clock. Take a breath and get ready. 2. Question one comes up. Read it, say the answer out loud first, then type it in the box. Then press Check and continue. I expect one short answer, like a number or one word — not a long sentence. 3. Do the same for question two, question three and question four. One at a time. Type, then press Check and continue. Speed is nice, but being right is nicer. 4. Here is my help for the four ideas, so you feel ready. An up arrow points to the sky. A square has the same number of corners as the sides you draw. To draw a shape, you follow a list of steps in order. And every program starts first and stops last. 5. When all four are done, the page shows how you did. I expect you to get most of them right. That means three or four out of four. 6. If you got fewer than that, do not feel sad. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Run the sprint again and try once more. You will be faster the second time — I promise! 7. Come and tell me your score. I will help you with the one that felt hardest. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. The page will show you it is done, and you can move on. Ready? Start question one now, and tell me when you finish. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello, artist! Today we are on the "Solve Real Problems" page. Here you use our unit words — direction, arrow, step, algorithm, square — in little real-life puzzles. We do this because giving good directions helps us in real places, like walking to the garden or drawing a window. By the end, you will be able to think out a direction problem and say your answer in your own words. You need your pencil, some paper, and your thinking voice. Get ready — here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first problem on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Ask yourself: what is this problem asking me? You can say it out loud to yourself or to your grown-up. I expect you to know what the question wants before you write anything. There are 4 problems on this page, and we do them one at a time. 2. Now work it out. Use your pencil and paper if it helps — draw the arrow, draw the square, or count the corners with your finger. Take your time, there is no rush. I expect real thinking on paper, not just a guess. 3. Type your answer in the box. Write your thinking too, in a short sentence, like "I counted the corners" or "the arrow points to the sky." Then press Check answer. I expect a full little sentence, not just one letter. 4. If your brain feels stuck, press Hint. Read the hint, then try again yourself. Getting stuck is normal — every artist and every programmer gets stuck. I expect you to press Hint and keep trying, not to leave the box empty. 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little cheer! Then go to the next problem and do steps 1 to 4 again. Do this until all 4 problems say right. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. This is your practice round, so your brain remembers it well. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. I expect the same careful thinking here, even though you have seen the problem once. 8. When a slide is finished, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the whole page is finished when all 4 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with problem one, read it twice, and tell me what you think it is asking you.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text:
Hello, artist! Today we take a short break from arrows and shapes. This page is called Stay Safe Online. It teaches three rules that keep you safe when you use a tablet or computer. We do this because ScratchJr and the internet are fun, and safe hands make happy artists. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. Here are all the steps. Step 1: Read every rule slowly. There are three rules on the page. Read one rule, then stop and think about it. Where you see a speaker button, press Listen and let the words be read to you. Listen with quiet ears. I expect you to read or listen to all three rules, not just the first one. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Say each rule in your own words. After each rule, close your mouth for a second, then say it out loud in YOUR words. Not the book's words — your words. Rule one is about checking if something is true. Rule two is about telling a grown-up if something worries you. Rule three is about other people's pictures and work. I expect one short sentence from you for each rule, like "I ask my mum if it is true."

Step 3: Give an example from your own life. For each rule, think of a real thing that could happen to you. Maybe you saw a funny video and you were not sure it was real. Maybe a game asked for your name. Maybe you drew a picture and put your name on it, because it is yours. I expect three little examples, one for each rule. You can say them to me here and I will listen! Step 4: Press I know these rules. This button is at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have read all three rules and said them in your own words. Pressing it tells the page that you are done. I cannot press it for you — the record of your work comes from you. How you know the page is finished: you have read all three rules, you have said each one in your own words with an example, and you have pressed I know these rules at the bottom. Ready? Start with Step 1 now. Read the first rule, and press Listen if there is a speaker. Then tell me what that rule means in your own words. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello, artist! Let's do this page together. I'll be your teacher and walk you through it. What this page is: it asks you to say HOW you think. You read a little question, then you tell me your thinking in your own words. We do this because a good computer helper can explain their steps, not just point. By the end, you will be able to say why your steps work, using our unit words: direction, arrow, step, instructions. What you need: your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. There are 4 prompts on this page. Start with the first one. Read the prompt slowly. Under it you will see key ideas, like direction, arrow and step. Those are the words I want to hear in your answer. Read them out loud once. Step 2.
