Now click in the box and write your explanation. Tell me three little things: what you know, what rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. For example: "I know arrows show direction. The rule is that steps go in order. So the first step must be start." Then press Check your reasoning. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check your reasoning again. I expect your own words — even short ones are perfect. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Ask yourself: did I use the key words? Did I say why? If you missed a key word, go back and add it. Then do the same for prompt 2, prompt 3 and prompt 4. Every explanation should use the key ideas. Step 4. Look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Do the same as before on each slide: write your thinking, press Check your reasoning, then press Show model explanation. To move on, press the arrow on the right. The little dots under the slide show which slide you are on. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you will know you are finished: all 4 explanations are written and checked, each one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with prompt 1 and tell me when it's done. I'm right here! 🌟

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Unit Challenge. This is the last page of Unit 11, "Be an Artist". It is a little quiz about arrows, steps and shapes — all the things you have been learning. We do it so you can show what you know, and so we can see what to practise again. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a comfy seat. You may keep your pencil and paper close by too. Here is what I expect from you: read every question twice, think first, then choose. Take your time — there's no rush. And remember, I really can't give quiz answers — but I promise you can get this. Here are the steps. Step 1. There are 12 questions. Read the first question slowly. Look at all the choices before you pick one. Ask yourself, "which one matches what I learned?" Some questions ask about words like direction, arrow, step or algorithm. Some ask what to do when something goes wrong, like mixing up left and right. Pick the answer that sounds most like our lessons. Then press Next question. Do this for every question, one at a time. Step 2. A little trick for tricky ones: if a question asks about a word, say the word out loud and tell yourself what it means in your own words. A direction is which way something moves. A step is one move, one square. If a question asks about drawing a shape, picture your pencil going right, down, left, up. If you are unsure, choose your best idea and keep going. Guessing your best is fine — never leave one empty. Step 3. At the end you will see your score. You pass with more than half of the questions right. Look at your score and smile — every question you answered taught you something. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4. If your score is not high enough, press Try again. This is not a bad thing! It just means one more practice round. Before you start again, come and tell me which questions felt hard, and we will go over that idea together. Then read each question extra slowly this time. Step 5. When your score is high enough, press Continue. That is you finishing Unit 11! You will know the page is finished when you have answered all 12 questions, seen your score, and pressed Continue. Ready? Go and read question one, then tell me how it goes. 🌟

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello, artist! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Unit Project page. Here is what it is. You will be an artist who draws with directions. You will draw a square window by following arrow steps: right, down, left, up. Then you will look at another list of steps, find the one wrong step, and fix it. We do this because computers only move when we give them good steps, in the right order. By the end, you will be able to make a shape all by yourself, just from a list of directions. Get these ready: a pencil, some paper (squared or dotted paper is best), and colours if you have them. A grown-up can sit near you to help. Here are the three things to do on this page. Step 1. Read the Unit Project box at the top. It tells you what you will make: a square window. Under it there is a list of things a good project has. Read the list slowly, one line at a time. If you cannot read a word, ask your grown-up or ask me. I expect you to tell me one thing from that list in your own words before we move on. Step 2. Now make your project, and tick each thing on the list as you finish it. Do it in small bits, like this. First, plan your steps: write or say the four arrows for a square — right, down, left, up. Second, put your pencil on the top-left dot and follow your steps to draw the square. Check it: a good square has 4 sides and 4 corners, and it is closed with no gaps. Third, look at the mixed-up list of steps on the page and find the one step that is wrong. Fourth, fix that step and draw the square again the right way. Fifth, add one thing to make your window nicer — maybe colour it, or draw curtains. Tick each line on the list only after you really did it. Step 3. When every single thing on the list has a tick, press the button that says My project is finished. Do not press it early. Pressing it is how the page saves your good work, so it must be you who presses it, not me. How will you know the page is done? Every item on the list is ticked, and you have pressed My project is finished. Then you are an artist who can draw with directions! Ready? Start with Step 1. Read the list, then tell me one thing a good project needs. Take your time — there's no rush. 🙂
